en: Having saluted the primordial Candraśekhara, the supreme light who is accompanied by Gaurī, [this work] Citramīmāṃsā composed by the illustrious Appadīkṣita [is begun].
I expand this *Arthacitramīmāṃsā*, which encompasses vast subjects and possesses clear meaning.
Poetry is first of all threefold, distinguished by the categories of *dhvani* (suggestion), *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion), and *citra* (the pictorial).
That in which the suggested meaning surpasses the expressed meaning is *dhvani*.
For example:

The first drops of rain lingered for a moment on her eyelashes, struck against her lower lip, and crushed by falling upon the swell of her breasts; then, slipping down her sides, they reached her navel only after a long time.

Here, by describing the action of the first drops of rain falling upon the body of the Goddess as she performs penance, her state of being established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is manifested through the expression of her condition. Thus, even during the first rain—which is a cause for agitation due to the pleasant ripening [of the skin] from falling upon a body long tormented by heat—her state of absorption remains unshaken. For instance:
"With eyes fixed on the tip of the nose, mouth closed, and perfectly motionless..."
One should meditate upon the God with the mind, having fixed one's gaze straight ahead upon the chest.

Thus they describe the posture appropriate for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). In that context, by the phrase "situated upon the eyelashes," the form of half-closing the eyes with the pupils fixed on the tip of the nose is indicated. This is because if the eyes were opened entirely, the eyelashes would have their tips pointing upward, and if they were closed entirely, the tips would point downward; in either case, it would be impossible for drops of water to rest upon them. Furthermore, since those drops falling from the eyelashes enter the mouth and fall upon the lower lip before trickling away, this indicates that the mouth is not closed.

Furthermore, by describing the falling of those [garments] from the elevated breasts, there is a compression of the chest. For if they remained in a downward position like something sluggish, their falling would not occur because of the constricted shape within the breasts. Even if they somehow fell and reached the three folds, they would move only obliquely across the folds and could not reach the region of the navel; and if the navel were closed, there would be no entry into it.

Furthermore, by describing the sequence of their falling from the eyelashes to the lips and so forth, her immobility is suggested; for if there were movement of the face and other limbs, it would be impossible for them to fall in that specific order from the eyelashes down to the lips, breasts, and so on. Moreover, through these very qualifiers, the world-transcending beauty of the Goddess is revealed.

By the word "stayed" (sthitā), the density of the eyelashes is indicated; by the word "moment" (kṣaṇam), their smoothness; by the description of the water drops striking the lower lip with force weakened by the falling of the lashes, the extreme delicacy of the lip; by the description of those drops becoming powder upon the elevation of the breasts as their force is weakened by the falling of the lashes and the lip, the extreme firmness of those two; by the statement that even when obstructed by the chest, the drops slip over the folds, the distinctness of the folds; and [by the fact that] all the drops [disappear] only at the navel...
Because the description of the entrance suggests that the navel is exceedingly deep, the suggested meaning here excels the expressed meaning.
Or, for example:
"The slope of the breasts has its sandal-paste completely washed away; the lower lip has its redness rubbed off..."
"Your eyes are far from kohl, and this slender body of yours is covered in horripilation.
O false-tongued messenger, you who do not understand the arrival of suffering for your own kin—
have you gone from here to bathe in the pond, and not rather to the presence of that base man?"

In this case, while the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*) remains "you went to the pond to bathe, and not to him," the phrase *adhamapadena* (by the word 'lowly') primarily suggests that you went to him specifically to dally. To explain: "lowliness" (*adhamatva*) means inferiority. And that [inferiority] arises either from birth (*jāti*) or from action (*karman*). In this context, a noble heroine (*uttamanāyikā*) would not speak of inferiority on account of birth; nor would she do so by means of any action other than lowly acts such as sexual union with a messenger (*dūtī*), which result in her own transgression.

Furthermore, everything prior to the enjoyment with the messenger-maid (*dūtī*) has already been endured; thus, it is not fit to be disclosed, for otherwise, the act of sending a messenger herself would be illogical. Moreover, since the "inferior act" (*hīnakarma*)—consisting precisely of the enjoyment with the messenger-maid sent by her own [rival]—can be known through proximate signs, the word "base" (*dhama*), which culminates in that very act, suggests that she went there specifically to sport with him.

Sentences such as "The slope of the breast, from which all sandal-paste has vanished" (*niśśeṣacyutacandanaṃ stanataṭam*) provide assistance there by disclosing the marks of sexual enjoyment. How so? In the phrase "The slope of the breast, from which all sandal-paste has vanished," the qualification "all" (*niśśeṣa*) is employed to preclude the possibility of an alternative explanation—that the sandal-paste was removed by the pulling of the upper garment—in order to establish the literal meaning: "You have gone from here to the pond to bathe."

Next, the mention of the "slopes" (*taṭa*) is intended to exclude the possibility that the falling away of the sandalwood paste occurred during bathing, thereby avoiding the implication of marks from sexual enjoyment. For if it were due to bathing, the falling away of the sandalwood paste would be observed everywhere; however, in your case, it is seen only on the slopes—the upper portions—of your two breasts, which indicates it was caused specifically by an embrace. Similarly, regarding the phrase "the lip with its redness rubbed away," the expression "rubbed away" (*nirmṛṣṭa*) describes the complete removal of the redness, thus precluding the alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*) that the slight fading of the previous color was merely due to the delay in taking betel. Thus, the redness was wiped away entirely.

Furthermore, by excluding the possibility of [the marks] being common to other causes such as bathing, the term "lower lip" (*adhara*) is specifically employed to reveal the signs of sexual enjoyment (*sambhoga*). Since the lower lip alone is seen to have its color rubbed away while the upper lip remains stained with *sarāga* (redness), this must be due to kissing. Regarding the phrase "eyes far devoid of collyrium" (*netre dūramanañjane*), the word "far" (*dūra*) is used to preclude the alternative explanation that the collyrium applied in the morning had merely faded slightly over time; the literal sense of "far" is "excessively. By this, the objection of temporal lapse (*kāla-anyathāsiddhi*) is refuted.

Furthermore, by excluding the possibility of a common bath, the underlying meaning residing in the heart is the revelation of the marks of sexual enjoyment (*sambhoga*), namely that "the edges [of your eyes] are far [from being stained]. In reality, however, through bathing at the [proper] time, the collyrium (*añjana*) would be wiped away entirely; yet in your case, there is this lack of collyrium only at certain edges of the eyes, and this is surely caused by kissing. In the verse, "This body of yours is thrilled and slender," the word "slender" (*tanvī*) at first sight refers to natural thinness, while "thrilled" (*pulakitā*)— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.)

The presentation of the signs of bathing: "Though thrilled with horripilation, she remains slender"—this is the connection established in the heart. For by that [ordinary] bathing, the body becomes thrilled and slightly swollen; yet this [heroine] is not so. Therefore, it is a piercing of the vital point that her thinness and the emergence of horripilation are produced solely by the torment of love.

Thus, when it is suggested by these words—that she has gone to that very place to sport with him through the inferior word (*adhamapada*)—this suggestion is connected as being consistent with the meaning "you have gone to the pond to bathe," which was the literal sense (*vācya*) in the previous state. Furthermore, the address "O deceitful woman" (*mṛṣāvādinī*) also culminates in a meaning that is consistent with the suggested sense. Consequently, since the suggested meaning of this [verse] also surpasses the literal meaning while the literal meaning remains subordinate, this too is an example of *dhvani*.
Where the suggested meaning does not surpass the literal meaning, that is *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).
For example:
"I am going, O Acyuta; can satisfaction ever arise from merely seeing you?
Yet, while we two remain thus in solitude, people will imagine otherwise.

May Hara protect you as he embraced the Gopī, whose body was thrilled with horripilation, she who was languid with the weariness of her futile stay, which had been signaled by the very turn of her address.

In this passage, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is: "O Acyuta (the Imperishable One), I have been waiting for so long with the intention of sporting with you by addressing you thus, yet that [pleasure] has not been obtained. However, since this suggestion serves to establish the literal meaning (*vācya*) expressed in the phrase, "her fatigue was rendered vain, as indicated by the manner of her address," it is subordinate to that literal meaning. Therefore, this is an instance of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).
Or, for example:
"At the end of the first watch, or at midday, or even later..."
"O beloved, will you not come here even when the entire day has passed?"—
with such words, a young woman, her voice choked with tears and shame, prevents her lover from departing for a land reachable only after hundreds of days.

In this case, "the entire day" is the ultimate limit, and the suggested meaning—that "beyond this I am unable to sustain my life"—effects the realization of the expressed meaning, which consists in the prevention of the beloved’s departure. Because it serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to that expressed meaning, it does not surpass it. Therefore, this too is *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).
Furthermore, that which is beautiful even when devoid of suggestion is called *citra* (ornamental poetry).
That is of three kinds: *śabdacitra* (verbal ornament), *arthacitra* (semantic ornament), and *ubhayacitra* (both verbal and semantic ornament). An example of *śabdacitra* is as follows:

"Before him, he beheld a forest of fresh *palāśa* leaves, filled with blossoming lotuses covered in pollen, with tender creepers swaying gently, fragrant with the abundance of flowers. Thus is *arthacitra* (poetry of striking meaning): [The example follows: *“yena dhvastamanobhavena balijitkāyaḥ purā strīkṛto yaścodvṛttabhujaṅgahāravalayogaṅgāṃ ca yo’dhārayat | yasyāhuḥ śaśimacchiro hara iti stutyaṃ ca nāmāmarāḥ pāyāt sa svayamandhakakṣayakarastvāṃ sarvadomādhavaḥ ||”* [Translation: "May that Mādhava—who, having destroyed the mind-born [Kāma], turned the body of the conqueror of Bala into a woman in ancient times; who wears as a necklace and bracelets serpents that have cast off their skins and supports the Gaṅgā; whose head they say bears the moon and whose name the immortals praise as 'Hara'—he who brought about the destruction of Andhaka, protect you at all times! [The commentary continues: Here, the word *sarvada* ("always giving") is applied to both Śiva (*Hara*) and Viṣṇu (*Mādhava*), yet it primarily denotes the latter through the sense of "bestowing everything" (*sarva-dā*). This is *arthacitra*. Furthermore, the word *umādhava* is applied to both Śiva and Viṣṇu, yet it primarily denotes the former through the sense of "the husband of Umā.

This too is *arthacitra*. Moreover, the word *andhakakṣayakara* ("destroyer of the Andhakas") is applied to both Śiva and Viṣṇu, yet it primarily denotes the former through the sense of "the destroyer of the Andhaka demons. This also is *arthacitra*. Thus, this verse is an instance of *arthacitra*. [The example continues: *“rājate rājyalakṣmīste bhuja evātra nānyataḥ | bhujageśvarabhogābha-bhujena bhuvi bhūtaye ||”* [Translation: "O King, the fortune of sovereignty shines here only in your arm, and nowhere else—for the sake of the welfare of the world, by means of your arm which resembles the coils of the Lord of Serpents. [The commentary continues: Here, the word *bhujaga* is applied to both "arm" (*bhuja*) and "serpent" (*bhujaga*). Yet, because the word *bhujageśvara* ("Lord of Serpents") is used, the primary sense is "serpent," and thus it is *arthacitra*. Furthermore, the word *bhoga* is applied to both "enjoyment" (*bhoga*) and "coils" (*bhoga*), yet because the word *bhogābha* ("resembling coils") is used, the primary sense is "coils," and thus it is *arthacitra*. Therefore, this verse is an instance of *arthacitra*. [The example continues: *“sāhityapāthonidhimanthanotthaśrīharṣamiśrāgamitasudhāṃśoḥ | prakāśate prauḍhatamā pratītirnabhastale gūrjarabhāṣayeyam ||”* [Translation: "This most mature understanding, like the nectar produced from churning the ocean of literature, has been obtained from the moon that is the poet Śrīharṣa Miśra; it shines in the sky of the Gūrjara language. [The commentary continues: Here, the word *sudhāṃśu* is applied to both "moon" (*sudhāṃśu*) and "poet" (*sudhāṃśu*, i.e., one who possesses nectar-like speech). Yet, because the word *miśra* is used, the primary sense is "poet," and thus it is *arthacitra*. Furthermore, the word *prauḍhatama* is applied to both "very mature" and "very bold," yet because the
"With its roots severed, the dust, shaken by the wind upon him as he was drenched in blood,
shone like the smoke previously risen from a fire that has been reduced to its embers.
An example of both types of *citra* (verbal and semantic figures) is as follows:
May that Boar grant you prosperity— he who, at the end of the aeon,
bore up the earth while shaking the waters of the ocean,
his auspicious war-drums clearly struck by the explosions of millions of stones tumbling from the peaks of the principal mountains shattered by the blows of his hooves.

Thus, we have already provided a detailed exposition elsewhere regarding these three types [of poetry] and the two varieties of *dhvani* and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*. Since *śabdacitra* (verbal artistry) is generally devoid of aesthetic flavor (*nīrasatva*), poets do not pay it much heed, nor is there much to be investigated therein; therefore, setting aside the portion concerning verbal artistry, an extensive and lucid investigation of *arthacitra* (objective artistry) is now commenced. Regarding this class of artistic figures (*citravarga*) to be considered, the verses of the ancient masters themselves are for the most part transcribed here, along with their definitions and illustrative examples.
Thus ends the section on the commencement of the work in the *Citramīmāṃsā*.
Now, the figure of speech known as Simile (Upamā): This single actress, having reached various painted stages,
delights the minds of connoisseurs by dancing upon the stage of poetry.

The description of similarity, such as "the face is like the moon," is first of all *upamā* (simile). That very same [simile] assumes the nature of various other figures of speech through different modes of expression (*uktibhaṅgī*). For instance: "the face is like the moon; the moon is like the face" is *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile). "The face is like a face" is *ananvaya* (self-comparison). "The moon is like the face" is *pratīpa* (counter-simile). "Having seen the moon, I remember the face" is *smaraṇa* (remembrance). "The face itself is the moon" is *rūpaka* (metaphor). "The heat is cooled by the moon-face" is... [and so forth].

Thus is *pariṇāma* (transformation). "Is this a face, or rather the moon?"—this is *sandeha* (doubt). "The cakora birds, thinking 'it is the moon,' pursue your face"—this is *bhrāntimān* (error). "The cakora birds, thinking 'it is the moon,' and the bees, thinking 'it is a lotus,' take delight in your face"—this is *ullekha* (multiple description). "This is the moon, not the face"—this is *apahnava* (denial). "Surely it is the moon"—this is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). "This is the moon"—this is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). "By the face, the splendor of the moon has been conquered"—this is *tulyayogitā* (equal pairing).

"In the night the moon and your face both rejoice"—this is *dīpaka* (illumination). "I am enamored only of your face; the *cakora* bird is enamored only of the moon"—this is *prativastūpamā* (counter-simile). "The moon in heaven and your face on earth"—this is *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration). "Your face bears the splendor of the moon"—this is *nidarśanā* (poetic indication). "Your spotless face surpasses the moon"—this is *vyatireka* (distinction). "Together with your face, the moon rejoices in the nights"—this is *sahokti* (joint expression).

"‘The face, beautiful with eyes like sprouts and graced by the moonlight of a smile’—this is *samāsokti* (speech of condensed meaning). ‘The face, resembling a lotus, has its attachment fixed upon Hari’—this is *śleṣa* (paronomasia). ‘Before the face, the moon is lusterless’—this is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). Thus, this simile (*upamā*) possesses the manifestations of many such figures of speech.

Just as the entire universe becomes known through the knowledge of Brahman, so too is this [simile] described here in its entirety, along with all its varieties, as being understood through the knowledge of simile."
Regarding this, they state its definition as follows:
"The charming similarity between two objects, both of which are capable of being the standard of comparison and the object compared, is called *upamā* (simile) by those who know poetry."

In the world, the word *iva* is observed to convey a sense of "as if" or "appearing like," as in: "Standing at a distance, Devadatta appears as if [he were someone else]. And how is it that by the phrase "by that which is established in itself" (*svataḥsiddhena*), the possibility of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is excluded? [Consider this example:
"Having abandoned the sky because its fullness was not eternal here, the new Lord of the Kākatīyas shines upon the surface of the earth, delighting the world with his own splendor like the moon."

Thus, in this very example of his own *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is established by its own nature. If it is argued that the moon is here imagined by the poet as having descended to the surface of the earth, then consider: "Poison from the orb of the moon, fire from sandalwood, or harsh speech from this mouth—such is an impossible simile (*asambhāvitopamā*)."

If this were said, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) regarding the "impossible simile" (*asambhāvitopamā*), because although the poison and the fire are established by their own nature, they are here imagined by the poet as originating from the moon and sandalwood respectively. For example: "If two separate streams of the waters of the celestial Gaṅgā were to fall in the sky, then [the chest of] this [hero], dark as a *tamāla* tree and adorned with a string of pearls, might be compared to them."

Thus, there is a total lack of coverage (avyāpti) in the case of a simile where the object of comparison is imagined by the poet. Furthermore, although the term "distinct" (*bhinnena*) was employed to exclude the figure of *anvaya* (self-comparison), it is also inappropriate [in this context]. [Example:
"Of that [mountain] which is the source of endless jewels, snow has not become a destroyer of its beauty..."

For this would result in over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in the following *upapādakopamā* (illustrative simile): "Indeed, a single fault sinks away amidst a multitude of virtues, like the spot on the moon amidst its rays. In that case, the specific faults and virtues—the stain and the rays—are included within the general categories of faults and virtues belonging to the object of comparison (*upameya*); therefore, they lack the quality of being "different from it" (*tadbhinnatva*). Now, suppose one were to define "being different from it" as the state of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) being delimited by a property that delimits the object of comparison (*upameyatāvacchedaka*) and is distinct from it. This too is not tenable.
[Consider the following verse: "Of her whose hand is a wave of water-drops held for the constant distribution of gold, and whose generosity is vast..."
"...speech is like thought, thought is like action, and fame is as stainless as action.

This is because there is no over-extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of the *raśanopamā* (chain simile), since the delimiters of the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna-tāvacchedaka*), such as "thought-ness" (*matitva*), do not lack difference from the delimiter of the subject of comparison (*upameya-tāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, in the case of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison), since both delimiters of the standards of comparison lack that difference [from the subject], the exclusion of that [simile] would be established by the aforementioned qualification alone; thus, the inclusion of the term "ekadā" (at one time) would result in redundancy. [Example:
"By the dust raised by the chariots, which resembled clouds..."

Furthermore, there would be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of "mutual comparison" (*parasparopamā*), which will be illustrated in the section on "comparison of the object of comparison with itself" (*upameyopamā*), as in: "making the sky like the surface of the earth, and the surface of the earth like the sky.

Now, if it is intended that the state of being distinct from that [object of comparison] consists in the upamāna being delimited by a property different from the delimitor of its own status as an object of comparison (*svopameyatāvacchedaka*), this too is not correct.
The thousand-rayed sun received from Tvaṣṭṛ a newly fashioned parasol;
with his crown not far from that silken cloth, he shone as if the Gaṅgā were falling upon his head.
Wandering from door to door, the mendicant thus learns by begging for new things.
"Do not be like me by not giving; by giving, may you become like yourself.

Furthermore, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases of identity-based similes (*abhinnadharmikopamā*), such as those involving a *caitya* (shrine) and so forth, because in those instances, the very property that delimits its own status as the object of comparison (*upameyatāvacchedaka*), such as "being the Supreme Lord," also serves as the delimiter of its status as the standard of comparison (*upamānatāvacchedaka*).

Moreover, the qualification "by way of a common property" (*dharmataḥ*) is also improper for the purpose of excluding *śleṣa* (punning), because in *śleṣa*, it is not merely a similarity of words that is expressed by the word "like" (*iva*), but rather a similarity of qualities (*guṇasāmya*) as well; thus, *śleṣa* is not excluded by that qualification.

[Objection: "But surely, in the former case [the city], there is 'possession of all arts' (*sakalakalatva*), meaning the presence of clamorous noise (*kalakala-śabda-sāhitya*); whereas in the orb of the moon, there is 'completeness of digits' (*kalā-sākalya*). Thus, a single common attribute is not obtained. [Response: Not so. For, by means of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole)—which is rooted in the identification of two distinct things based on their similarity (*śleṣa*) and takes the form of "non-difference where there is difference"—a commonality of attributes is achieved. Indeed, the figure of speech *upamāna* (simile) does not require that the shared attribute be primarily common to both the object of comparison and the subject of comparison.
Consider this example: "This Pāṇḍya king has long necklaces resting upon his shoulders; he is anointed with fragrant sandalwood paste (*haricandana*)."

"In such passages as 'The king shines like the lord of mountains, whose peaks are reddened by the morning sun and which seems to emit a gushing waterfall,' we accept that even things like the *hari-candana* tree, the young woman, the act of abduction, and the waterfall—which are indicated through the relationship of prototype (*bimba*) and reflection (*pratibimba*)—function as common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

If it is objected: "In cases such as *sakalakalam*, if there is equality of qualities (*guṇasāmya*), then it would simply be a simile (*upamā*)," [the reply is: Why should it not be a simile even if there is merely an equality of words? For it is certainly not an established rule that only the equality of qualities and so forth—distinct from the words—is the cause of a simile, while the equality of words is not.

"Just as the moon is so called because of its delighting [coolness], and the sun because of its scorching heat, even so did that king become 'Anvartha' (True to His Name) through his pleasing of the subjects.

In this instance, although there is a similarity of words in the form of names that follow their literal meaning (*anvarthanāmarūpa*), an *upamā* (simile) is observed; however, Maṅkhaka and others maintain that even when a simile is suggested, the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone is the cause for the emergence of that suggestion, not the simile. This is because *śleṣa*, having no scope apart from other figures of speech, is powerful and thus subordinates other figures. Even when a simile appears, it is *śleṣa* itself that serves as the cause for its manifestation.

Furthermore, just as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is shown to subvert *upamā* (simile) by relying merely on the similarity of words (*śabdasāmya*) when a simile presents itself, so too it can be argued that when a simile presents itself based on the mere similarity of qualities obtained through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) founded upon *śleṣa*, [the latter] can likewise subvert it. Therefore, in accordance with that [principle], there is no need for a separate investigation into the similarity of qualities (*guṇasāmya*) in such cases.

As for what Rudraṭa, while attempting to justify the presence of *upamā* in examples such as "sakalakalam," stated: "In 'sphuradurumahimā,' there is neither *upamā* nor *samuccaya*, but rather... [he was mistaken].
"Even here, a commonality consisting of mere sound is possible.

By this, it is stated that there is merely a similarity of words; the intention is that even by relying on such a mere similarity of words, a simile can be established, and not with the intention that a similarity of qualities is impossible even through the determination of non-difference (*abhedādhyavasāya*). This is because, even in the case of *śliṣṭa* (pun-based) adjectives, all [theorists] resort to the identity [of the objects] through the determination of non-difference in other figures of speech. Therefore, by the phrase "on account of its attributes" (*dharmataḥ*), the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) cannot be excluded.

In reality, however, in examples such as "sakalakala," there is only a simile (upamā); thus, the qualification "by its attribute" (dharmataḥ) is redundant. Furthermore, the domain of *śleṣa* (punning) distinct from other figures of speech will be demonstrated in its own section. Moreover, the argument that *śleṣa* sublates other figures because it lacks a distinct domain is also untenable; for the status of being "without scope" (niravakāśatva) is lost merely by the existence of its own domain, without requiring a domain distinct [from others].

The worldly maxim that an ornament must have a distinct subject matter does not apply here; for even though there is no separate subject matter for the gems other than gold, they are established as a distinct type of ornament because they serve as the cause of beauty while being supported by gold. Otherwise, the status of the gold—which has space available—being an ornament through the gems set within it without gaps would be contradicted.

Nor is this the logic accepted by those learned in grammar (*vākyavid*), for [the rule] "one sacrifices with a word" (*pad juhoti*) and so forth remains established merely by having a scope, even when there is no scope such as the *āhavanīya* fire-ritual [which applies to the rule] "one sacrifices in the latter half," just as it does in the case of "one sacrifices with a word. Nor is this the unique logic of this specific treatise [on poetics], because even when there is no scope for hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) and so forth in cases like "simultaneous mention" (*sahokti*), they are treated as distinct figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) precisely because they do not contradict it. Non-contradiction is thus identical here as well.

Therefore, it is incorrect to say that the figure of speech *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is the cause for the emergence of the suggestion of a simile (*upamāpratibhotpattihetu*) here; on the contrary, it is the simile itself that is the cause for the emergence of the suggestion of *śleṣa*. For, in the context of describing a city, the suggestion of another meaning based on the words *sakala* (all) and *asākalya* (incompleteness) is not possible. Furthermore, regarding the statement "the similarity of the subject with another" made for the purpose of excluding *pratīpa*, the use of the word "another" (*anyena*) is improper. This is because the term "another" is redundant when used with the word "different" (*bhinna*). Moreover, if the meaning of "by another" is "by something other than the subject under description," namely, by something non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), then—
"Other demons also fell upon the crores of monkeys, like the dust raised in battle falling into the rivers of their blood.

This definition would suffer from non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of this *samuccitopamā* (cumulative simile), because in that instance, the falling of the dust into the blood is also described as being an integral part of the battle. If, however, the meaning is "by something other than the subject of description (*varṇya*), whether it be itself or not," then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure *pratīpa* (the inverse), which consists of imagining something as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) when it is incapable of even that status due to its excessively superior qualities. For example: [Example omitted per instructions]
"O Hālāhala poison, do not be arrogant, thinking, 'I alone am the teacher of the most dreadful things,' dear child;
for indeed, there are many words of the wicked in this world that are like you.

Here, there is *pratīpa* (the inverse comparison), because the comparison is established with the words of the wicked—which are being described—as being equal to Hālāhala, even though that [poison] cannot tolerate such an extreme degree of defectiveness as a point of comparison.

In this context, the phrase "of the subject of description" (*varṇyasya*) is incorrect; for it would fail to apply (*avyāpti*) to the case of a simile mixed with *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), such as: "The moonlight, soiled by darkness, shines before your fame. In that instance, since it is fame alone that is the subject of description, the moonlight is not the subject of description.

Furthermore, what is the meaning of the statement "the similarity of the subject of description (*varṇya*) must be expressed through another"? Does it mean that the similarity residing in the subject of description must be expressed as having another as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); or that the similarity, in whatever way possible, must be expressed as being defined by both the subject and the non-subject of description; or that the similarity must be expressed as having the subject of description as its locus (*anuyogin*)? In the first case [if it means the former], consider the following: "‘This lotus and the face of her whose eyes are tremulous like those of a startled deer, and who possesses the luster of a necklace of fresh, red rubies—these two are equal’—this thought produces joy in the heart. [In this example, the similarity is expressed with the lotus as the counter-correlate.]

Thus, there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of the "simile based on similarity resting on both" (*ubhayaviśrāntasādṛśyopamā*). In the second [definition], the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) remains even in the case of a well-known *pratīpa* (contrasting simile). Likewise, in the third, since the intended meaning is obtained merely by the phrase "similarity of color," the inclusion of the word "by another" (*anyena*) is redundant. Furthermore, the qualification "at once" (*ekadā*) is also improper for the purpose of excluding *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile); for even if it excludes over-extension in cases like "the sky is like the water, the water is like the sky"—where the reciprocal simile proceeds by alternation—it fails to exclude it in such cases as: "By that beauty of his, which blossomed simultaneously, the two immediately attained mutual equality. [The *upameyopamā* occurs here despite the simultaneous occurrence.]
"Your eye, with its pupil both quivering and soft, and the lotus, with its bee moving within"—
since this [definition] applies simultaneously to both, the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is not avoided.
Moreover, in this way:
"A woman of shapely hips is like moonlight, a delight to the eyes; she is like a goddess, a cause of intoxication; she is like sovereign power, attracting all the world."

Thus, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the definition in the case of *mālopamā* (garland simile), where the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is distinct [in each instance], because in that case, the similarity is established multiple times. Nor should it be argued that *mālopamā* is merely a combination of many individual similes (*bahūpamā*), and that therefore the definition exists for each of those [individual similes] separately. For if that were so, the same would apply to *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile), which is likewise merely a combination of similes and counter-similes (*upamāpratīpa*). Furthermore, the definition would fail to cover the *parasparopamā* (mutual simile) illustrated in the section on *upameyopamā* with the verse beginning "By the dust raised by the chariots" (*rajobhiḥ syandanoddhūtaiḥ*). Moreover, the claim that the word "expressed" (*vācya*) must be included in the definition in order to exclude instances of suggested simile (*vyaṅgyopamā*) is also incorrect.

"In this case of *tattvākhyānopamā* (simile of stating the true nature), as described by the verse: 'This is not a face; these two are not bees; these are the eyes,' because the similarity is so clearly manifest, that [definition] would result in the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*), since the similarity (*sāmya*) is not explicitly stated."

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as: "Your face, with its tremulous eyes and the radiance of visible teeth, shines like a lotus with hovering bees and discernible filaments," where the simile of the qualified (*viśiṣṭopamā*) is implied by the similes of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇopamā*). Moreover, there would be the consequence of non-pervasion in the case of a simile where the word expressing the comparison is elided (*vācakaluptopamā*), such as "The woman is dark" (*śastrī śyāmā*), and in the case of a simile containing a word that indicates similarity, such as "A face, the friend of the moon" (*candrasuhṛn mukham*).

Furthermore, in the phrase "is to be expressed" (*vācya*), is "being expressible" (*vācyatā*) stated as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), or as something to be restated (*anuvādya*)? In the first case, [one might cite]:
"Leading a vast army coming from the eastern ocean, he shone like Bhagīratha leading the Gaṅgā fallen from the matted locks of Śiva."
In such cases as this, the definition would indeed apply:
"He first went toward the East, equal to Prācīnabarhis,
as if threatening with his banners shaken by the wind, which were unfurled."

In such cases [as the first example], it would not apply. In the second case, where in the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) there is a mention (*anuvādyatā*) for the purpose of negating similarity—as in "The moon is not equal to this spotless face"—this definition would also apply there. Nor can it be specified that the subject must be something other than the counter-positive of the negation (*niṣedhāpratiyogitva*).
For instance, consider: "Though having only his sword as a companion, he overcomes vast hosts of enemies;
this man of great luster is by no means full of pride like other base people."

Thus, even with this exclusion, there remains the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Nor can it be argued that the definition must be qualified by the condition "not being included within the category of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the negation.
[For example: "O bee, why do you wander aimlessly here and there in the forest?
Though you roam everywhere, you shall never find anyone equal to Mālatī."

Thus, there is a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of the "omission of the standard of comparison" (upamānaluptā), because when the attainment of similarity is negated, the commonality itself is included within the category of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin). Therefore, the definition stated by Vidyānātha is also untenable.
As for that definition stated in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*: "That which,

in accordance with established convention, is the frequent conjunction of common attributes between two things capable of being compared to one another— that is considered here to be simile (*upamā*)."

Thus it is said. That [type of simile] also consists in the description of mutual similarity between qualities, actions, and so forth—as in: "The pollen of the fruits of the *elā* plants, crushed by horses and flying upward, becomes equal in scent to the temples of intoxicated elephants."
This [definition] is under-extended (*avyāpta*) in the case of such similes as:

"The orb of the moon, resembling the impression left by the pressing of the high breasts of a pregnant Hunnish maiden— broadened and bent by the friction of her lover— reveals this first footstep of Viṣṇu, tawny like a mature lotus stalk, with its fingertips."

In cases such as "the orange fruit vying with the chin of a freshly shaven Hun," which lacks a well-known object of comparison, and in the case of a "fancied simile" (*kalpitopamā*), [the definition] is over-narrow (*avyāpta*).

Furthermore, that which was stated by the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*: "Simile (*upamā*) exists when there is a similarity between the object of comparison and the subject of comparison, characterized by an equality of difference and non-difference."

In the case of similarity (*sādharmya*), there are three modes of presentation: predominance of difference, as in *dīpaka*, *tulyayogitā*, *dṛṣṭānta*, *prativastūpamā*, *sahokti*, *vyatireka*, and so forth; predominance of non-difference, as in *rūpaka*, *pariṇāma*, *bhrāntimat*, *ullekha*, and so forth; and the equality of both, as in this present simile (*upamā*).

"In this case, since there is a distinction between the standard of comparison (upamāna) and the object of comparison (upameya) by way of their unique characteristics, yet non-distinction by way of a common attribute, there is indeed equality between the two"—this [definition] is also clearly flawed due to over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison). Therefore, its definition is difficult to state. To this, it is replied: "If the operation known as the 'standard of comparison' is intended [to be expressed] until the completion of the action, then that is the poetic figure of *upamā*."

The operation of comparison (*upamāna-vyāpāra*) is the operation that brings about the act of comparison (*upamiti-kriyā*), namely, the description of similarity. The meaning is that if this [operation] is intended to extend as far as the completion of the act of comparison, then it constitutes the figure of speech *upamā*. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure of contrast (*vyatireka*). For although there is a description of similarity in such instances as "The moon is not equal to your spotless face," because the similarity itself is negated; and in such instances as "Nor like other base people," because the qualities that serve as the basis for that similarity are negated, the act of comparison is not completed. Nor is there over-extension to the figure of non-comparison (*ananvaya*).

Even in that case, since one's own similarity to itself serves merely as a gateway for the exclusion of other similar things—just as in the case of non-factual explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as the weeping of Rudra or the cutting out of the omentum (*vapā*), which function as censure or praise—the act of comparison (*upamiti*) is not actually accomplished. Otherwise, that very thing would be its own fruit, as Bhāmaha and others state: "Where there is the relation of object of comparison and subject of comparison between the same thing by means of itself, they call that 'non-comparison' (*ananvaya*) because of the intended expression of non-similarity."

For this very reason, the authors of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* and others maintain that even when described, the similarity of a thing to itself does not cohere; thus they derive the term *ananvaya* (non-coherence) from the fact that there is no connection [of the object] with itself. Consequently, just as water becomes entirely free of turbidity when the application of *kataka* powder causes the suspension of impurities and the powder itself subsequently dissolves, so too in instances such as "Rāma is like Rāvaṇa," when the description of similarity to oneself effects the exclusion of all other similar things, the comparison (*upamā*)—in reality even with respect to oneself—is thereby negated.

Since the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa is impossible [to conceive], it is "incomparable" (*anupama*); in this very case, the poet’s intention lies precisely in the non-actualization of the act of comparison. Thus, there is no room for the suspicion of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure *ananvaya*, because the act of comparison is not brought to fruition. The same applies to *pratīpa* (the counter-comparison) where the comparison is not actualized, as in:
"Listen, O lotus-eyed one, to this censure on earth:
the moon is compared to your face by the vulgar!"* *The example provided is from the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.*
In such cases as this, there is no suspicion of over-extension (ativyāpti), because of the absence of the actual accomplishment of the act of comparison (*upamiti*). For example:
"O blessed lady, why do you bear this unbearable pride with your pair of eyes?
Indeed, such blue lotuses exist in every direction within the lakes."

Thus, both *pratīpa* (the inverse comparison) and *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) must certainly be included; therefore, the fact that the definition does not encompass them is not a defect. For instance, the *pratīpa* cited as an example is merely a specific variety of *upamā*. This is because, just as the description of similarity when it concerns the subject (*prakṛta*) constitutes *upamā*, it cannot constitute a separate figure of speech even when it concerns the non-subject (*aprakṛta*). This is on the same grounds as [the figures of] *smṛti* (remembrance), *rūpaka* (poetic identification), *sandeha* (doubt), *bhrāntimān* (error), *anekadhāgrahaṇa* (multiple apprehension), *apahnuti* (concealment), *sambhāvanā* (poetic fancy), *asamālaṅkāra* (the unequal), *abhavadvastusambandha* (connection with a non-existent thing), *nirdiṣṭa* (directed), and *samarthana* (justification). These all fall under *upamā* despite their different forms.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate that for those [figures] as well, they constitute figures such as *smaraṇa* (recollection), *sasandeha* (doubtful), *bhrāntimad* (error), *ullekha* (multiple description), *apahnuti* (concealment), *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), *nidarśanā* (illustration), and *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) only when they have the contextual subject (*prakṛta*) as their object, whereas they would constitute different figures altogether when they have a non-contextual subject (*aprakṛta*) as their object. Furthermore, it will be shown in various places that recollection and the other figures function as ornaments even when they have non-contextual subjects, just as they do when they have contextual subjects.

Furthermore, there is no such restrictive rule regarding simile that it must necessarily consist of the description of a similarity between the subject (prakṛta) and the non-subject (aprakṛta). This is because, in the examples of "simile by conjunction" (*samuccayopamā*) and others, the status of being a simile is accepted even when the description of similarity occurs only between two subjects or only between two non-subjects. Similarly, it is logical that the description of a similarity between a subject and a non-subject is also simply a simile. Consequently, even the "mutual simile" (*upameyopamā*), which involves a reciprocal comparison between a subject and a non-subject, does not attain the status of a distinct figure of speech separate from the aforementioned mutual simile.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasanga*) that even the *parasparopamā* (mutual simile), which will be illustrated in that same section, would have to be considered a distinct figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*). Furthermore, it would follow that figures such as *anyonyabhrānti* (mutual error) and others would also become distinct figures of speech. Nor should it be argued that because the description of similarity and its separate treatment are identical in the cases of *ananvaya*, *pratīpa*, and *upameyopamā*, it is improper to claim that *ananvaya* is not a form of *upamā* while the other two are.

Because the disparity is evident: on the one hand, where the process of comparison (*upamiti*) is accomplished, there exists the ground for the application of the word "comparison" (*upamā*); and on the other hand, where that process is not accomplished, there is merely a semblance of it. With this very distinction in mind, in the definitions of *tulyayogitā*, *pratīyamānopamā*, and so forth, an effort was made solely to exclude non-connection (*ananvaya*), and not to exclude *anupameyopamā* and the like.

Although figures such as *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) are included within the category of *upamā*, their separate enumeration is not contradictory because they possess specific varieties of charm produced by the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) meaning and so forth, just like *rūpaka* (metaphor) and *pariṇāma* (transformation). In verses such as "If both [streams] were to flow separately in the sky," the absence of a formal definition (*lakṣaṇābhāva*) is not a fault. For if such two streams were to exist, then a comparison could be made; however, they are not possible. Therefore, since nothing can be compared to them, the *upamiti* (the act of comparing)—which is synonymous with *upamā*—is not accomplished. Thus, there is no comparison at all.

Nevertheless, if one were to accept [the presence of] *upamā* (simile) there, it would result in the word *upamā* being treated as a mere technical term (*pāribhāṣika*) in that context; rather, the figure of speech there is a specific variety of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). For this very reason, in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, after enumerating the types of *atiśayokti* with the words, "The attribution of otherness to the subject at hand, and the conceptualization [of identity] upon the statement of 'if' (*yadyartha*)," the conceptualization upon the statement of 'if' is illustrated by the example: "If the body of the nectar-rayed moon were spotless during the full moon (*rākā*), then her face would suffer defeat in comparison."
If there were a flower set upon a fresh sprout, or a pearl resting on bright coral,
then it might imitate her radiant smile as its luster spreads across her copper-hued lips.

This, then, is an example of what is termed "produced simile" (*utpādyopamā*), which is based on a standard of comparison imagined by the poet. In that case, since the definition [of simile] exists precisely because the production of the act of comparison is accomplished through the imagined standard of comparison—which is rendered plausible—there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Nor does this lead to a lack of pervasion in the case of an "improbable simile" (*asambhāvitopamā*) such as "poison like the orb of the moon," for although the act of comparison is accomplished there by means of an improbable standard of comparison, the production of the act of comparison still exists in accordance with the poet's intention (*vivakṣā*), since that very intention is what the poet has intended to express.

For the definition of simile (*upamā*) is not stated as "the accomplishment of the act of comparison based on the actual existence of the object of comparison," but rather as that which is based on the poet’s intention (*vivakṣā*). For this very reason, the qualification "intended" (*vivakṣita*) in the verse is most meaningful. Otherwise, the definition would not apply even in cases such as "The moon is like the face," because since the excellence of luster residing in the moon does not actually exist in the face, there would be no other way [to establish the simile] than by following the poet’s intention.

Nor should it be argued that even in the case of *ananvaya* (non-comparison), the accomplishment of the act of comparison of a thing with itself is possible through the poet’s intention; for when the poet’s intent is to manifest absolute incomparability, such an intention cannot arise.

In such instances as "O bee, why do you wander in vain? and so forth, although the result is the negation of similarity with respect to those objects currently perceived—by means of stating the non-perception of the locus of similarity—there is nonetheless the accomplishment of the act of comparison (*upamiti*) because the existence of similarity in the unperceived [object] is admitted; thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). For this very reason, since the object of comparison is not specifically mentioned, it is a case of the elision of the standard of comparison (*upamānaluptā*). Likewise:
"If the similarity being described by the poet does not exist in its own nature, yet it culminates without resorting to a negation, that is *upamā*."
This definition should also be kept in mind:
*Upamā* (simile) is the description of similarity that brings about the accomplishment of the act of comparison;
or, *Upamā* is the description of similarity which does not terminate in its own negation.

Thus, this twofold definition of the general nature of simile (*upamā*) is precisely what constitutes the definition of the figure of speech *alaṅkāra*, when qualified by the absence of defects and the absence of being a subordinate suggestion (*avyaṅgya*). In cases such as "qualified simile" (*viśiṣṭopamā*) and others, because the similes consisting of the qualifiers and so forth serve as the means for establishing the qualified simile and other figures that constitute the expressed meaning (*vācya*), they possess only the status of "subordinate suggested meaning" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*)—namely, being a "suggestive element that serves to establish the expressed meaning" (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*)—and thus are not considered *alaṅkāras*. Therefore, there is no fault of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in that regard. In examples such as "This is not a lotus, but rather a face," there is no figure of speech of simile.

However, because its power is implied by the negation, both "error" (*bhrāntimān*) and the "simile" (*upamā*) that establishes it are suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*). Nevertheless, since Daṇḍin includes even "error" and the like within the category of simile based merely on their foundation in similarity (*sādharmyamūlatva*), he employs such a designation as "simile of factual description" (*tattvākhyānopamā*); thus, there is no fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) even in that case. This is the general direction [of the argument].

That simile (*upamā*) is of two kinds: complete (*pūrṇā*) and elliptical (*luptā*). It is complete when all four—the object of comparison (*upamāna*), the object compared (*upameya*), the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*), and the word expressing the comparison (*upamāvācaka*)—are employed. It is elliptical when one, two, or three of these are omitted.

In the *pūrṇā* (complete) [type of simile], there is sometimes the indication of the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) by way of its recurrence (*anugāmitva*); sometimes by way of the relation between the thing and its counterpart (*vastuprativastubhāva*); sometimes by way of the relation between the original and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*); sometimes through paronomasia (*śleṣa*); sometimes through metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*); sometimes by relying on a different compound; and sometimes through the mixing of these as appropriate. However, in the *luptā* (elliptical) type, such divisions do not exist, because in that case the common property is necessarily recurring. Rather, its divisions will be stated according to another classification. Among those, an example of the recurrence of the property in the *pūrṇā* is as follows:

"I salute Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the world, who are joined together like word and meaning for the sake of the comprehension of word and meaning. It is well known that there is an eternal relationship between word and meaning, as expressed in the principle: "The relationship of a word with its meaning is innate. Furthermore, it is extremely well known that there is no separation between these two—Umā and Maheśvara—any more than there is between the moon and its light. Thus, in this case, the common attribute consisting of their state of eternal connection is indicated by way of a pervasive correspondence (*anugāmitā*).

Although the description of Umā and Maheśvara as being eternally connected like word and meaning suggests their possession of unsurpassed mutual love, their great majesty, and so forth, nevertheless, this does not constitute the designation of *dhvani* (suggested sense) or *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion). Indeed, in this case, the perception of beauty does not arise solely from the appearance of contact with the suggested sense; rather, it arises also from the appearance of the variety of the expressed meaning (*vācya*). Thus, in most instances, various figures of speech are illustrated while disregarding the suggested sense—such as the *rasa* and other elements that may occur there—as well as other distinct figures of speech.

The "object-to-counter-object" relation (*vastuprativastubhāva*) consists in the twofold mention of one and the same property due to the difference in its correlates. However, this [relation] does not occur in its pure form; rather, it is everywhere intermingled with the "image-and-reflection" relation (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), whether by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a qualificand (*viśeṣya*). In reality, the "image-and-reflection" relation consists in the twofold mention of two properties that are distinct, yet which are determined as non-different due to their mutual similarity. In that regard, the status of being a qualifier for the object-to-counter-object relation is as follows:

"As she departed, repeatedly turning her neck and bearing that face which resembled a lotus with its stalk bent back—the side-long glance of that long-lashed-eyed woman, smeared as it were with both nectar and poison, has been deeply embedded in my heart.

Here, between the neck (*kandara*) and the stalk (*vṛnta*), which are indicated through the relationship of the original and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), a single attribute is specified by the two words *valita* (turned) and *āvṛtta* (bent back) as a qualifier. An example of [the same attribute] as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*) is as follows:

"She, the virtuous woman, was seized by him with force, trembling with fear, like a creeper shaken by the wind by that exceedingly restless monkey. Here, between "fear" (*sādhvasa*) and "wind" (*vāta*), which stand in the relation of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), the single attribute of "trembling" (*kampita*) and "shaken" (*adhūta*) is indicated as the common predicate. An example of a pure *bimba-pratibimba* relation is: "This Pāṇḍya, with a long necklace resting upon his shoulder," and so forth. Here, the lion and the moon, as well as the twilight glow and the pearl necklace, are indicated through the relation of the original image and its reflection.
An example of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows:
"O King Narasiṃha, every single one of your enemies,
fallen from their own positions, possesses a likeness to the ocean (pārāvāra)."
An example of figurative usage (*upacāra*) is as follows:
"Then, as the sun with its rising rays ascended from the golden mountain,
the people drank him in with their eyes and faces in wonder, as if with lotuses."
In this instance, "blooming" (vikāsa), which is a property of flowers, is metaphorically attributed to the eyes, which are the objects of comparison.
An example based on a specific type of compound (samāsa) is as follows:
"By that maiden, whose face was like the moon, her eyes were made to bloom like water-lilies."

"With a mind as clear as water, he became auspicious, like the world being created anew by autumn. Here, the qualifying phrase "with a face-moon that has waxed" functions through a shift in compound structure with respect to both the Goddess and autumn. Regarding the mixing [of figures], the mixture of "pervasive presence" (*anugāmitva*) and the "relation of image and reflection" (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) is as follows:
"By means of his royal qualities, which were both formidable and lovely, he became [the source of] sustenance for his dependents..."
"Unassailable yet approachable, like the ocean with its aquatic jewels.

Here, the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*)—namely, being unassailable and approachable—is established by depending on the relationship between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) between the qualities of the king and the aquatic jewels.
An example of the mixture of *anugāmitva* (pervasive recurrence) and *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows:
"O child, now that your brother has gone to his death, our great lunar dynasty will for a long time lack splendor due to the absence of progeny,
like the ocean deprived of the churning of Mount Mandara.

Here, the quality of being "devoid of splendor" (śobhārahitatva), which gains its existence by depending on the pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *santāna*, serves as the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*).
An example of the blending of *anugāmitva* (pervasive presence) and *upacāra* (metaphorical transference) is as follows:
"Beholding the army of the Kuru king, which was surmounted by a banner with a blazing weapon,
[the moon] embraced it with trembling— like a beloved woman— with sweat born of fear."

In this instance, with respect to the quality of being "following" (*anugāmin*) due to its trembling nature, the state of being a "wanderer" (*cārin*) attained by the act of embracing is metaphorically attributed to fear.
An example of the mixture of "being following" and the recourse to a different type of compound is as follows:
"With hair disheveled by the wings of hawks, their garments drenched in blood like thick evening clouds..."
"The quarters of the sky became like women in their menses, unfit for being looked upon.

Here, by resorting to different types of compounds for the two qualifiers "dusty with the wings of hawks" and so forth, their commonality is established; thus, the shared attribute "unfit for being looked upon" nourishes an excellence of beauty.
An example of the mixture of the relations of *vastu-prativastu-bhāva* (correspondence) and *bimba-pratibimba-bhāva* (reflection and reflected image) is as follows:
"By signs, those lakes, whose transformations were concealed, became as if serene, like waters hiding crocodiles;
having taken leave of the King of Vidarbha and returned his honors under the guise of gifts, they departed.

Here, between "concealed" (*saṃvṛta*) and "hidden" (*gūḍha*), which have entered into the relationship of *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and reflection) regarding the "wrath" and "crocodile," a single attribute is expressed by both words; thus, there is a *vastu-prativastu-bhāva* (correspondence of things) intermingled with *bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*. Furthermore, there is a *bimba-bhāva* (original image status) between the "signs of satisfaction" and "serenity."

An example of the blending of the states of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and *bimbapratibimba-bhāva* (the relation between the original image and its reflection) is as follows: "The king's daughters, rejoicing at the destruction of Pārtha and harboring feigned anger, shed tears,
like lakes whose waters are heated by the sun on the outside but possess cool water within."

In this instance, regarding the word *bāṣpa* ("tears"), beauty arises from observing the relationship of "original image" (*bimba*) and "reflected image" (*pratibimba*) among the adjectives qualifying both the king’s son and the lake.
An example of the mixture of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) and the relationship of original image and reflected image is as follows:
"She, it is said, was consoled by her husband—that fierce woman—after he had promised her two boons."
"The earth, sprinkled by Indra, vomited [the serpents] like two snakes submerged in a hole.

Here, in the phrase "sprinkled by Indra," the act of vomiting by both the simile (the upamāna) and the object of comparison (the upameya)—referring to the two groups of serpents—is figurative (*upacarita*), because the primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) is impossible for both, and because that primary meaning would be vulgar (*grāmyatva*). As they say:
"Terms such as *niṣṭhyūta*, *udgīrṇa*, and *vānta* depend upon figurative function (*gauṇavṛtti*)."
"But this [figure], though exceedingly beautiful, falls into the category of the vulgar.
Thus, other mixtures of two [figures] may also be understood.

An example of the mixture of *anugāmitva* (pervasive presence), *bimbapratibimbabhāva* (the relation of original and reflection), and the recourse to *samāsa-bheda* (differentiation through compounding) is as follows:

"She, whose navel was as beautiful as a whirlpool, passed by that king—who was destined to become another's wife—just as a river flowing toward the ocean passes by a mountain encountered on its course.

Here, the word *vyatyagāt* ("passed by") is the common attribute (*anugāmidharma*). Between the two phrases "destined to become another's wife" (*anyavadhūrbhavitrī*) and "flowing toward the ocean" (*sāgaragāminī*), there is the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*). In the phrase "whose navel was as beautiful as a whirlpool" (*āvartamanojñanābhiḥ*), there is the employment of a specific type of compound (*samāsabheda*). Thus, these elements are combined.

An example of the blending of *anugāmitva* (pervasion), *śleṣa* (paronomasia), and *upacāra* (metaphorical attribution) is as follows: "Here has arrived the season of spring, like Hanumān— its lovely filaments kissed by the breeze, its leader the bright orb of the moon, and it being gazed upon with longing eyes by women separated from their lovers."

In the verse beginning with "atrāturadṛṣṭivīkṣita," there is *anugāmitā* (pervasive correspondence); in the word "rāmādi," there is *śleṣa* (paronomasia); and in the word "cambita" when referring to the spring season (*vasanta*), there is *upacāra* (metaphorical transfer)—thus, there is a combination of these. Other varieties of such combinations should likewise be discerned by oneself. Regarding the examples of the *bimba-pratibimba* (original and reflection) relationship, there is a certain distinction: in some cases, the state of being original and reflection arises between two things whose similarity is either well-known or perceived through the similarity [of other attributes].

For example: "This Pāṇḍya king has a long necklace resting upon his shoulders," and so forth. In some cases, due to the lack of established similarity, there occurs a relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba*) between two things that have assumed a common attribute through some manner or other; for instance: "By her, whose face possessed the radiance of the full moon... and so forth. Here, indeed, although the autumn season and the heroine possess a similarity that is not inherently well-known, they are treated as a prototype and its reflection precisely because they have assumed a common attribute through the employment of a specific compound, such as *vivṛddhānana* ("expanded face").
In any case, without the perception of some commonality (*sādharmya*), the relationship between the original image and its reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*) is simply not possible.
Now, consider this: "Just as you are possessed of virtues in the world, so too is your enemy devoid of them."

"Thus, this [type of] simile is known as the 'Inverse Simile' (viparītopamā). How, then, is the establishment of such an Inverse Simile possible? For in that case, there is no perception of similarity (*sādharmya*) based on an attribute that is either explicitly mentioned (*śrūyamāṇa*)—such as "possessing qualities" (*saguṇatva*) and "being devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇatva*)—or even one that is merely implied (*pratīyamāna*). This is not a fault; for even there, the perception of similarity between those two occurs through an implied attribute such as "absolute" (*ātyantika*) or "inherent" (*svābhāvika*). Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the similarity expressed by the word *yathā* would be entirely without a basis. Thus, the full (*pūrṇā*) variety has been illustrated.

The elided [simile] (*luptopamā*) is of eight kinds: elision of the expressive word (*vācaka*), elision of the quality (*dharma*), elision of the object of comparison (*upamāna*), elision of both the expressive word and the object of comparison, elision of both the quality and the object of comparison, elision of both the quality and the expressive word, elision of both the expressive word and the subject of comparison (*upameya*), and elision of both the quality, the object of comparison, and the expressive word. The examples in their respective order are as follows:

"Know me, Kumbhodara by name, equal to Nikumbha, to be the servant of the Eight-formed One (Śiva), whose feet have favored you by placing themselves upon the back of the bull, white as Mount Kailāsa, as he desires to mount it."

In this context, in the phrase *kailāsagauram*, there is the elision of the denotative term (*vācakalopa*). In the phrase *nikumbhatulyam*, there is the elision of the attribute (*dharmalopa*). The elision of the denotative term occurs everywhere as mandated by the rules governing compound formation (*samāsavidhārakaśāstra*). However, the elision of the attribute is optional (*vaicchika*), since it is possible to express "equal to Nikumbha" by specifying the grounds of comparison, such as power (*prabhāva*) and so forth. As it is said: *Yaccorāṇāmasya ca samāgamo yacca tairvadhob'sya kṛtaḥ |* *Upatanaṃ etadakasmāt āsīdbata! kākatālīyam ||* "That the thieves encountered him, and that they killed him—this sudden occurrence was, alas, truly 'crow-and-palm' (fortuitous)."

In this context, within the scope of the compound formation (*vṛtti*), the words *kāka* (crow) and *tāla* (palmyra tree) function as the actions inherent in the crow and the palmyra tree respectively. Thus, by the rule "after a compound, [the suffix *cha* is added] when that [comparison] is the object" (*samāsācca tadviṣayāt*), which serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) for the sense of "like" (*iva*), there is a compound formed according to the rule *sup supā*. In both cases, the objects of comparison are, respectively, Devadatta’s arrival and the sudden attack of the bandits. Consequently, the result is that the meeting of Devadatta and the bandits is similar to the occurrence of the crow and the palmyra tree.

Then, in the sense of "like the crow and the palm fruit," the suffix *cha* (forming *-īya*) is applied according to the rule *samāsācca tadviṣayāt* [Pāṇini 5.3.106], which pertains to the second sense of the particle *iva*. Thus, the meaning is that just as the death of a crow occurs by means of a falling palm fruit, so too the death of the one [attacked] occurs by means of the bandits who have suddenly descended. As the venerable Bhāṣyakāra said: "In that case, there are two senses of *iva*: 'crow-going-like' and 'palm-falling-like' is *kākatālam*; 'like *kākatālam*' is *kākatālīyam*.
And this has been explained by Kaiyaṭa:

"In this context, the arrival of the crow is the simile for Devadatta’s arrival, and the falling of the palm fruit is the simile for the attack of the bandits. However, the killing of the crow by the palm fruit is the simile for the killing of Devadatta. The common property here is the occurrence of something unexpected. Thus the author of the *Vṛtti* says: "By that, what is called 'crow-and-palm-fruit-like' (*kākatālīya*) refers to a marvelous occurrence that has happened unexpectedly."

Furthermore, in this instance, because the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—consisting of the crow’s arrival, the palm fruit’s falling, and their meeting, as well as the crow’s being killed by the falling fruit—is not explicitly stated, there is an elision of the standard of comparison in the *pratyayārthopamā* (simile based on the meaning of a suffix). In the *samāsārthopamā* (simile based on the meaning of a compound), there is an elision of both the expressive word (*vācaka*) and the standard of comparison. In the very same context, if the third quarter were read as "kim iva brūmo vayam idam" ("What indeed can we say of this?"), then in the *pratyayārthopamā*, there would be an elision of the attribute (*dharma*) and the standard of comparison; and in the *samāsārthopamā*, there would be an elision of the attribute, the standard of comparison, and the expressive word. Here, the mere elision of the attribute is optional. [As in:

However, in the case of the "triple elision" (*trilopa*), the elision of the common property may also occur optionally, as in the second reading of the second quarter of the verse beginning *yac cotpāṇām asya ca*, where the simile functions within a compound. However, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśikā* and others have shown that the complete [upamā] is of six kinds, while the defective (*luptā*) is of nineteen varieties according to some—based on internal subdivisions such as the omission of the attribute (*dharmaluptā*)—and of twenty varieties according to others. In this regard, the following is the distribution: first, the complete [upamā] is twofold, being either expressed by words (*śrautī*) or implied by meaning (*ārthī*). That which possesses words such as *yathā*, *iva*, and so forth, which denote similarity alone, is the *śrautī*. That which possesses words such as *tulya*, *sadṛśa*, *asaṅkāśa*, and so forth—which extend to the substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by similarity—is the *ārthī*.

Thus, the *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile) is of six kinds—occurring in a sentence (*vākya*), a compound (*samāsa*), and a secondary derivative (*taddhita*)—each being twofold. The *dharmaluptā* (omitted attribute) is also divided in the same manner as the *pūrṇā*, yet it is of five kinds because the *śrautī* (expressed by particles) form is not possible in a *taddhita*. The *vācakaluptā* (omitted word for "like") is of seven kinds: in the *karmakarman* and *ṇamul* suffixes; in the *kyac* and *kyap* suffixes denoting object and location respectively; in the *kyaṅ* suffix; in the *ṇini* suffix; and in a compound. The *upamānaluptā* (omitted standard of comparison) is of two kinds, occurring in a sentence and a compound. The *dharmavācakaluptā* (omitted attribute and word for "like") is of two kinds, occurring in the *kvip* suffix and in a compound.

The *upamāna-luptā* (omission of the standard of comparison) is of two kinds: that which omits the attribute (*dharma*) and that which omits both the word expressing the attribute and the standard of comparison. The *upamā-luptā* (omission of the simile itself) is of one kind, occurring only in the *kyac* suffix. The *dharmavācakopamāna-luptā* (omission of the attribute, the word expressing it, and the standard of comparison) occurs only in a compound (*samāsa*). As they say:

"It is twofold—complete (*pūrṇā*) and omitted (*luptā*)—and each of these is further divided into the verbal (*śrautī*) and the conceptual (*ārthī*). These two types [of the complete] occur in sentences (*vākya*), compounds (*samāsa*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*)."

Likewise, when the suffix *ṇini* is used and in compounds, it is proclaimed to be of seven kinds;
