Here, all five types of *dharmaluptopamā* (simile with the common attribute omitted) are demonstrated. Among them, "mūrtiḥ sthānavasudheva" (his form is like the earth of the nine regions) is an instance occurring in a sentence (*vākyagā*). "Bhasabhinmaṇīva kaṇṭhaprabhā" (the luster of his neck is like a jewel set in gold) is an instance occurring in a compound (*samāsagā*) and is *śrautī* (based on direct assertion). In both cases, if the verb "shines" (*bhāti*) were employed, that very [verb] would be the common attribute (*sādhāraṇo dharmaḥ*), and thus it would not be *dharmaluptā*; therefore, it is not employed.

However, a *śrauti* (direct) application of the suffix *vat* derived from a word ending in the genitive or locative case in the sense of "like" (*ivārtha*) is not possible when [the base] is *dharma*, because there is no ease of syntactic connection for *dharma* as the point of reference (*upādāna*). Nor should it be said that a *taddhita* suffix prescribed in the sense of "like" under the governing rule "in the sense of 'like' (*iva*), when denoting a representation (*pratikṛti*)" lacks expectancy without the mention of *dharma*; for we observe such usage as "intellect sharp as the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass" (*kuśāgrīyā buddhiḥ*), "curd like a mountain" (*śaileyaṃ dadhi*), and "a face like the *puṇjarīka* flower" (*pauṇjarīkaṃ mukham*).

Therefore, in that case, the *śrauti* [metaphor] with the *dharma* elided can be illustrated by means of a *taddhita* suffix; for the suffixes prescribed under the governing rule "in the sense of 'like' (*iva*) when denoting a representation" (*ive pratikṛtau*) are ordained only in the sense of similarity (*tulyārtha*). Otherwise, since those suffixes would not extend to the substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by similarity, the inclusion of the word "like" (*iva*) in the rule would be contradicted by the observed grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the object of comparison (*upameya*), as in the expression "intellect like the tip of a whip" (*kaśāgrīyā buddhiḥ*).

In the three sentences beginning with *susadṛśa-śama-*, there are respectively [similes] based on the sense (*ārthī*) residing in the sentence, in the compound, and in the secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Here, although the suffix *-deśya* is prescribed in the sense of "slightly incomplete" (*īṣadasamāpti*), it is employed in the sense of similarity (*sādṛśya*); and because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it results in the meaning of "similar. Now, it is correct to say that when words such as *sadṛśa* ("similar") are used, it is an *ārthī* [simile], since it culminates in the substratum qualified by similarity. But when words such as *sādṛśya* ("similarity") are used, how is it? Is it *śrautī* (based on the word) or *ārthī*? For example: *"parasparākṣisādṛśyamadūrojjhitavartmasu |"* [etc.]

In passages such as, "Beholding the pair of deer whose gaze was fixed upon the chariot," and so forth, some claim this is *ārthī* (implied) [simile]. Therein, they argue that because the suffix (*taddhita*) base denotes the substratum (*dharmī*) first, and the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) subsequently denotes the similarity, it is *ārthī*. We, however, maintain that in reality it is *śrautī* (expressed). Even though the suffix base denotes the substratum, it is the similarity—which is denoted by the primary suffix—that alone connects with the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). For example:
"Seeing whom, like a sight of a lamp, the mind-born [god of love] instantly perished along with his pride. [In this case, the similarity is directly expressed by the suffix.]
I worship Him whom those who perform supreme devotion treat as their own inner chamber within their hearts; whom they quickly treat as a young maiden;
who acts as the central pillar in the mansion of the three worlds; and upon whose left side, which speaks with the voice of a cuckoo, rests the wish-fulfilling vine, dark as a blue lotus.

Here, all seven types of *vācakaluptā* (elliptical omission of the indicator) are demonstrated. Among them: in the sense of "seeing like a lamp," there is *dīpadarśam* [in the form *dīpadarśaṃ paśyan*] using the *ṇamul* suffix after an accusative; in the sense of "perishing like a moth," there is *kīṭanāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ* using the *ṇamul* suffix after a nominative; in the sense of "behaving as if in the inner apartments," there is *antaḥpurīyati* using the *kyac* suffix after a locative; in the sense of "behaving like Kumāra (Skanda)," there is [the formation] using the *kyac* suffix after an accusative; and in the sense of "behaving like the foundational pillar at the creation of the three worlds," there is *mūlastambhāyate* using the *kyaṅ* suffix after a nominative.

The *vācakaluptā* (omission of the denotative word) is to be seen respectively in the formation of the *ṇini*-suffix in "kokilālāpinī" in the sense of "one who calls like a cuckoo," and in the compound "kuvalayaśyāmā" in the sense of "dark like a blue water-lily.

"May the worship of the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) grant me [blessing], casting aside all other fickleness of mind— that worship which is seen to be neither surpassed by anything else in its endearment and benefit, nor even heard of as having an equal."
Here, in the compound *yatsamam* and in the sentence *yena sadṛśam*, both types of the elision of the standard of comparison (*upamānaluptā*) are demonstrated:
"Alas! My mind wanders in vain; for while Maheśvara is present, has anyone been heard of who is equal to him, or has anyone been remembered as his equal?"
May the six-legged bee [of my mind] always remain steadily upon the two lotus-feet of that one who possesses such feet, and may it likewise dwell within her moon-bright face."

Here, all seven types of *vācakaluptā* (elliptical expression of the indicator) have been demonstrated. Among them: in the sense of "seeing like a lamp," there is *dīpadarśam* [in the form *dīpadarśaṃ paśyan*] using the *ṇamul* suffix with the object; in the sense of "perished like a worm," there is *kīṭanāśam* [in the form *kīṭanāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ*] using the *ṇamul* suffix with the agent; in the sense of "behaving like a harem within one's own heart," there is *antaḥpurīyati* using the *kyac* suffix with the locus; in the sense of "behaving like Kumāra (Skanda)," there is [the form] using the *kyac* suffix with the object; and in the sense of "behaving like the root-pillar at the creation of the three worlds," there is *mūlastambhāyate* using the *kyaṅ* suffix with the agent; [and finally], *kokila*...

In the sense of "speaking like a cuckoo" (*kokilālapati*), the form *kokilālāpinī* occurs with the suffix *ṇini*; and in the sense of "dark like a blue lotus" (*kuvalayam iva śyāmalā*), the form *kuvalayaśyāmalā* occurs in a compound (*samāsa*). These should be understood as instances of the *vācakaluptā* (elliptical) [metaphor], occurring respectively.

Thus, this classification of *pūrṇā* (complete) and *luptā* (elliptical) metaphors, being restricted to specific cases of sentences, compounds, and suffixes, serves merely to demonstrate proficiency in the technicalities of grammar; it does not deserve to be expounded in a treatise on poetics (*alaṅkāra-śāstra*) to any great extent. Nor is this an exhaustive classification of all elliptical [metaphors].

To explain: the elision of the attribute (*dharmaluptā*) has been shown in the case of sentences, compounds (*samāsa*), and secondary derivatives (*taddhita*); it is also seen in the case of reduplication (*dvirbhāva*). For example: *paṭupaṭureva dattaḥ*. Here, because the rule "reduplication of a quality-word when expressing a manner" (*prakāre guṇavacanasya*) prescribes reduplication in the sense of similarity, the meaning is "one who is similar to clever. For one who, though actually unskilled in the sciences and so forth, acts as if he were clever, is called *paṭupaṭuḥ*. This [type of elision] is not, however, the elision of the attribute in a sentence.

Because the status of a single word is established by the rule "the subsequent [compounds] are like *karmadhāraya*," which prescribes the treatment of a compound, this [type of ellipsis] does not occur even in a compound as a case of "elliptical omission of the attribute" (*dharmaluptā*). Some have shown that "elliptical omission of the denoter" (*vācakaluptā*) occurs in six ways without the suffix *ṇini*; others, including it with *ṇini*, show seven ways. It is also seen in the case of the suffixes *kkip* and primary derivatives (*taddhita*), as in:

"That Śambhu, by worshipping whom even the world of transmigratory existence becomes full of happiness for his devotees—[if] a mortal does not worship him, he is indeed a mere corpse, failing to achieve his own welfare."

Thus [it was said]. This has been explained below. The elision of the standard of comparison (*upamāna-luptā*) has also been shown in both compounds (*samāsa*) and sentences; it is also seen in secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), as in: "Alas! This which has arrived all of a sudden is truly 'like the fall of a crow and a palm fruit' (*kākatālīya*). The elision of both the word expressing the comparison and the standard of comparison (*vācaka-upamāna-luptā*) has not been illustrated by its very nature; yet that too is seen in the compound *kākatālīya*, which serves as the base form. The elision of both the property (*dharma*) and the standard of comparison is also seen in the secondary derivative *kākatālīyām*. The elision of both the property and the word expressing the comparison is seen not only in the *kvi*-formation and the compound, but also in the secondary derivative.

"For mortals in this world worship him whose lower lip is like a blooming moon-lotus"—this was indeed cited previously. Therefore, this classification by the ancients regarding the elided [upamā] is merely an indication of the general direction, and not an exhaustive classification. As for the other varieties of simile shown in the *Kāvyāloka* and other works, they should all be sought in those very sources; they have also been briefly indicated here during the discussion on the examination of definitions. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate some of its varieties in the section on *rūpaka* (metaphor).

Furthermore, this simile is briefly of three kinds. In some cases, it rests solely upon its own variety, as in: "That dust, its root severed by blood... and so forth. In some cases, it is intended to establish a stated meaning, as in: "Of him who is the source of infinite jewels... and so forth. Or, for example: "The sound of the breaking of forest trees, which causes anger to the hero and steals the sleep of the lion, serves only to bring about the destruction of the wicked man, just as it leads to his own death through the fault of killing one who trusts him."

In some cases, that [suggestion] is primarily suggestive (*vyaṅgyapradhānā*). It is threefold, according to whether the suggested element takes the form of a fact (*vastu*), an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), or a sentiment (*rasa*). Among these, an example of suggestion as a fact (*vastudhvani*) is as follows: "By the heroes in battle, his splendor was beheld—reddened by the intense glow of wrath, with rays crimson like the thick blood flowing from the frontal globes of scent-elephants blinded by pride."
"In whose hand the sword is like the wrathful sidelong glance of Kālī.
Here, by describing the similarity between the sword and the angry glance of Kālī, the fact (*vastu*) is suggested that the destruction of the entire enemy force will be accomplished in an instant.
An example of *alaṅkāradhvani* (suggestion of a figure of speech) is as follows:
"O King, upon your blossoming glories, white as the mass of rays from the moon, this station of Viṣṇu shines like a bee upon a white lotus.

Here, through the figure of simile (*upamā*), there is the perception of the vastness of the glories compared to the white lotus, and the smallness of the sky compared to the bee; thus, the figure of "Excess" (*adhika*)—characterized by the lack of proportionality between the locus and the thing located—is suggested. An example of the suggestion of aesthetic flavor (*rasadhvani*) has been illustrated in the verse beginning with "Like word and meaning" (*vāgarthāviva*).
In some cases, all three types of *dhvani* are observed in a single instance, as for example:
"Look! Here, on a lotus leaf, a crane is seen, like a pearl-oyster shell resting within a vessel made of emerald."

This statement was made by a clever woman to indicate the place of their rendezvous; she had understood through gestures the intention of a secret lover who, wishing to ask "What shall be our meeting place? but not daring to do so openly before the public, had questioned her. Here, by describing the crane perched on a lotus leaf as resembling a crest-jewel set in an emerald vessel, her state of being at ease is suggested through the perception of its immobility, which is similar to that of the jewel.

By this, the secluded nature of that place is suggested; thus, there is *vastudhvani* (suggestion of a fact). Furthermore, because it reveals that "this very spot is a rendezvous for us two," there is *sūkṣmālaṅkāradhvani* (suggestion of the subtle ornament) consisting in the revelation of a subtle meaning that was previously unperceived. Likewise, because the description conforms to her intention, the mutual emotion of love (*ratibhāva*) is suggested; thus, there is also *rasadhvani* (suggestion of rasa).

Now, it is well known that the suggestion of rasa and so forth is of the "imperceptible sequence" (asaṃlakṣyakrama) type; how then can it be said here that it is suggested by means of a resonance (anuraṇana)? Do not say so. Where the manifestation of rasa occurs through the power of the determinants (vibhāva), consequents (anubhāva), and so forth, there it is of the imperceptible sequence type. But elsewhere, even the suggestion of rasa and so forth is indeed of the perceptible sequence (saṃlakṣyakrama) type.

This has been stated by the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta: "Although aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), emotion (*bhāva*), and so forth, are only suggested (*dhvanyamāna*) as the meaning and are never directly expressed (*vācya*), nevertheless, not all of them fall within the scope of that [suggestion] where the sequence is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*). For this very reason, even the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* [cited] the verse: "While the divine sage was speaking thus in her father’s presence, Pārvatī, with her face cast downward, counted the petals of her play-lotus."
In this instance, he cited the transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*) known as shame (*lajjā*) as an example of resonance-suggestion (*anuraṇanavyaṅgya*).

Now, following the context of suggestion through simile (*upamā*), the various types of suggestive similes (*upamādhvanayaḥ*) are demonstrated. Among these, an example of suggestion based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) regarding simile is as follows:
"Scattering a profuse shower of rays upon the flowers of the moon, the treasury of digits..."
"Some attain awakening while others do not; that is simply their own inherent nature.

When several students learn a science from a single teacher, some become proficient while others do not. This distinction among them is not caused by any difference in the teacher’s method of instruction, but rather by their own inherent nature. To convey this point, the primary subject (the students) is compared to an irrelevant subject (the moon) through the device of simile: just as the moon scatters its rays without distinction upon all flowers, yet only some bloom while others do not—this scattering of rays [is the cause].

Even the distinction between awakening and non-awakening is produced solely by their respective natures. In this instance, because the words *go*, *sumanas*, and *kalānidhi*—which possess double meanings—are incapable of being replaced by synonyms such as *vāk* (speech) and so forth, there is a suggestion (*dhvani*) in the form of a resonance rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*).
An example of a suggestion of a simile (*upamādhvani*) rooted in the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*) through the expressed matter (*vastu*) is as follows:
"O wind, blow from where my beloved is; having touched her, touch me as well."
"The touch of my limbs is upon you; the meeting of my gaze is with the moon.

Here, by the power of *ārta* (the piteous), the phrase "the meeting of my gaze is with the moon" suggests that the moon possesses a resemblance to Sītā’s face. An example of the suggestion of a simile (*upamā-dhvani*) through a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is as follows:
"By those who saw you then in battle—your forehead struck by the falling edge of a sword, the front of your chest made crimson by the flow of abundant blood, and rending your enemies—"

"In them, curiosity vanished before the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva), who was radiant with the mass of flames from the fire of his eyes produced by the unbearable burning of the bodies of Kāma. Here, there is the figure of speech *viśeṣokti* (poetic exception), consisting in the performance of one task while another is impossible; for, based on the description that as he beheld you of the aforementioned form, the sight of the Enemy of the Cities—characterized by the aforementioned attributes—took place. This is because the act of seeing exists even when the action [of burning] has ceased. Although this meaning is not directly expressed (*vācya*), it is nonetheless suggested (*vyaṅgya*) through the description of the subsiding of curiosity.

By that, you were then situated like a city in such a state; thus, the simile (*upamā*) is manifested. Thus, the examples of simile and so forth have been cited. Now, the defects of simile are considered: deficiency, excess, difference of gender, difference of number, lack of similarity, and impossibility—these they call the six defects of this [simile]. Among these, the inferiority of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) relative to the subject of comparison (*upameya*) is deficiency; superiority is excess. Both of these are threefold each, according to genus (*jāti*), measure (*pramāṇa*), or quality (*dharma*). Regarding that, examples of deficiency and excess pertaining to genus and measure are as follows:
"A most reckless act has been committed by you, as if you were outcasts (caṇḍālas).
"This sun shines like a spark of fire.
"This ruddy goose (cakravāka), seated upon a lotus-throne, is resplendent."
"At the beginning of the Yuga, the Lord Creator seems as if desiring to fashion forth all creatures.
"Your navel is like the netherworld (Pātāla), your breasts are like two mountains,
and this staff-like braid of hair is like the descent of the Yamunā."

In this instance, the subject matter is utterly degraded by comparisons such as those with *caṇḍālas* and the like; thus, these two defects—deficiency and excess—are subsumed under the category of *anucitārthatā* (inappropriateness of meaning). As for the defects of deficiency and redundancy in terms of attributes (*dharma*), they are exemplified as follows: "That sage, marked by his girdle and wearing a garment of black antelope skin, shone like the moon embraced by a dark cloud."

"In that passage: 'Clad in yellow garments and grasping his Śārṅga bow, the Dark One assumed a form both charming and terrible, like a cloud at night, possessing lightning as its weapon, being joined with the moon.

Here, in the first [example], there is deficiency because the specific attribute of the standard of comparison (the cloud), namely its possession of the *mauñjī* (girdle) as a reflection of the *taṅilla* (thunderbolt), is not mentioned. In the second, there is excess because the mention of the moon is superfluous due to the non-specification of the object of comparison, such as the conch and so forth."
An example of difference in gender and number is as follows:
"O King, through a lack of fortune, even that which was in my hand has slipped away like a wish-fulfilling gem;
I have eaten barley-meal, like a pure woman of good family."

These two are included within the varieties of *prakaraṇabhaṅga* (subversion of the context). How so? Here, attributes such as "slipping from the hand" cannot serve as a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*). This is because this [simile] is only applicable where there is identity of gender and number between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), due to its lack of connection with both when such identity is absent. Thus, the status of being the standard of comparison or the object of comparison belongs only to that which is qualified by the expressed attribute. However, a simile can be established through an implied attribute.

Furthermore, when one of the two—the object of comparison (*upamāna*) or the subject of comparison (*upameya*)—possesses a qualifier while the other does not, this constitutes the fault of breaking the uniformity of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇaprakramabhaṅga*). Some, however, state that differences in time, person, number, meaning, and so forth are also faults. For example:
"Even though the opportunity for action toward the fruit has arrived, he remains indifferent to removing that [obstacle]..."
"I shall abandon the daughter of the King of Videha, just as [the sage] abandoned the ocean-girdled earth at his father’s command.

Here, the phrase "ocean-girdled earth" (*samudranemim*) connects with "I abandoned" (*atyajam*), but not with "I shall abandon" (*tyakṣyāmi*). An example of a difference in persons (*puruṣabheda*) is as follows:
"O Lord of Men, standing there with merely your body, you appear like one whose prosperity has been bestowed by sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*)."
"Having yielded its fruit through the forest-dweller’s gathering, it remains like a stalk of wild rice (*nīvāra*) left behind.
Here, the word *nīvāre* connects with "appears" (*ābhāti*), and not with "shines forth" (*ābhāsīti*).
An example of the distinction between injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth is as follows:

"For you who have attained all blessings, any other thing to be wished for would be redundant; may you obtain a son who conforms to your own virtues, just as your venerable father obtained you, O worshipful one. The construction connects with "obtained you" (*alabhata*), and not with the benediction "may you obtain" (*labhasva*).

The faults of *asādṛśya* (dissimilarity) and *asambhava* (impossibility) result in the fault of *anucitārthatā* (inappropriateness of meaning) within the figure of simile (*upamā*). *Dissimilarity* (*asādṛśya*) is illustrated as follows: "I string together the moon of poetry, which has rays in the form of extensive meanings. Here, the similarity between poetry and the moon is not well-known. If a similarity between meanings and rays were well-established, then—by way of the relationship between an original image and its reflection—the similarity between the poetry and the moon, though currently unknown, might be brought about. But even that is not the case. Or, for example: [text omitted].
"This Vindhya mountain, with its waterfalls gushing from dense groves,
is like Lord Śiva himself, with the mass of flames from the fire flashing from his forehead-eye.
An example of the impossible (*asambhava*) is as follows:
"The face of the young woman, its eyes smeared with tears,
was seen last year like a lotus whose petals are sprinkled with frost.

Here, although a similarity exists between "eyes smeared with tears" and "petals sprinkled with frost" through the relationship of object and reflection (*bimba-pratibimba-bhāva*), the very fact that a lotus is not conventionally established as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for a face is the defect.

Now, the exceptions to these defects are demonstrated as they occur. Among those accepted by poetic convention, deficiency or excess in terms of genus (*jāti*) and measure (*pramāṇa*) are not considered defects. For example:
"The moon is equal to your face; your face is like the moon.
The atom (*dvyaṇuka*) is similar to wine; the waist is like an atom."

In this case, there is no impropriety whatsoever due to its being well-established by poetic convention (*kavisamaya*). When the object of comparison (*upameya*) possesses either fewer or more attributes than the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), these discrepancies in quality—whether it be one-to-one correspondence, the purpose of establishing commonality through multiple attributes, the purpose of attaining a specific nature for the subject, or some other purpose related to the matter at hand—are not considered defects. For example:
"Like the shore of the Ocean of Milk with its mass of foam, like an autumn night with a full moon..."

"In this [verse], 'She, wearing fresh linen garments, shone all the more while holding a mirror,' the inclusion of the additional qualifiers— the linen garment and the mirror— belonging to the object of comparison (upameya) serves the purpose of providing multiple points of comparison for a single qualifier. "And the shore of the Ocean of Milk with its mass of foam, and the autumn night with its full moon..."
"He pierced her, who was dressed in linen and holding a mirror of spotless luster.

In the reading of this very verse, the employment of multiple attributes belonging to the object of comparison (*upamāna*) for the purpose of two similes based on a single common attribute (*aikadharma-upamā*) means that the superiority of the object of comparison in terms of its attributes is not a fault.
Thus addressed by the king, his eyes became motionless in meditation...
"For a mere moment the sage remained there, like a lake with sleeping fish.

Here, the qualifying attribute *dhyānastimitalocana* ("with eyes motionless in meditation") is provided specifically to establish the possession of a common property; thus, its inclusion as a deficiency is not a fault.
"The twilight, possessing the luster of a night thick with darkness, appeared before them, receiving the sound of their bowstring."
"Tāḍakā, with her moving earrings of skulls, was like a dense Kālikā [cloud] filled with cranes.

Here, the qualifier "dense" (*nibiḍā*) serves to establish the possession of a common attribute—namely, the appearance of a thick night—for the *kālikā*; thus, its presence is not a fault of redundancy.
"Kumudvatī obtained from the descendant of Kakutstha a son named Atithi..."
"Consciousness [attains] clarity from the final watch of the night.

Here, the qualification "named Atithi" is for the purpose of obtaining a specific attribute of the subject (*dharmī*); thus, deficiency is not a fault. "Just as divine water assumes other flavors, yet remains a single flavor..."
"In every place and in every quality, you remain thus in these various states, yet you are changeless.

Here, the qualifier *dvayam* (the pair) is intended to bring out a specific characteristic of the subject (*dharmin*); therefore, its presence is not a defect. This should be understood to apply even when the purpose is another effect, such as the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) of composing the current narrative.

Consequently, a defect of deficiency or excess occurs only when there is no mention of a corresponding counterpart (*prativiseṣaṇa*) for the qualifiers of the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), which—being devoid of utility for any other matter at hand—are conceived as having a single purpose through the relation of image and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*) by way of a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

Even in the case of attributes belonging to other purposes, there is an additional merit if they are made common through their persistence or by the mention of a specific qualification. For example, in the verse beginning with *jyāninādamabhigṛhṇatī*, the epithet of the object of comparison (*upameya*)—*jyāninādamabhigṛhṇatī* (seizing the sound of the bowstring)—is also common to the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). This is because, while it serves to avoid the impropriety of killing a woman by showing that the female demon (*tāḍakā*) herself appeared with the intent to kill and was the first to rush forward before being slain by Rāma, it is also applicable to Kālī through poetic exaggeration (*atiśayokti*), as she too is characterized by her association with thundering.

Because of the persistence of that qualification. For example, in the verse beginning “He approached that king,” although the phrase “she who was to become the wife of another” implies a transgression [of propriety], the qualifying attribute “flowing to the ocean” is specified in relation to her.

There is no fault where, despite a difference in gender or number, the word expressing the general quality does not undergo a change in its essential nature, because it is capable of conforming to both; as in: “By the king’s qualities, which were both formidable and lovely. Also: “His appearance, possessing sweetness, was unlike other women.”
"They assumed a supreme beauty, like her own graceful charms.
Even when a word denoting a universal (sāmānyābhidhāyipada) undergoes a change in its own form, differences in gender and number are observed in the usage of great poets:
"Though he is hateful, the learned man is esteemed by that suffering person, just as medicine is [esteemed]."
"Even a beloved person, if wicked, must be abandoned—like a finger bitten by a serpent. "The moon wanes even when it has waxed full; likewise, one who is equal to a foe may fall.
But he (the king) increased in proportion to them, and did not become diminished like those two."

In such cases as these, there are numerous examples regarding differences in tense (*kāla*) and other factors. Vāmana states: "In instances such as these, because they are established by worldly convention, a difference in gender (*liṅga*) and so forth is not a defect. Thus, in the determination of merits and defects, the heart of the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*) alone is the authority. For it has been said by Daṇḍin:
"Neither a difference in gender nor number, nor even deficiency or excess, is sufficient to constitute a flaw in a simile, provided that no agitation arises in the minds of the wise."
"This eunuch walks like a woman," "This woman speaks like a man," "He is as dear to me as my own life," or "Knowledge is acquired like wealth."
"O protector of the earth, like you, the king of the gods shines resplendent;
by his splendor, the king is able to ascend to the height of the sun.
In this way, such good fortune never deserts him at any time.
And there is sometimes a sense of agitation in the usage of those skilled in speech, as for example:
"The moon is white like a female swan; the sky is stainless like a lake."
A soldier devoted to his master is like a dog; a firefly shines like the sun [only] when it is near the sun.
"Such [a comparison] is avoided by the virtuous; let the reason for this be considered.

Thus, when it is well-established by poetic convention (*kavisamaya*), dissimilarity (*asādṛśya*) is not a defect—as in "fame white as the moon," and so forth. When there is an intention to express the impossibility of the object of comparison (*upameya*), the impossibility of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is not a defect—as in "poison as if from the orb of the moon," and so forth. Furthermore, even in a constructed simile (*kalpitopamā*) where the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is based on wordplay (*śliṣṭa*) and which delights the hearts of connoisseurs, lack of conventional renown (*aprasiddhitva*) is not a defect—as in: [Example follows]
"Like the intellect of a poet, it is rich in iron; like the hour of dawn, its wheels are well-fitted;
like the form of Hara, it shines while laughing, endowed with smokeless fire.
"The orange fruit vies with the chin of a freshly shaven, intoxicated Hun."
In such cases as these, other types of exceptions to the [rules on] defects should likewise be considered by the learned.
Thus ends the section on Simile (*upamā*) in the *Citramīmāṃsā*.
Now, the "Comparison of the Compared" (*upameyopamā*) is defined.

If the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison exists between two things by way of alternation, that is Upameyopamā (Reciprocal Simile); it is proclaimed to be of two kinds.

If it is said that when two things are described [as being mutually compared], that is called *upameyopamā* (the comparison of the object of comparison with the standard of comparison), then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure of *tulyayogitā* (parallelism). For instance, in the following verse: "At that time, when the people were distressed, two became especially beautiful: the king standing at the head of his army, and the moon, both whose service of their feet was capable of dispelling the heat."

Thus, because the description of a single common attribute is applied simultaneously to both the king and the moon, it was stated [by the author] that this occurs "alternately. Nevertheless, as it is said: "The dust from the elephants, sprinkled with rut-fluid, and from the impact of the hooves of the horses, attained the state of mud on the path of the leader; and even the mud attained the state of dust."

In this case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*). For there, dust (*reṇu*) and mud (*paṅka*) are described as possessing the nature of mud and dust respectively in alternation. Therefore, it was stated that [the figure must involve] the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*). Even if one says that "Upameyopamā" is where the status of being both the standard and the object of comparison is described, there would still be over-extension in the case of an *upamā* where the similarity rests on both [sides], such as: "And their departure became simultaneous with the state of women distressed by the pain of separation."

Nor should it be argued that there is no over-extension (ativyāpti) because in those cases there is only the presentation of "being the object of comparison" (upameyatva)—defined as being the locus of similarity—for both [terms], and not "being the standard of comparison" (upamānatva)—defined as being the relatum of similarity; for this would result in the undesirable consequence of failing to include instances of "object-of-comparison-and-standard-of-comparison" (upameyopamā) where the two are suggested (vyaṅgya). Therefore, it was stated [in the definition] "alternately" (paryāyeṇa).

Even so, in order to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as the "repeated simile" (*aśanopamā*)—namely, "speech is like thought, thought is like action, and action is like thought"—where both thought and action possess the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) through their occurrence in different turns of expression, one must intend that in one turn an entity is the standard of comparison with respect to a certain thing, and in another turn it is the object of comparison with respect to that very same thing.
It has been stated that this [simile] is of two kinds. The twofold nature of the *dharma* (attribute) arises from its being common or from its being the actual object itself—as in:
"Your face is like a lotus, fragrant, pleasing to the eyes, and rosy with the intoxication of wine;
and the lotus is like your face."

"The ponds, with their lotus-faces possessing true luster, and the women, with their lotus-mouths possessing true luster; where the ponds appear like women, and the women appear like ponds"— these are the examples in sequence.

In this regard, the following is considered: there is an over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) of the definition in the previously cited instance of simultaneous *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile), namely, "By that beautiful [glance] which opened simultaneously... Nor should it be suspected that this is not an *upameyopamā*, but merely a case of a simile resting on both [terms]; for since the mutual comparison is established by the phrase "mutual likeness," the meaning of the constituent parts—namely, "the simile [is] by means of the object of comparison"—remains unchanged for both.

Furthermore, by explicitly stating the mutual opposition that is established even through implication, one obtains the result of excluding a third similar object. Moreover, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the previously cited "mutual simile" (*parasparopamā*), such as "by the dust raised by the chariots. Nor can that be considered a "simile of the compared with the comparer" (*upameyopamā*), because there is no cognition of the exclusion of a third similar object. Additionally, it would lead to an inconsistency in the classification [of similes] stated as, "this is proclaimed to be of two kinds."

In this case, there is neither a commonality of attributes (*sādhāraṇya*) nor a relationship of primary object and its counterpart (*vastuprativastubhāva*). When the sky is compared to the ground, being pervaded by dust is the common attribute; however, when the ground is compared to the sky, the elephants and the clouds stand in the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*). Because they are thus utterly distinct, this very fact results in the exclusion of the third type of *samāsokti*.

When the similarity of one thing to another is described, and the similarity of that [second thing] to yet another is also described—even if it is already established by implication—it serves to exclude a third similar object; this is indeed the seed for its resulting purpose. However, this is not possible when there is a difference in attributes (*dharma-bheda*), even as it is in the case of the commonality of attributes (*dharma-sādhāraṇya*). For instance, by describing the sky’s similarity to the ground through dust, the ground’s similarity to the sky by means of elephants in the form of clouds is not established by implication.
Furthermore:
"Just as a father is [pleased] by a son intent on his service, so too is he by that [son] who has a daughter... [and so forth].

"Likewise, the son became possessed of a father by means of that father who was exceedingly affectionate. Herein lies the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the "simile consisting of an inverted relationship between the subject and its reflection" (*vyatyastadharmibimbapratibimbakopamā*). For here, both the son and the father are the subjects (*dharmin*) functioning respectively as the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*). Of these two, those very qualities—being a father and being a son—are presented as falling within the scope of the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*). And the quality that establishes the commonality in the form of the relationship between the original image and its reflection is the excellence (*praśastya*) conveyed by the suffixes *matup* and *ini*. In this context, those two suffixes are used in the sense of praise (*praśaṃsā*).

The son is "possessed of a father" because the mere relationship [of being a son] cannot be predicated [without reference to the father]. And thus, the fact that both the son and the father possess a praiseworthy father and possess a praiseworthy son is obtained as a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) through the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (original and reflection) combined with the *bimba-pratibimba* (original image and reflected image). Furthermore, regarding those two—the father and the son—their possession of a praiseworthy son is qualified by the phrase "intent upon propitiation," which is combined with the *bimba-pratibimba* relation.

Furthermore, in this *dharmyupamā* (comparison of the subjects), it is clear that the very father who serves as the standard of comparison for the son becomes the object of comparison (*upameya*) when he is designated as the prototype (*bimba*) in the description of the reflection (*pratibimba*) that establishes that [similarity]. Nor is this a case of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison). In the comparison between the two subjects—the son and the father—the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) consists of "possessing a praiseworthy father" and "possessing a praiseworthy son," which exist in the relation of *vastu-prativastu* (corresponding entities) and are interwoven with the relation of prototype and reflection.

However, the excellence resulting from the excess of affection and devotion between father and son, both of whom are established in the pinnacle of Dharma, constitutes a common attribute shared by the followers (*anugaka*). This is because it conforms to the nature of the previous examples. Although the meaning—that the son is also praised for his devotion to his father, and the father is also praised for his affection toward his son—is obtained through the *samuccaya-upamā* (cumulative simile), this does not result in the exclusion of the third type of *sabrahmacārin*.

Nor should it be argued that because there is an absence of two synonymous terms joined by two *iva* words in this case, the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) would not be excluded even when qualifying the synonym; for while there is an absence of two synonymous terms joined by two *iva* words at the level of the expressed meaning (*vācyakakṣā*), where the comparison is between "son" and "father," at the level of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyakakṣā*), there is the presence of two synonymous terms, namely "father" and "protector. Indeed, it is not intended here that both synonymous terms must be expressed, such that the over-extension could be excluded merely by the absence of two synonymous terms joined by two *iva* words.

For if that were the case, it has been stated that there would be no commonality between the suggested *upamā* and the *upameyopamā*. Nor is there an *upamā* here between the two subjects (*dharmin*) alone; rather, for the sake of establishing the commonality between the qualities (*dharma*) as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), only non-difference (*abheda*) is perceived, and not actual comparison (*upameyatā*), which is what is expressed [in the following example]:
"Like a lotus-pond, I drank in again and again the face of that slender-limbed woman, which was like a lotus—just as I, like a bee, drank in [the nectar]."

In such instances as these, since we observe even a simile (*upamā*) between a slender woman and a lotus plant when they stand in the relation of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), the similarity between the two attributes (*dharma*)—even though it serves as a common property (*sādhāraṇīkaraṇa*)—is also a cause for the simile. Therefore, the suspicion of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case is unavoidable. Consequently, this definition is perceived as being indeed untenable. To this we reply:

"That which consists of a mutual comparison (*upameyopamā*)—whether understood through another individual instance (*vyakti*) or by means of another function (*vṛttyantara*)—and which rests upon a single attribute (*ekadharmāśrayā*), is considered *upameyopamā*."

Due to the qualification "by each other," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *raśanopamā* (chain-simile). And due to the qualification "either by individual instance (*vyakti*) or by another mode of function (*vṛttyantara*)," there is no over-extension to the simile where similarity rests upon both [the subject and the object]. For that simile which—by means of a word whose sense is an option (*vikalpa*) consisting of mutual exclusion—is characterized as having a mutual correlative (*parasparapratiyogika*), and which is either cognizable by an individual instance independent of another mode of function regarding its own object, or cognizable by another mode of function independent of the individual instance regarding its own object—that is *upameyopamā*.

Consequently, in a simile where similarity rests upon both [the upameya and the upamāna], there is the operation of *vyakti* (suggestion) regarding the aspect of mutual opposition, while there is another mode of function (*vṛttyantara*) regarding the aspect of the simile consisting of similarity; thus, because these two are blended, there is no fear of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the general definition, the inclusion of both *vyakti* and *vṛttyantara* is intended as being embraced by their non-exclusion of one another.

For thus, in the verse "Was this indeed grasped from the female deer?", the definition would fail to apply to the *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile) when it is understood through direct denotation (*vyañjanā*) without depending on another function (*vṛtti*) and does not constitute a figure of speech, as well as when it constitutes a figure of speech and is understood through another function independent of direct denotation.

Although in the case of suggested *upamā* based on inference, because the word acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), its power residing therein must also be required; and in examples such as "the sky is like water, water is like the sky," where the common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is itself implied, the manifestation (*vyakti*) of that [power] is required regarding the aspect of the property—nevertheless, the mutual independence between [manifestation and power] is impossible. For manifestation consists in being independent of any other function (*vṛttyantara*) with respect to the object of similarity qualified by the state of being a mutual correlate; whereas [the power] consists in being independent of the manifestation of that very object.

And there certainly exists another mode of function (*vṛttyantara*). This very [definition] is also a specific definition of the form of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) that does not depend on individual instances (*vyakti*). In that context, by the removal of the word "individual instance," this qualification results in [the meaning]: "to be understood solely through another mode of function. Consequently, there is an exclusion of the simile (*upamā*) where similarity rests upon both [the subject and the object]. Nor should it be argued that, because in that [simile] one alone possesses the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and not both, its exclusion is already accomplished by the word "mutual" (*anyonya*) itself, making this [qualification] redundant.

In the description of similarity between the contextual (*prākaraṇika*) and the non-contextual (*aprākaraṇika*), although the status of the object of comparison (*upamāna*) belongs only to the non-contextual one, when both are contextual, there is a cognition of mutual comparison due to the absence of a deciding factor (*vinigamanā*). Because of the qualification "having a single common property" (*ekadharmāśrayatva*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the mutual comparison in the verse beginning with "by the dust raised by the movement of the chariots" (*rajobhir syandanoddhūtaiḥ*). By the force of the aforementioned qualification alone, there is also no over-extension to the verse beginning with "the father [was honored] by him intent on propitiation" (*pitā samārādhanatatpareṇa*) in the *Umā* [episode].

In both cases, this is because the two similes rely upon different attributes (*dharma*). This meaning should be understood as follows: when something is compared to another by means of a certain attribute—whether that attribute is common [to both] or consists of qualities such as color or substance—that very same [attribute] is used for the comparison of the latter with the former as well. It does not mean, however, that they must rely upon a single recurring attribute (*anugāmi-dharma*), because such an attribute is absent in the case of the description of things in the relationship of image (*bimba*) and reflection (*pratibimba*), or of real and unreal entities. This is the general direction of the argument.

This, however, is the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) that serves as the basis for the figure of speech known as *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile). But the inclusive and non-overlapping definition is as follows: "When two things, which are similar, mutually function as the object of comparison by excluding a third [dissimilar] entity, that is considered *upameyopamā*."

Thus it should be understood. Here, the qualifier *anyonyena* ("mutually") is intended to exclude the specific variety of *pratīpa* (the "counter-poetic" figure) expressed as "I alone am the teacher of the most cruel [deeds].
Now, the examples. Among these, an example where the attribute (*dharma*) is common through its persistence (*anugāmitayā*) is as follows:
"The sky is like the water, the water is like the sky; the swan is like the moon, and the moon is like the swan."
"The stars have the form of water-lilies, and the water-lilies have the form of stars.

This is an instance where the common property is implied (*pratīyamāna-sādhāraṇa-dharma*). An instance where the common property is expressed (*vācya-sādhāraṇa-dharma*) is as follows: "Fragrant, delighting the eyes," and so forth;
or for example:
"This king of elephants shines like a mountain, and the mountain shines loftily like a king of elephants; the stream of ichor flows like a waterfall, and his waterfall flows like a stream of ichor.

Here, because two instances of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) mutually support one another, there is an additional excellence of aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*). An example of the relation of *vastu-prativastu-bhāva* (correspondence of subject and counterpart) is found in the verse beginning with "sacchāyāmbhojavadanā" ("her face is like a beautiful lotus").

This is the distinction between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) regarding the state of "thing-for-thing" (*vastu-prativastu-bhāva*). An example is: "By that beauty, simultaneously manifested... and so forth. Even there, the previously mentioned varieties should be inferred according to their possibility.
Thus ends the section on the Simile of Reciprocity (*upameyopamā*).
Now, *ananvaya* (non-comparison):
*Ananvaya* is considered to occur when one and the same thing serves as both the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*).

By the force of the word "only" (*eva*), it is understood that this occurs within a single act of comparison. Consequently, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figures of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) or *raśanopamā* (chain comparison). An example: "The sky has the form of the sky; the ocean is like the ocean. This is an instance where the common property (*dharma*) is implied.
As it is stated regarding the expressed object (*nirdiṣṭadharma*):
"Not only does that very woman with shapely hips shine with extreme loveliness like another woman with shapely hips;
even her playful gestures, which are the abode of the dance of the weapons of Love, are like her own playful gestures."
Now, one might object:

"Having thus completed his forest exile by his father's command and having assumed the kingdom, Rāma attained an equal disposition toward virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and likewise maintained the same conduct toward his younger brothers."

In this case, a single entity possesses both the status of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), yet there is no *ananvaya* (non-correspondence) here. This is because, through the metaphorical conjunction (*samuccayopamā*), what is intended to be conveyed is merely his equal conduct toward the goals of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, as well as toward his younger brothers; there is no intention to exclude any other similar object. Likewise, in the verse: "I shall leave the daughter of Vaideha behind, just as [one leaves] a wheel with good rims at the command of a father," there too, the self possesses both the status of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison. Even in that instance, there is no *ananvaya*.

This is because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) consists solely in the exclusion of other similar instances—namely, that "I am not to be restrained from abandoning Sītā due to her censure, just as [the sun] is not restrained from descending to the earth by the command of its father"—and there is no intention to exclude anything else. Likewise:
"The thousand-rayed one (the Sun) took up the new umbrella fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ for him;
with his head close to its silk cloth, he shone as if it were falling upon his own head."

In these and similar cases as well, the relationship of subject and object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) between one and the same thing is clear. However, in these instances, the relationship of subject and object of comparison does not exist between the action of falling and the action of being born among the common attributes (*dharmas*) and so forth; nor elsewhere between the abandonment of the earth and the abandonment of Sītā, nor in another case between the falling into the Gaṅgā and the placing of the silk garment. Nowhere, indeed, does the relationship of subject and object of comparison belong to the very same substratum (*dharmin*). This is because, even when there is a connection with a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭānvaya*), it is appropriate for the transfer (*saṅkrama*) of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) [to occur]. Thus it should be understood.

Just as [the king] attained impartiality toward virtue, wealth, and pleasure, so too toward his younger brothers—in such a manner, even when a single entity is established in the relationship of both the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), if one were to conceive of a transference of its qualifiers, then in examples such as "this Pāṇḍya has a long necklace resting on his shoulder," there would also be a relationship of *upamāna* and *upameya* between the necklace and the waterfall (as in the previous example). Consequently, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total disappearance of the category of illustration known as the "reflection" (*bimbapratibimba*).

Furthermore, for those theorists of poetics (*alaṅkārika*) who accept the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison even in cases of non-difference—as in the expression "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa"—the sublation of the substantive (*viśeṣyabādha*) is unavoidable. Therefore, the application of the maxim "for [a qualification applies] when the qualified [is affected]" (*saviśeṣaṇe hi*) is appropriate for the Mīmāṃsakas of grammar (*vākya-mīmāṃsaka*), but not for the Mīmāṃsakas of poetics (*alaṅkārika-mīmāṃsaka*).

For those who specialize in the analysis of sentences (*vākyamīmāṃsaka*), believing that the relationship of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*) cannot exist where there is no difference, imagine that in expressions such as "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa," the battle of today is compared to the battle of the previous day, or that the sky of this *kalpa* is compared to the sky of another *kalpa*, and so forth. Therefore, if it is argued that according to the view of the *ālaṅkārikas*, the definition [of simile] is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) because in these cases there is a relationship of comparison between one and the same thing—here we reply:
"That which is a self-comparison by itself must possess a common attribute (*anugāmin-ekadharmin*)."
This figure, whose name is true to its meaning, is called Ananvaya (Non-comparison).

Because of the qualifiers "of its own" (*svasya*) and "by itself" (*svena*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal comparison) or to *raśanopamā* (chain comparison). Because of the qualifier "having a single recurring attribute" (*anugāmyekadharmikā*), there is no over-extension to the specific varieties of comparison cited above. Although the recurring attribute is present in parts such as "he attained an equal state" (*samāṃ vṛttiṃ prapede*), nevertheless, it is not a single one; for it is intermingled with the attributes of virtue, wealth, pleasure, younger brothers, and so forth. For this very reason, the inclusion of the word "single" (*eka*) is also purposeful.

The term *anvartanāmadheya* (the name "following after"), however, is not included within the formal definition [of the figure]. Rather, it is intended merely as a justification for the fact that the figure *ananvaya* (non-comparison) occurs only when there is a common property (*ekadharma*) that follows [itself] by itself, and not otherwise. For when there is identity of the property, a comparison of a thing with itself does not "follow" (*anveti*); thus, the name *ananvaya* becomes etymologically significant (*anvartha*). Furthermore, by virtue of being based on the meaning of "not following," it must extend as far as the result of manifesting the state of being incomparable (*anupamatva*).

But when there is a distinction between properties (*dharma-bheda*), that which is delimited by one property cannot be compared to itself as delimited by another property; thus, there is no such thing as "non-connection" (*ananvaya*) there, nor is the result of "unlikeness" (*anipamatva*) obtained through the dependence on a basis of meaning that lacks connection. This is the definition that serves as the cause for the state of being non-connec ted (*ananvayatva*). As for the mere definition, however, one should follow what Bhāmaha stated: "Where [the object] would be [compared] to that very same [object] by that very same [means]."

In the specific type of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) expressed as, "If two separate streams were to arise in the sky," there is an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because one imagines a similarity (*sāmya*) for the purpose of highlighting incomparability; therefore, to exclude that case, the qualification "by that very [thing]" (*tenaiva tasya*) is included.
This *ananyaya* (self-comparison) can also be suggested (*vyaṅgya*), as in:
"O Govinda, today which has dawned for me now that you have come to my house..."
"This joy of yours shall arise in due time only from your return once again.

Here, in these words of Vidura addressed to Śrī Kṛṣṇa who has arrived at his home, the statement—phrased as "this joy born of your arrival shall occur only through your return again after a long interval, and not by any other means"—suggests that the joy arising from your arrival is comparable only to itself and not to anything else. For this purpose of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), the qualification "non-suggested" (*avyaṅgyatva*) in the definition of the figure *ananvaya* (self-comparison) should be understood as before.
Thus ends the section on *ananvaya*.

Now, the figure of speech *smaraṇālaṅkāra* (recollection): Recollection based on similarity which takes another object as its support shall be the figure of speech *smaraṇālaṅkṛti*, provided it remains unmanifested (*avyaṅgya*).
For example:
"Even as a peacock with its beautiful plumage flew up from near his horse, he did not take it as a target for his arrow."
"Instantly his mind went to the mass of hair of his beloved, which was strewn with a parasol and garlands, its tresses loosened by passion.
Or as it is said:

Seeing before him a certain woman emerging from the water— who had inspired wonder even in the gods, whose beautiful hands were like shimmering lotuses, and who resembled the goddess Śrī herself— Śauri recalled the churning of the ocean.

In one case, from the perception of something similar, there arises a memory of an object possessing similar qualities; in the other, from the perception of something dissimilar, there arises a memory of the churning of the ocean, which possesses a similar splendor. In both instances, the nature of being a memory of another object rooted in similarity is indistinguishable. For this very reason, the term "another object" (*vastvantara*) is included in the definition for the purpose of encompassing both similar and dissimilar cases. "O Saumitri, surely let us take shelter at the foot of a tree; the sun is blazing fiercely. What talk can there be of the sun's heat? Here, O Lord of the Raghus, this moon is rising!"
"My child, how is this known by you? For whom does he carry the deer?
Where are you, my beloved, O fawn-eyed Jānakī with the moon-like face?

Here, from the recollection of her eyes—which are connected to the deer that was heard of—there arises the recollection of Sītā who resembles them, as well as the recollection of Sītā herself who is connected to them. However, this [recollection] is merely suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and is itself the object of poetic ornamentation (*alaṅkārya*). To exclude such cases, the qualification "not being suggested" (*avyaṅgyatva*) is added.

"The mountains all around shine exceedingly high, and the oceans are vast and immeasurable; yet you bear even these without any fatigue—salutations to you! While I was beginning to praise you again and again out of wonder, saying 'I shall extol,' at that very moment I remembered Your Foot which bears this earth, and my words were then silenced. The recollection of the Lord, who is the "Mountain-Bearer" (Bhūbhṛdbhuja) in relation to the Earth being praised, is not based on similarity; therefore, the figure of speech here is not *smaraṇa* (recollection). Rather, because the transitory emotion (*sañcāribhāva*) of recollection serves as a subordinate element to the dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love for the Lord as the object of devotion, it constitutes the figure of speech *preyaḥ*.
"Having promised 'So be it,' and having dismissed Umā—who was of some sort—he, the subduer of Smara, went toward the seven sages who were composed of light.

Here, the recollection (smṛti) is rooted in anxiety. Since there is no particular strikingness (vicchitti), it is not a distinct figure of speech (alaṅkāra). To exclude both of these cases, the qualification "rooted in similarity" (sādṛśyamūla) has been added. Thus, these figures of speech based on commonality (sādharmya), which apply to both difference and non-difference, have been demonstrated.

Thus ends the section on the ornament of recollection (*smaraṇālaṅkāra*). Now, regarding the figure of speech based primarily on non-difference (*abhedapradhāna*), the metaphor (*rūpaka*) is first defined:
When that which is being superimposed serves as an embellishment for the object of superimposition, whose form is not concealed,
that is considered *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification).

Here, by the phrase "of the object of superimposition" (*āropaviṣayasya*), there is an exclusion of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), because in those two cases the face and so forth do not constitute the object of superimposition. By the phrase "whose form is not concealed" (*atirohitarūpiṇaḥ*), there is an exclusion of *sasandeha* (doubtful), *bhrāntimad* (erroneous), and *apahnuti* (concealment), because in those figures the object is obscured by doubt, error, or denial.

By the term "coloring" (*uparañjaka*), they state that *samāsokti* (synecdoche) and *pariṇāma* (transformation/metaphorical identification) are excluded; for in those two figures, there is no quality of "coloring" characterized by the imposition of the identity of the object [upon the subject], since in *samāsokti* there is an absence of even the cognition of identity through the mere superimposition of behavior, and in *pariṇāma*, because the object itself undergoes the assumption of the identity of the superimposed [subject], there is no assumption of the identity of the superimposed upon the object. Thus they say.

In this regard, the following is considered: with what kind of distinction between superimposition (*āropa*) and identification (*adhyavasāya*) does [the author] intend to exclude *utprekṣā* by the phrase "of the object of superimposition"? If the distinction intended is that superimposition is the apprehension of non-difference between the expressed object and the subject, whereas identification is the apprehension of the subject's non-difference from the object through the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object, then *utprekṣā* would necessarily have superimposition as its very basis.

In that case, because there is no swallowing (*nigaraṇa*) of the object—the face—due to its being explicitly named in the expression "Surely the face is the moon," over-extension (*ativyāpti*) would remain unavoidable there. Alternatively, the distinction between the two is this: superimposition (*āropa*) is the cognition of identity (*tād-rūpya*), whereas identification (*adhyavasāya*) is the cognition of non-difference (*tad-abheda*). In a metaphor such as "The face is the moon," one perceives merely that the face possesses the form of the moon—that is, the quality of being a moon—but not the actual non-difference from the well-known moon.

If it is argued that in a poetic exaggeration (*atiśayokti*) such as "the moon," where the face is the object, it is precisely their non-difference (*abheda*) that is perceived, we say no; for it is equally possible to conceive the opposite. Nor should it be said: "The moon-face of deer-eyed women surpasses even the moon, for while it is being drunk by the gods, it never diminishes."

Thus, this is a description of the distinction of the moon-like face from the well-known [actual] moon; for when there is a cognition of non-difference, in a *rūpaka* (metaphor), it is indeed a cognition of identity (*tādūpya*). On the other hand, a "metaphor with parts" (*sāvayavopamā*) implies a "qualified simile" (*viśiṣṭopamā*).

In the verse, "Then he set out toward the north, like the sun," the attainment of a commonality (*sādharmya*) between Raghu—who has set out toward the northern direction with his arrows to uplift the northerners—and the distinguished sun—who has set out toward the northern direction with his rays to dry up the waters—is achieved through the realization of the implied meaning. Thus, in some instances, the fact that one simile implies another simile results in this conclusion by way of the sense (*arthāt*).

In some cases, through the simile of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇopamā*), the simile of the qualified (*viśiṣṭopamā*) is understood from the simile of the qualifier, just as the injunction regarding the collection of primary and subsidiary elements of the archetype (*prākṛta*) is understood from the injunction regarding the modified primary element (*vaikṛta*). Both of these are cited as instances of partial metaphorical representation (*ekadeśavivartin*). In other cases, through the simile of the parts (*avayavopamā*), the qualified simile is understood, just as the injunction for the performance of the primary rite as qualified by all its parts is understood from the collection of individual injunctions concerning the parts and the primary rite. This, however, has been demonstrated in the examples of the "simile whose scope comprises the entire subject matter" (*samastavastuviṣayopamā*).

This is an example where a qualified simile (*viśiṣṭopamā*) is understood through a subordinate simile (*avayavopamā*) within a single sentence. It is also seen with a difference of sentences—as in: "The more a wicked person, soiled by impurity like a hand, approaches a good man, the more he [the good man] becomes of stainless luster, like a mirror."

Here, by means of a partial simile (*avayavopamā*), a specific simile (*viśiṣṭopamā*) is understood: just as a hand soiled with dust, rubbing a mirror more and more intensely, makes it increasingly stainless, so too a wicked person, rubbing a virtuous man more and more intensely, makes him increasingly pure. In some cases, by means of a specific simile, the similes for its constituent parts are understood, just as the prescription of the qualified object implies the prescriptions of its qualifiers and the qualified attributes. For example: "Your face—with its tremulous eyes and the radiance of visible teeth—shines like a lotus with bees hovering about and filaments clearly visible."

Here, through the comparison of the qualified [subject] with the qualified [object], the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood between the bees and the eyes, the filaments and the luster of the teeth, and the lotuses and the faces, which constitute their respective parts. Thus, there are countless varieties of simile (*upamā*). For example:
"The mind of lovers is conquered by the sprout-hands of the creepers and the lotus-hands of the passionate women;

Thus, there are countless varieties of metaphors (*rūpaka*), such as the "girdle-metaphor" (*raśanārūpaka*) and others. For it is said in the *Kāvyāloka*—(under a different title or a variant reading): "Since the varieties of metaphor and simile are limitless, only a mere indication of their direction has been shown by the wise; the rest should be inferred."
Thus ends the section on Metaphor (rūpaka).

"In the case of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*), [it is said]: 'That slender woman, having even crossed the impassable river of bashfulness, entered the heart of Nala.
And: 'Because it causes the wheel to revolve, and because it is avoided from afar by those with false views...'"
Because you sport within the depths of the Upanishads, O Mādhava, I consider you alone to be a mosquito.

Furthermore, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of inference (*anumāna*). This is because [the following examples] serve as useful means for the intended effect: in the case of *bhrāntimān* (error), regarding the blooming of the moon; in *apahnuti* (concealment), regarding the eyes of celestial women being granted celibacy (*brahmacarya*); in *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), regarding the pair of jars being turned into rivers; and in *anumāna*, regarding the whirling of Mādhava’s discus. In the case of *apahnuti*, according to the maxim of the "intentionality of that" (*tatkratu-nyāya*)—"As one worships him, so one becomes"—there is utility in granting celibacy to the eyes of celestial women whose self-restraint has been surpassed.
As it is said: "By the mere conversation of a friend, the internal affliction that persists perishes."
"For the fever born of separation is indeed pacified by the lovely moon of the beloved's face.

Thus, there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a *pariṇāma* mixed with a simile (*dṛṣṭāntasaṅkīrṇa*), because that which is being superimposed (*āropyamāṇa*)—being included within the category of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—is employed for the sake of the effect of the subject (*aprakṛtakārya*).

On this point, they say: the meaning of the definition is that *pariṇāma* (transformation) occurs when the object being superimposed is useful for the nature of the subject (*prakṛta*). This being the case, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the examples of *rūpaka* (metaphor) and so forth cited earlier. For in those cases, the objects being superimposed—such as the sun, eyes, flowers, and the moon—are capable of performing their respective functions, such as crossing, seeing, protecting, and blooming, by means of their own nature alone; thus, they do not depend upon the identity with the subjects—the pair of feet, the lightning, the face, and the moon—for those purposes.

Nor is there an impossibility of the aforementioned *pariṇāma* (transformation). For *pariṇāma* is accepted only in cases where something being superposed is described as being useful for a certain action, yet because it cannot inherently be so useful, it requires the attainment of the nature of the subject (*prakṛta*). An example is: "The intoxicating-eyed woman gazes with her clear lotus-eyes. Here, the usefulness of the lotus for the act of gazing is indeed described; for, by the rule regarding compounds such as *mayūravyaṃsaka*, the meaning of the final member of the compound is predominant.

Nor should it be argued that, by resorting to a *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison), the primary status belongs to the first member of the compound, and thus it must be accepted that the eye alone is connected to that utility. This is because the general property (*sāmānya-dharma*) is employed in the word "prasannena" (by the clear one); for according to the rule, "that which is compared with [words such as] *vyāghra* etc., when the common property is not employed," the formation of the *upamita-samāsa* is taught only when that [common property] is not employed. Furthermore, the lotus's utility for the act of seeing is not possible in its own right. Therefore, since it requires attaining the nature of the subject's eye under discussion, this is the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation).

[Objection: But if this were so, then even in cases such as "that which [is crossed] by mind, speech, and body," since the utility of rafts and the like for birth, destruction, and so forth—indicated by words such as "crossing"—occurs precisely through their nature as feet and so on, the consequence would be that those [feet, etc. too are subject to transformation (*pariṇāma*). [Reply: Not so. For the utility [of something] is understood as occurring through that very nature which possesses the capacity to accomplish the primary meaning first perceived from the word expressing the effect. And since the capacity to accomplish the primary meaning of words such as "raft" is established as residing only in the rafts themselves, there is no such consequence.

Therefore, what has been cited is indeed a *rūpaka* (metaphor), and there is no over-extension [of the definition] to those cases. Now, even if the aforementioned over-extension is avoided, consider this: "He has that unprecedented method of reversing his tongue; that fickleness of his ears; that gaze which, through intoxication, forgets the distinction between self and other—what more need be said? O bee, you have forgotten everything! That this elephant, even though its trunk is now empty, is still to be served—O brother, what is this obsession of yours? [In this verse, the elephant's trunk is metaphorically identified with the bee's tongue, etc. How is this to be explained?

Thus, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the definition of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), because in that case, the elephant’s flapping of its ears and the bee’s flitting about, though themselves "unrelated" (*aprakṛta*), serve as causes for the effect characterized by the abandonment of service [to the king], precisely by being identical in nature to the flapping of the ears and the flitting about of the [king's] own elephant. For the elephant’s flapping of its ears is not the cause for the bee’s abandonment of service in the same way [as the bee’s own flitting about is].

Likewise, in that case, the distortion of the tongue and the state of being rendered empty are the causes [of the fault], whereas intoxication (*mada*) is, on the contrary, the cause for indulging in them; thus, its status as a cause for their abandonment is cast far away. Even so, the fact that they are established as causes for abandonment can only be justified by attributing to the elephant-drivers and others—though not the primary subjects—the identity of the wicked king and so forth. Furthermore, the aforementioned non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) remains in the case of the *pariṇāma* illustrated by the phrase "by conversation with a friend" alone.

In that case, since the bee (*makhu*)—like the moon—is not the subject under discussion (*aprakṛta*), it lacks utility as something belonging to the subject under discussion (*prakṛtātman*). To this it is replied: in the phrase "as something belonging to the subject under discussion" (*prakṛtātmanā*), the word *prakṛta* refers merely to the object [of description]. Thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the example cited for *paruṣāpamā*. Furthermore, "utility" is intended here with respect to an effect that makes known the subject under discussion. In the example of *aprastutapraśaṃsā*, there is utility with respect to the abandonment of serving an elephant—which makes known the abandonment of serving a bad master; thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) there either. And so:
"That which is being superimposed exists as having the nature of the locus of superimposition..."
"The transformation (*pariṇāma*) is illustrated when there is utility for the subject at hand (*prakṛta*).
This definition by Vidyānātha is to be refined by explaining the term *prakṛtasya* as "of the subject at hand [which is] the incoming element" (*prakṛtāgama*).
Furthermore, this *pariṇāma* is of two kinds: through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
An example by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is as follows:

"Having himself crossed the celestial river that serves as a garland upon the head of the Lord of Beings, he, the third [brother], provided a ferryman with a fare consisting of his friendship for the son of Sumitrā;
then, followed with difficulty for a moment by Śabara maidens whose breasts reached their armpits and whose eyes were raised in curiosity, he set out for Citrakūṭa, the mountain."

Here, the *ātapa* (sunlight) being superimposed becomes useful for the purpose of Guha’s assistance by attaining the form of friendship with Saumitri (Lakṣmaṇa), who is the object [of the superimposition]; thus, this is *pariṇāma* (transformation). There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because both terms share the same case-ending.
An example of non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) is as follows:
"With clusters of *punnāga* flowers, [he made] necklaces; with garlands of *kesara*, [he made] waist-bands."
"And with earrings and ear-ornaments, they prepared to sport in the forest.

Here, the necklaces and other ornaments being superimposed are suitable for the forest-sport precisely because they take on the form of the *puṃnāga* groves and so forth, which serve as the objects of the superimposition; thus, this is a *pariṇāma* (metaphorical transformation). There is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) due to the difference in case endings. And this lack of coreferentiality can also occur in a *rūpaka* (metaphor), as for example:

"To Him who has Tārā as the crest-jewel upon His head, who is the support of the world, whose neck bears the luster of a rain-cloud, who is uniquely adorned by the embrace of the Mountain (Pārvatī), who wears the river (Gaṅgā) as a crest-ornament, who is marked with a tilaka by His glance, who is embraced by Nārāyaṇa, who wears serpents as bracelets, and who has the mountain (Kailāsa) as His wife—to that Lord, this is my salutation.

In this [verse], there is no grammatical distinction between the two bases of superimposition (*āropyamāṇa*), namely the river and the glance, and the two objects of superimposition (*viṣaya*), namely the crest-jewel and the tilaka. Or, for example:
"The double appearance of the flower-arrowed god (Cupid), the redundancy of the celestial trees, the alternative option for the wish-fulfilling gem, the repetition of the sun-born Vāsava (Indra),
and the duality of the Lord (Viṣṇu) who delights in the sport of crushing the lord of the Daityas— may the illustrious King Nṛsiṃha be victorious in this world, bringing joy to the learned.
