Here, there is a difference in grammatical case between the subject, the king, and the correlates, Cupid and the others.
Now, what is an example of suggestion (*vyaṅgyatā*) through *parimāṇa* (measure)?
"O Narasiṃha, Lord of the Earth, who are we to describe you?
Even after surpassing a king, his fame continues to expand."

Thus it was stated by the Vidyādhara. Here, since the word *rāja* (king) is used to refer to the moon (*candra*), the metaphorical identification (*pariṇāma*) is suggested because the king—who is being superimposed there—is perceived as being fit for the action of attacking. This, however, is incorrect. For in this context, metaphorical identification is accepted only when there is an expectation that the superimposed object (the king) must undergo a transformation into the nature of the subject (the moon). As it has been said: "The wise call that a metaphorical identification (*pariṇāma*) where the subject transforms itself into the form of the object of superimposition for the sake of performing the intended action."
But Vidyānātha has illustrated this:
"This distress of yours will be pacified by serving at the feet of the King; how could dwelling at the roots of thorny trees bring it to peace? Thus he says.

In this case, there is no occurrence of the defect mentioned previously. For when service to the king’s feet is the subject at hand, the service to the moonbeams—which is superimposed upon it—functions as a cause for the cessation of heat precisely by virtue of being service to the king’s feet. Although the word *tāpa* (heat) is common to both physical heat and mental distress, what is intended here is specifically the distress born of the loss of the kingdom; and in the removal of that [distress], service to the moonbeams is inherently incapable. Nevertheless, this remains an illustration according to the opinion of the ancients.

For they believe that because the phrase "by serving the feet of the king" is constrained by the context, there occurs a function based on the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla-vyañjanā*) with respect to the service of moonbeams, which is not the primary subject. In reality, however, even with regard to a non-contextual meaning, the function of words is indeed denotation (*abhidhā*), as we shall establish in the section on *śleṣa* (paronomasia); thus, here too, in the phrase "by serving the feet of the king," the function regarding the service of moonbeams is also denotation alone.

Therefore, since the apprehension of the identity between the relevant (prastuta) and the irrelevant (aprastuta) occurs through the very mode of relation (*saṃsarga-vidhi*)—just as in cases such as *śleṣa*-based hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—and since its utility for the present context is obtained through the third [case-ending], there is no requirement for the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) anywhere; thus, this is not an example of the suggested metaphor (*pariṇāma-dhvani*). Furthermore, this objection applies equally to the previous example. Here, however, is an example:
"O mind, you have long endured suffering; abandon your anxiety!
Is there not the cool moon of the toe-nails of Śauri’s lotus-feet?"

Here, by demonstrating the true nature of the moon-like toenails of Hari’s lotus-feet to one afflicted by long-standing heat, the *pariṇāma* (transformation) is suggested: "Devote yourself to that very [moon]; through devotion to it, this heat shall reach pacification. Thus has *pariṇāma* been defined as distinct from *rūpaka* (metaphor).

In this regard, while the distinction between *rūpaka* (metaphorical identification) and *pariṇāma* (transformation) remains established—wherein in *rūpaka* the subject (*prakṛta*) assumes the form of the non-subject (*aprakṛta*), whereas in *pariṇāma* the non-subject assumes the form of the subject—it is on the basis of that very distinction that Cakravartin has described their difference in a different manner. In the case of *pariṇāma*, as in the example "the heat is pacified by the moon-like face," the face remains with its own nature unobscured; for it is the moon itself, acting as the face, that serves as the cause for the pacification of the fever of separation. And it has been said:
"When the object [of comparison] is superimposed with the form of the subject [of comparison], and the subject is thereby concealed..."
"In that case, there is the state of being a form (rūpakatva) through the connection with coloring (rañjana).
But when the object does not deviate from its own form, then the assumption of another's appearance is considered transformation (pariṇāma). Thus [it is said].

In this regard, the following must be considered: the concealment of the object in a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) does not consist in its form being hidden, as is the case with the true nature of mother-of-pearl due to the error of silver; for it is impossible for the object to be concealed by a superimposition that is voluntarily assumed (*āhāryāropa*).

Furthermore, in the *Śārīraka*, regarding the passage "One should meditate upon that which shines yonder as the Udgītha," an objection is raised that if the Udgītha were accepted as the object of the vision of the Sun, its own nature as the act of chanting (the Udgītha) would be obscured—just as the true nature of mother-of-pearl is obscured when it is the object of the vision of silver. However, this is refuted by the fact that it has already been stated that an imposed (āhārya) vision does not cause such obscuration. Nor is there the status of being subordinate to the object of cognition (*viṣayopasarjanatva*), for that would be equally applicable even in the case of transformation (*pariṇāma*). This is because in both cases, there is no difference in that the compound belongs to the class beginning with *mayūravyaṃsaka* (where the latter member is predominant).

For this very reason, the view that "concealment" (*sthagana*) consists in being qualified by the subject (*viṣayin*) is also refuted, because the subject is itself the thing to be qualified (*viśeṣya*). Therefore, since the distinction between concealment and non-concealment lacks a basis, the difference of *pariṇāma* from *rūpaka* must be established solely through its application as the nature of the object (*viṣaya-ātmanā*). Enough with this prolixity.
Thus ends the section on *pariṇāma*.
Now, [the figure of] *sasandeha* (Doubtful).
"That cognition which, due to similarity, results in a non-ascertainment of the contextual meaning while relying upon that meaning—this is held by those who know it to be *saṃdeha* (doubt).
And this doubt is of three kinds: pure (*śuddha*), containing a certainty within (*niścayagarbha*), and ending in a certainty (*niścayānta*). As examples in order:
O crest-jewel of kings, having brought the wealth of your enemies into the forest,
you saw a pure fragment of a snow-stone among them;
[mistaking it for a casket], what was to be spoken, what was to be ground, what was the wealth, and what was this thing to be thrown away?
"Or what deity is this?"—thus the dull-witted Pulinda people, their minds uncertain, [asked].
"Is this the sun? But he is surely accompanied by seven horses. Is it fire? Yet it does not constantly spread in all directions."
"Having gazed at you for a long time in battle, your opponents entertain doubts as to whether you are Kṛtānta (Yama) himself, borne upon his buffalo.
"Is that a lotus in the lake nearby, or is it the face of a young woman that shines forth?"
"Having hesitated for a moment, he concluded thus by means of the indirect gestures (*dṛṣṭi-bhaṅga*) of those who dwell with the swan.

So they say. Here, this must be considered: regarding the word "sāmyāt" (on account of similarity), is the ablative used here with the intention of expressing a cause as a result—like in the expression "he dwells because of food"—or is it intended to express a cause in its own right? In the first case, the meaning would be that [the figure] has the manifestation of a similarity with something not under discussion as its result. If that were so, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the example "having brought [the enemies]," and so forth.

For in that case, the poet’s intent is not to manifest a resemblance between the moon-vessel and a musical instrument (*vādya*) and so forth; rather, it is to manifest the king’s extraordinary majesty by showing that the city of his enemy has fallen into such a state. Regarding the second [alternative], does the phrase "on account of similarity" intend for only a single similarity with the non-contextual (*aprakṛta*) to serve as the cause for the emergence of the various alternatives of doubt? Or is there no restriction, such that multiple similarities may also serve this purpose? In the first case, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in examples such as "Is this the sun? and so on.

For in that case—such as "Is this Lakṣmī, or Urvaśī, or Rambhā, or Menakā?"—there is a single similarity consisting in the equality of extraordinary beauty amidst the alternatives of being Lakṣmī and so forth; whereas here, in the alternative of being Mārtaṇḍa (the Sun), there is the similarity of being the destroyer of all in an instant, and in the alternative of being Kṛtānta (Death), there is the similarity of being the slayer. In the second [definition], there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure of speech *vikalpa* (alternative), such as: "In this battle-front, either bow your head like Kaliṅga, or [lower] your bow like Karahāṭa."

In this regard, when a powerful king has set out on a conquest of the quarters, he should act as the King of Kaliṅga did in battle against a superior foe: "Overpowered by one more powerful while desiring unshakable prosperity,
one should adopt the behavior of a reed, never that of a serpent."

Thus, following this maxim, he bowed his head, desiring to avoid the certain loss of his own royal fortune; or rather, bend your bow in such a way that King Karahāṭa—who, following the maxim "Fortune is gained through victory, while celestial maidens are won through death," was eager for battle—bent his bow. For, due to the instability of the mind’s conviction regarding the meaning [of the advice], which is induced by the examples of those respective kings' conduct, there arises a doubt concerning the appropriate instruction of a trusted person.

Nor should it be argued that there is no such basis for cognition in that verse, and thus there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*); for even if one intends to include the basis for that cognition within the definition itself, [the following example applies]: "Bending down when grasped while living, and rising up once released—Are these the younger or the elder buckets of the water-wheel? How difficult they are to discern!"

Because this would lead to the fallacy of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as those cited above—namely, in the *sandehālaṅkāra* (the figure of speech of doubt) where the doubt is based on a subject that is itself the object of uncertainty—and because, just as in the case of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) there is a distinction between the expressed and the implied, here too, by observing two types of examples, one must accept a twofold division based on the distinction between the expressed and the implied.

Furthermore, what is meant by "non-determination" (*anavadhāraṇā*)? If you say it is "having the nature of non-certainty" (*aniścayātmakatva*), then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), such as the example to be cited later—"Because of their state of being unopened, they are like the curved crescent moon"—which consists of a probability of identity with something non-contextual based on similarity. If you say that what is intended is "the apprehension of multiple alternatives (*koṭi*) bound together by mutual exclusion through contradiction," even so, [it would still apply to] "Some suspected it to be the moon's spot... [and other similar cases].

There would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as the following, where *apahnuti* (concealment) is about to be illustrated: for there, just as with the particle *vā* (or), the mutual exclusion of the respective views is established by the presentation of those positions, whether through doubt or through alternative options.

"In the creation of this [woman], was Prajāpati the author? Or was it the moon, the bestower of luster? Or was it Madana himself, whose sole essence is the sentiment of love (*śṛṅgāra*)? Or was it the month that brings forth flowers?"
"How could that ancient sage, dulled by the constant study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from worldly objects, be capable of creating this enchanting form?"

Thus, there is a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the example of *sasandeha* (doubtful figure), because in that case, while the subjects of doubt—the moon and so forth—are indeed multiple, the mode (*prakāra*) is everywhere one and the same: being the creator of the woman who is the subject of description. Consequently, since there is an absence of "multiple alternatives" (*anekakoṭikatva*), it cannot be argued that this is not a *sasandeha* because it lacks a common ground for comparison (*sāmyanimittatva*), as is the case in the following doubt: "Has she gone from here? Where has she gone? Has she gone home, or has she gone into my heart? In such a case, doubt is certainly admissible.

Taking as the basis for comparison the heroine’s resemblance to the moon by virtue of her luster, and her resemblance to a flower by virtue of her fragrance and delicacy, there arises a doubt: "Is the moon, who is a treasury of luster, the creator of this [heroine] through the excellence of his own luster, or is the spring, through the excellence of its own flowers? Because of this doubt, the portion "Is he not Love himself, whose sole essence is erotic passion?"—even though it culminates merely in the abundance of her erotic charms and lacks any direct basis for comparison—nevertheless, since the two attributes belonging to the moon and the spring do serve as the basis for that [doubt], it constitutes a *sandehālaṅkāra* (poetic figure of doubt).

And thus, the claim that [the definition] "resting upon the subject matter at hand" is also untenable— on the grounds that it lacks pervasiveness (*avyāpti*) because the aforementioned doubt does not rest upon the heroine who is the object of description— if this is argued, we reply: "The figure of speech known as Doubt (*sandehālaṅkāra*) is considered to be a cognition resting upon various objects that are mutually exclusive, which is based on similarity or touches upon the actual object."

Although conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) also possesses the quality of taking as its object multiple mutually exclusive and contradictory meanings, nevertheless, those objects do not exclude one another in their entirety; rather, while not precluding the possibility of obtaining the other alternative, they exclude the attainment of their own opposite only within the context of their own attainment. For instance, when the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice or barley" presents an option, the rice does not entirely exclude the barley from the sacrifice, nor does the barley entirely exclude the rice.

If that were the case, it would follow that this scripture lacks authority because it would neither provide a definitive determination nor prompt one to act. Rather, [authority resides] only in the context of each person's own performance of the rite. For this very reason, when someone asks out of doubt, "Should one sacrifice with rice or with barley?", the sentence "One should sacrifice with rice or with barley"—which is identical in form to the question itself—is seen to be the decisive factor, the remover of the doubt rooted in the question, and the prompter of action.

In the interrogative sentence, the particle *vā* serves to exclude all other alternatives; in the assertive sentence, it serves to exclude that [specific] alternative—such being the distinction between them. Likewise, in the example of the figure of speech *vikalpa*, since both systems of political science (*nītiśāstra*) are authoritative, it is appropriate to practice either one according to the desire for the results prescribed therein. Thus, because the bowing of the head and the bending of the bow do not exclude each other in every respect, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to the figure of speech *vikalpa*.

In the case of denial (*apahnava*), although there is a mutual exclusion of all aspects, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because there is no contact with the meaning of the word "or" (*vā*). For in that instance, the mutual exclusion of the alternatives is obtained through the presentation of different opinions, such as "some [say]" or "others [say]"; however, there is no contact with the meaning of the word "or. Nor is there over-extension in the case of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*); for in that case, since the two sides of the doubt—which possesses one side as predominant—lack equal strength, there is no contact with the meaning of the word "or."

In the illustrative example beginning with "In the act of her creation," although there is an absence of reliance on multiple alternatives that mutually exclude one another, there is nevertheless reliance on an object consisting of various properties (*dharmin*) of such a nature; thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*), and everything is clear.
An example of the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the figure of speech "Doubt" (*sandeha*) is found in the *Varadarājavasantotsava* composed by the preceptor Vakṣaḥsthalācārya of our lineage:
"Beholding a certain woman of golden complexion, as if she were the Goddess Śrī herself..."
The boon-granting [Lord], overcome by doubt, gazed at his chest.

Here, although the doubt is expressed through words (*śabdopātta*), that much alone does not constitute a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*). Rather, it is because the doubt—which is the cause for the figure—is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) by the phrase "he gazed at his chest," consisting in the thought: "Is Lakṣmī still situated upon his chest, or has she descended from there and stands before him?"—that this is an instance of *sandehālaṅkāradhvani* (the suggestion of the figure of doubt). As in:
"And beholding her enjoyment in the mirror, as her lover sat behind her..."

In the verse, "Beholding her own reflection after [his], she performed various [actions] out of shame," although the word *lajjā* (shame) is employed to convey the perception of specific *anubhāvas* (consequents) indicated in a general way by the phrase "various [actions]," there exists *dhvani* (suggestion) in the form of the manifestation of that shame in accordance with the *rasa*, through its own *vibhāvas* (determinants) and *anubhāvas*.

Although many forms of doubt may be suggested by the phrase "he looked at his chest," such as: whether he was filled with doubt as to which of the two—the Goddess Lakṣmī or the woman seen before him—possessed the superior form; or whether he was filled with doubt as to how Lakṣmī, who prides herself on having no equal in beauty, would behave upon seeing her standing right in front of her; or whether he was filled with doubt as to where this woman should be placed upon his chest.

Nevertheless, since all doubts are rooted in similarity (*sādṛśya*), even though a doubt based on difference (*vyatireka*) might here be possible, it is entirely appropriate that this serves as an illustration of the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the figure of speech "Doubt" (*sandehālaṅkāra*), because it is somehow rooted in similarity. Thus ends the section on the figure of speech "Doubt. Now, "Error" (*bhrāntimān*).
Where there is the experience of something being superposed upon an object whose own nature is concealed due to a resemblance approved by poets, that is considered *bhrāntimān* (the figure of error).

By the term *pihitātmani* ("in one whose self is concealed"), what is intended is the natural conceptualization (*kalpana*) by the poet’s imagination of the experience being superimposed, precisely because that [experience] possesses the capacity to conceal the object. Therefore, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to figures such as metaphor (*rūpaka*). An example: "A cat licks at the moon's [reflection] in a skull, thinking it is milk; an elephant gathers [the moonbeams] threaded through the gaps in trees, thinking them to be lotus stalks."
"At the end of lovemaking, even a woman steals the garment of those lying on the bed"—
thus, the moon, intoxicated by its own radiance, deludes this world;

here, because the description extends from the onset of passion to its consummation, the delusion is entirely natural, yet it is composed by the poet’s imagination to highlight the brilliance of the moonlight.
In some cases, there is a charm arising from a successive elaboration of a delusion:
"O King Ballāla, a Kirāti woman wandering through the city of your enemy, having gathered scattered jewels, has her limbs agitated by the suspicion that they are pieces of a massive khadira log."
Having applied pieces of sandalwood paste upon it, she closes her eyes like buds and fans herself;
the swarm of bees chasing the fragrance of her breath creates a sense of uncertainty.
In some cases, there is aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) arising from a succession of errors whose authors are different.
The bees kissed her breasts, mistaking them for flower-clusters jingling with sound;
her hands, trembling with fear, were bitten by parrots as they mistook them for tender sprouts;
and as she spoke to stop them, she was struck by cuckoos who took her voice for the warbling of their own kind.
Thus, O lion among the lords of the Colas, even the forest is no refuge for the deer-eyed wives of your enemies.
In some cases, this occurs by means of a mutual confusion of objects, as in: "The bee, mistaking it for a *palāśa* bud, alights upon the beak of a parrot."
"He too, mistaking it for a rose-apple fruit, desires to seize that bee.
"O Lord of the Earth, when your fame is in full bloom, even Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and Śiva desire to climb upon it and rest there."
In this instance, the figure of speech *bhrāntimat* (the presence of error) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

Doubt (*sandeha*) and confusion (*vibhrama*), which are rooted in similarity (*sādṛśya*) and difference (*anyatva*) respectively, do not serve as the instigators of the figures *sasandeha* and *bhrāntimat*. For example:
"To conquer this steadfast one, the reckless [warrior], providing his bowstring with arrows..."
He cast even those glories earned by conquering the three worlds into doubt;
and by the wrestler Cāṇūra, whose entire chest was crushed by the blow of Dāmodara’s hand,
the sky was seen as if it were filled with a hundred moons.

In the first case, there is the doubt of a loss of reputation resulting from the rashness of engaging in a battle difficult to conquer; in the second, there is the delusion of the moon caused by a severe blow to a vital spot.
Thus ends the section on *bhrāntimad* (delusive error).
Now begins the figure of speech *ullekha* (multiple description).
Because of the diversity of its signs, this single time appears in many ways.
The mention of that [object] by means of a single [word] is called *ullekha* (mentioning).

*Ullekha* (multiple description) occurs when a single object, which is capable of possessing various attributes, is depicted in multiple ways by different perceivers due to the distinction of the causes consisting of its connection with those respective attributes.
For example: "The fame of [the king] is the Ganges; he is the snowy mountain Himavat; he is the mountain of sunrise for the splendor [of his enemies];
he is the mountain that churns the ocean of the enemy army; and he is the Rohaṇa mountain for the multitude of jewels that are his virtues."

Thus, in the case of the *mālārūpaka* (garland-metaphor), since there is a multiplicity of descriptions (*ullekhana*) in various ways—such as being the Snowy Mountain (*tuṣārādri*) and so forth—based on the distinct causes consisting in the connection with attributes such as the king’s fame and the like, the term "by many" (*anekena*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to that [figure]. In that instance, the multiple description is not based on a difference of perceivers; therefore, there is no over-extension.
[Example: "The learned, the brave, women, and the elderly gaze with curiosity upon him who has arrived, a treasure-house of learning, valor, beauty, and asceticism."

"In your radiant fame, both elephants and serpents, suspecting it to be a lotus stalk and milk respectively, repeatedly lick the tips of their tongues. In this example of *bhrāntimat* (the figure of error), there is a licking by multiple perceivers—in the form of elephants and serpents—of a single fame through multiple modes such as its being a lotus stalk or milk. To exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in that case, the phrase "due to a difference in cause" (*nimittabhedāt*) was stated. Therein, the single whiteness residing in the fame is the cause for both instances of licking.

Although there is indeed a difference in the causes—namely, the desire for their respective beloveds and food—in the case of the elephant and the serpent, nevertheless, by the phrase "due to a difference in causes," what is intended is the absence of a single common cause; thus, that [example] is excluded. Its inclusion [in the category of *saṅkara*] is merely stated as its essential nature (*svarūpa*) in the words "due to a difference in causes. Even so, consider this:
"Some recognize the face as the moon because of its luster, others as a lotus because of its fragrance; we, however, say that the two have attained identity through ascetic power."

Thus, one might suspect an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition to cases of concealment (*apahnava*). To avoid this, the "multiple delineation" (*anekadhollakhana*) must be qualified by the condition that it is untouched by negation (*niṣedhāspṛṣṭatvena*). In those cases, the first two types of delineation involve a negation that is understood through the force of presenting another's opinion (*paramata*); therefore, there is no over-extension.
Furthermore, this *ullekha* is of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) and mixed with other figures of speech (*alaṅkārāntarasaṅkīrṇa*).
Among these, the pure type is as follows:

"Śauri was seen with curiosity by the elderly as 'Gajatrāta' (the Savior of the Elephant), by the young women as 'Śrīkānta' (the Beloved of Lakṣmī), and by the girls according to his actual appearance.

Here, Kṛṣṇa was seen by the elderly— who, fearing the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), sought freedom from it— as the Primordial Being (*Ādipuruṣa*) who once protected the terrified elephant Bhīta with His skin.

He who is the eternal beloved even of Lakṣmī, renowned for her fickleness, because of his skill in the arts of love—this divine youth was seen by longing young women; he was seen by children according to their own nature as possessing a form and dress exactly as they were. Because he is thus described through various forms that exist as actual reality in every instance, this is the "pure" (śuddha) type.
Or, as in the *Harṣacarita*, in the description of the Śrīkaṇṭha region:

It was regarded as a grove of asceticism by sages, a temple of love by courtesans, a hall of music by dancers, a city of Yama by enemies, a wish-fulfilling gem by supplicants, a teacher’s household by students of learning, a city of the Gandharvas by singers, the workshop of Viśvakarman by artisans, a field of profit by merchants, the abode of rogues by bards, a gathering of the virtuous by the good, an adamantine cage by those seeking refuge, and a circle of libertines by the profligate.

It was perceived by the learned as a transformation of the world; by travelers as a mere resting place; by those seeking refuge as a cavern of the Asuras; by the ascetics as a hermitage of the Śākyas; by the lovers as the city of the Apsarases; by the bards as a great festive assembly; and by the Brahmins as the very girdle of the earth.

In this case, because the location abounds in ascetic groves and the like, there is a commingled *ullekha* (multiple description) of those ascetic groves and so forth. Therein, if the nature of being the city of Yama and the rest is connected merely as an embellishing attribute (*uparañjakatvamātra*), then there is a commingling with *rūpaka* (metaphor). If, however, it is within the scope of being experienced as having that very identity (*tādrūpyānubhavagocaratayā*), then there is a commingling with *bhrāntimān* (error). Furthermore, this *ullekha* is composed even when the agent is insentient, for the purpose of proclaiming the excellence of the qualities of the object described; as, for example, in that same [work], in the description of Harṣa:

"He is 'without affection' because of his wealth; 'unreliable' because of his vices; 'fond of suppression' because of his senses; 'difficult to approach' because of the Kali age; 'sapless' because of his addictions; 'timid' because of his lack of fame; 'of difficult-to-grasp mental fluctuations' because of the god of love; 'devoted to women' because of Sarasvatī; 'impotent' because of the wives of others; 'an ascetic of wood' because of the mendicants; 'a rogue' because of the courtesans; 'discipline' because of his friends; 'a laborer' because of the Brahmins; and 'without allies' because of the enemy warriors—he who, though being one, is perceived in many ways."

Even figures such as *bhrāntimat* (the figure of error) are composed with insentient agents, as in the following example: "When the rays of the moon, diverse in their brilliance, have come into contact with the rays of various gems and thus reached the number of a thousand, the lotus-beds indeed assume the state of full-blown red lotuses, thinking: 'Surely this is the sun, the lord of day, even though it is night. And so forth.

"Honey-seeking bees and thirsty cakora birds alike pursue you, who are fragrant, beautiful, and full of grace. Here, *ullekha* (multiple description) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*). In the verse beginning with "learning, valor, and beauty," if [the king's] learning and so forth do not rest merely as causes for the curiosity of beholding their true nature, but rather find their finality in being the cause for the curiosity of beholding him—just as in the case of the multiple descriptions of his scholarship and so on—then even there, because the specific charm produced by the manifoldness inherent in *ullekha* is understood, *ullekhālaṅkāra* is suggested.

Even in the case of the verse: "Regarding one and the same woman, there are three distinct conceptions: for the wandering ascetic, the lover, and the dog, she is respectively a corpse, a mistress, and food," this is also accepted as *ullekha* (multiple description); thus, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition.
Now, another variety of *ullekha* (multiple description):
"Even in the absence of a difference among perceivers, they call that *ullekha* where a single object is described in multiple ways due to a difference in its substrates."

In this regard, due to the distinction of objects (*viṣaya*), there is a manifold manifestation (*anekadholllekha*) which is both pure (*śuddha*) and mixed (*saṅkīrṇa*). An example of the pure is as follows: "May that fortune, characterized by compassion, manifest—[fortune] which is not meager at the waist, expansive at the hips, red at the lower lip, and wide in the eye; [and] which possesses a compassionate nature in the heart."

In such passages as, “Guru in speech, Pṛthu in chest, Viśāla in mind, Janaka in austerity, Sumitra in splendor, Sumantra in counsel, Budha in assembly, Arjuna in fame, Bhīṣma in the bow,” there is a mixture with *śleṣa* (paronomasia). In “She was like a flight of swans in her gait, like cuckoos in her speech, like ruddy geese in her love for her husband, like the rainy season in the swelling of her breasts, and like a lotus in her private parts,” there is a mixture with *saṅkīrṇa* (conflation). In “Yudhiṣṭhira in truthful speech,” and so forth, there is a mixture with *rūpaka* (metaphor).
In passages such as "equal to Yudhiṣṭhira in truthfulness," one should infer that this is a case of *ullekha* (poetic conceit) mixed with *upamā* (simile).
An example of this *ullekha* occurring through a difference in substrata (*ādhikaraṇabheda*) is as follows:
"For a moment, the sun became an umbrella over the expanding [palace] of the destroyer of Bali..."
May He whose head bears a jewel, whose forehead has a tilaka at its edge, whose ears are adorned with earrings,
who has a discus on His shoulder, a supreme gem upon His chest, the Lotus-Seated Lord (Brahmā) at His navel,
and an anklet upon the feet of Him who traversed the three worlds— may He protect you from all calamity.

Here, there is a mixture of metaphors (*rūpaka*). It is also mixed with a description (*ullekha*) based on the distinction between various perceivers situated facing those respective limbs, starting from the middle of the Lord’s forehead and extending to the edge of his ears; for it is impossible for a single observer to see the sun both in the middle of the forehead and at the vicinity of the ear simultaneously.

"His majesty’s prowess—consisting of fire within hearts, water in the hollows of the eyes, wind in the breaths, earth in the limbs, and ether in the voids—was seen as if embodied within the harems of the slain rival kings."

In this context, the description of the identity between the effects of majesty—such as heat, steam, and so forth—which are denoted by words like "fire" and "water," and the majesty itself, constitutes the figure of speech *hetu* (causation); thus, there is a commingling (*saṅkara*) of these figures. According to another school of thought, it is a commingling of *rūpaka* (metaphor). [The verse continues: "They act as musk on the surface of the forehead; they play as bees upon the lotus-face; they serve as dark Tamāla buds for ear-ornaments even upon the head."
"May those splendors of Śrīkaṇṭha’s throat grant you auspiciousness—splendors which act as blossoming blue lotuses upon your ear and serve as black aloe-wood pastes upon the slope of your breasts.

Here, there is a commingling with the figure of Simile (Upamā). Some, however, say that because of the appropriateness of the respective substrata, although the suffix *kvip* is employed for the sake of Simile based on the possibility of identification (*tādātmya*) with musk-patches and the like, it ultimately results in Poetic Fancy (*Utprekṣā*); thus, they call this a "Poetic Fancy initiated by Simile" (*upamopakramotprekṣā*). According to that view, it is a commingling with Poetic Fancy. In this manner, the commingling with other figures of speech should also be inferred. Thus ends the section on *Ullekha*.
Now, *apahnuti* (concealment):

"The attribution of something else through the negation of the subject at hand, based on similarity, is *apahnuti*; it is of two kinds, according to whether there is a distinction or non-distinction of the sentence."

The inclusion of the qualification "distinguished by similarity" (*sāmya-viśiṣṭa*) is necessary because [the definition] would otherwise over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to: (1) *rūpaka* (metaphor), which consists merely in the imagination of identity; (2) *ākṣepa* (paraleipsis), which consists merely in the negation of the object, as in "I am not a messenger; the burning of the fair one's limbs is due to the excessive sun"; and (3) *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), where both [identity and negation] are present but devoid of specific qualifying attributes, such as "Kāma is not five-arrowed, but rather possesses countless arrows."

Nor is there over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of a simile expressing reality (*tattvākhyānopamā*), such as "This is not a lotus; it is indeed a face," because although there is a negation of lotus-ness and a conceptualization (*prakalpana*) of face-ness in that object, the term "conceptualization" (*prakalpana*) refers specifically to superimposition (*āropa*). The definition was not stated using the gerund suffix (*ktvā*)—as in "having negated the object, there is the superimposition of another due to similarity"—because that would result in non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the examples to be cited later, where the negation occurs after the superimposition.

And this [metaphor] operates through syntactic split (*vākyabheda*) in three cases: when there is the direct employment of negating particles such as *nañ*; when it occurs through the presentation of another's position (*parapakṣa*) and so forth; and when the negation is understood by implication (*arthāt*). Furthermore, it operates without syntactic split in two cases: when words such as "deceit" (*chadman*), "disguise" (*nibha*), or "pretext" (*vyāja*) are employed to establish the unreality of the object; and when words such as "form" (*rūpa*), "body" (*vapus*), or "name" (*nāman*) are employed, which result in the unreality of the object. Within that [latter case], there is a twofold division: superimposition preceded by concealment (*apahnavapūrvaka āropaḥ*), and concealment preceded by superimposition (*āropapūrvako 'pahnavah*).
Examples in order:
"This is not a blemish acquired in the past by the daughter of the mountain, whose luster has matured; rather, this is the reflection of the moon’s own body.
I believe it is this very form of his, cool with the trickling nectar, that shines forth."
"Tired from lovemaking, the lady of the night lies fast upon his chest.
Or as it is said:
"This is not the circle of the sky, but an ocean; these are not stars, but clusters of fresh foam."
"This is not the moon, but the lord of serpents coiled; this is not a spot, but Murāri reclining.
In the former case, there is *niravayavāpahnuti* (partless concealment); here, the distinction is that it is *sāvayavā* (with parts).
"Some took the mark [on the moon] for a hare; others considered it the mud of the ocean."
Some indeed praised the spotted deer, while others desired the shadow of the earth;
for that which appears at night on the moon, dark as a fragment of split sapphire, we declare to be the thick, swallowed-up darkness residing within its belly.

In this instance as well, there is a superimposition preceded by a negation (*apahnava*). The negation is established through implication (*arthasiddha*) by the presentation of the opponent's position:

"He who always dwells upon the clusters of blue lotuses that are the eyes of blossoming celestial nymphs—clusters surpassed [in beauty] by his self-restraint—and who does not reside upon the peacock with its lovely plumage; may that Kumāra bestow upon you the glory of the splendor of celibacy (*brahmacarya*)."
In this instance, there is a verbal negation preceded by superimposition (*āropa*):
"The scar of the wound from the friction of thousands of rocks at the base of the mountain that serves as the churning-stick throbs within the moon;
the 'shadow-deer' is but a hare—this is the vulgar talk of the world, a popular maxim followed blindly by those who merely follow the crowd."

Here too, there is a denial preceded by superimposition (*āropa*), and that is established by implication through the citation of the speech of a common person (*pāmara*). These are examples distinguished by syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*):
"Alas, friend! Behold how great is this enmity of Smara toward this world of lovers made emaciated by separation from their beloveds; for instance:"
"Under the guise of bees shimmering upon the mango trees in the grove,
he has, as it were, carved out kālakūṭa poison for every arrow.
Surely, in this deer-eyed woman who pours forth the nectar of her loveliness— "
"The God of Love, consumed by Śiva, fell upon her broad hips;
this column of smoke rising from the hollow of her navel, signaling the extinction of the embers of his limbs, now transforms into the form of the line of hair."

In the former case, the statement “there are no mango trees with bees” leads to the understanding that they are actually arrows tipped with *kālakūṭa* poison, by virtue of the word *chala*, which denotes a false assertion. In the latter case, the understanding that this is not a line of body hair but rather a column of smoke arises from the power of the word *vapuḥ*, which results in a false conclusion.

Some, however, maintain that this is an *alaṅkāra* (poetic figure) where, just as there is a denial for the sake of manifesting similarity, there is also a denial of similarity for the sake of the denial itself. As they say:
“Where there is a denial for the sake of manifesting similarity, that is *apahnuti*.”
"Where there is similarity for the purpose of denial, that too is *apahnuti* (concealment). And they cite as an example:
"Having first drawn [her] with a firm grasp by her hair, and having pressed her face against his own face..."

"He clings to my neck with his own neck, spreads his arms as he presses a firm embrace upon my breasts, and, fixing his attachment upon my hips, falls at my feet—he who is such a beloved of mine! O girl, shame has been cast aside; no, no, you simple-minded one, how could a mere bodice cause embarrassment?"

In this instance, having concealed the intended beloved (*priya*), there is the superimposition (*āropa*) of being a *colaka* (a small garment); and for that purpose, there is first the presentation of a quality similar to the beloved’s garment. Here, this statement of concealment (*apahnuti*) is formulated in accordance with the view of Bhaṭṭa and others, who do not accept *vyājokti* as a distinct figure of speech. However, those such as Rucaka and others, who maintain that *vyājokti* is the concealment of a manifest object (*udbhinnavastunigūhanam*), hold that even here it is simply *vyājokti* and not *apahnuti*.

Daṇḍin, however, disregarding the rule that denial (*apahnuti*) must be rooted in similarity (*sādharmya*), defined it as "the mere indication of something else after having denied something," and gave this example:
"Denial (*apahnuti*) is the suggestion of another meaning by means of denying something; for example:
'Smara is not the five-arrowed one; his arrows are a thousand.'"
"Sandalwood, moonlight, and the gentle southern breeze—
this very creation consisting of fire is cooling for me, but [hot] toward others.
"The moon is considered 'Amṛtāṃśu' (Possessor of Immortal Rays) by name."
"This very essence of the object is quite different, its rays dripping with poison.
However, *apahnuti* (concealment) based on similarity is designated by him as *upamāpahnuti* (concealment by way of simile).
An example of *apahnutidhvani* (suggestion of concealment) is as follows:
In a portrait painted by a slender maiden trembling with curiosity, one girl has finished drawing the discus and is now painting the son of Suparṇa;
then another, her hand perspiring, quickly wipes this away.
"In his hand he holds a bow of flowers, and above it he draws a sea-monster (*makara*).

In such passages, the suggestion of *apahnuti* (concealment/denial) should be illustrated. For here, by the drawing of the discus, the eagle, and the sea-monster, someone suggests: "This is not an ordinary man, but rather the lotus-eyed one (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*, i.e., Viṣṇu). Another woman, however, with the intention that even for him such a form is impossible, suggests: "This is not even the lotus-eyed one, but rather the god of love (*manmatha*)," thereby wiping away both [previous suggestions] by drawing a flower-arrow and a sea-monster-banner.
Thus ends the section on *apahnuti*.

Now, the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (Poetic Fancy): "O wise ones, that wherein the subject under description is imagined as something else due to its connection with the attributes of another, that indeed they call *utprekṣā*."
For example:
"The *palāśa* flowers, curved like the young crescent moon and not yet fully blossomed, shone with an intense redness like the nail-marks of Spring upon the forest grounds as they met."

Here, the *palāśa* buds under discussion are conjectured to be nail-marks because they possess the qualities of curvature and redness associated with the non-contextual (aprakṛta) nature of nail-marks. Conjecture (*tarka*) is mere possibility, not certainty. For while the presence of its [the object's] qualities is a cause for the mere possibility of identity with it, it is not a cause for certainty—unlike a logical mark (*liṅga*), which possesses both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Nor should one suspect that this is a simile (*upamā*), on the grounds that the word "like" (*iva*) here refers to similarity.

In this case, since it is possible to speak of nail-marks even when they exist somewhere else [on other women], there is no need to postulate the qualification of being connected to a forest region where the hero has met with the heroine in spring. This is because such a qualification is only useful for the purpose of conceiving an identification (*tādātmya*) between the *palāśa* buds and the nail-marks. Thus, wherever else there is the postulation of a qualification used for conceiving an identification with something non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), in all such instances, it should be understood as *utprekṣā*. For example:
"She who bore a creeper-like slender body with a vine of hair like a swarm of bees..."
"...like a braid reflected [in water], liberated from impurity.

Where an object of comparison (*upamāna*) can be described even by means of a simple braid, the conceptualization of specific qualifiers—such as "due to purity" and "reflected in front"—is unnecessary; rather, they are employed for the purpose of suggesting a possibility of identity (*tādātmya-sambhāvanā*). However, where an object of comparison is presented without such qualifiers that serve to suggest a possibility of identity, the word *iva* refers solely to similarity (*sādṛśya*), and thus it constitutes the figure of speech known as Simile (*upamā*).

Intending this very distinction, the Cakravartin stated: "If this portion consisting of comparison attains establishment through worldly usage," and so forth. Daṇḍin also stated that the word *iva* functions as a suggester (*vyañjaka*) of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*):
"By words such as *manye*, *śaṅke*, *prāyaḥ*, *nūnam*, and others, as well as by similar words, poetic fancy is manifested."

Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such terms as *tarkayāmi* (I conjecture), *sambhāvayāmi* (I imagine), *jāne* (I know), *utprekṣe* (I fancy), and *syāt* (it might be). And in this regard:
"If I were Brahmā once again, having extracted the entire quality of fragrance from the musk-deer's navel, I would deposit it upon the tongues of the wicked."
In such instances as, "If fire were not hot, if water were not cold;

then Rāma, firm in his vows, might indeed be a speaker of untruth," the phrase "due to the connection with a property" (*dharmasaṃbandhāt*) is stated in order to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For in those cases—whether they belong to the domain of the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) according to the rule "and when there is a statement of 'if,' there is a conceptualization [of the contrary]," or to the domain of the figure of speech *saṃbhāvanā* (poetic fancy) according to the rule "fancy is a conjecture that 'if it were thus,' it would be another thing"—such a representation occurs entirely without a factual basis. Nevertheless—

[If one were to define it simply as] "I suspect Satyavat’s face possesses beauty surpassing all others, by which that deer-eyed Sāvitrī was made to tremble," and so forth, there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). To exclude this, the phrase "due to the connection with the attribute of another" (*anyadharmasaṃbandhāt*) was stated. In that case, since the conjecture is made precisely through her own attribute—namely, being the cause of the agitation in Sāvitrī’s heart—there is no over-extension.

In the verse: “‘I suspect that Bharata, having heard the news from Hanumān, has come out to meet me with his army, since a dust cloud arising from the earth rises ahead, reddened by the twilight,’”—the qualification *anyatvena* (as something other) is added here to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*). In this case, although the rising of dust ahead is observed elsewhere as well, it is inferred here specifically as the factual reality of Bharata’s coming out to meet him, based on its connection with the cause; it is not inferred as something else. Thus, there is no over-extension.

In the verse: "O Narasiṃha, O protector of the earth, we know you to be the god of love (Makaradhvaja); otherwise, how could your arrows be flowers?"—the term "upatarkitam" (suspected/contemplated) is used here to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*). For in that case, regarding the figure of speech *anumāna* (inference), the king's status as the god of love is determined through the mark (*liṅga*) of being possessed of flower-arrows, which is pervaded by the state of being the god of love; it is not a mere matter of poetic fancy (*sambhāvanā*).
The moon seems as if smeared with collyrium; the gaze of the does is as if dulled;
the coral vine is as if its sprouts have withered; the luster of gold is as if turned dark;
and I perceive a touch of harshness, as it were, emerging in the throats of the female cuckoos.
And alas, in the presence of Sītā, the plumage of the peacocks seems as if it were covered in shame.

Here, the term "prakṛta" (the contextual) is mentioned to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*). In that case, because of the proximity of Sītā’s face and other features—which possess unsurpassed beauty—and because this proximity causes even the conventional objects of comparison (*upamāna*) such as the moon to appear inferior, one conceives of the application of collyrium and the like to the non-contextual [objects] such as the moon to account for their perceived inferiority; thus, there is no over-extension. But even so, consider this:
"O Daughter of the Earth, hearing of our heroic exploits—those which caused the gods and demons to bow down in submission before the effortless conquest of the entire three worlds—"

"In this passage—'With a mind stained by hatred for her husband, will she remain affectionate toward me? For the love of women is fickle, being agitated by a desire for ever-increasing qualities of excellence'—Sītā, whose heart is in reality fixed solely on her husband, is suspected of fickleness because of her association with that quality of fickleness observed elsewhere [in women]. Yet, there is no figure of speech (alaṅkāra) called *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) here; for since only the mere thought conducive to accomplishing Rāvaṇa’s desired end is described, there is an absence of any particular strikingness (*vicchitti-viśeṣa*)."

Furthermore, it should not be argued that in the phrase "due to the connection with another property" (*anyadharmasaṃbandhāt*), the term "property" (*dharma*) is intended here—just as in the case of simile—to mean a quality that delights the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*), and not merely any common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*). For if that were so, there would be no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as: "The Lord of the Raghus ran, imagining that this creeper, lovely with its clusters of blossoms, was surely Sītā," because even though femininity (*strītva*) and the like serve merely to suggest the possibility [of identity], they lack the status of a common property that delights the hearts of sensitive readers, and thus do not function as the instigator of the figure of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). If that were the case, then in the verse cited above, [the definition would fail to apply].

If it is argued that this is not so because [the definition] would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) here due to the inclusion of "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*), and that "being induced" (*āhāryatva*) cannot be a qualification of *tarka*, since one must state that "in this case, the imaginative possibility (*sambhāvanā*) is non-induced (*anāhāryā*)," and that if that were the case, then because the imaginative possibility in "I suspect the activity described by Hanumān" is also non-induced, the phrase "by way of being other" (*anyatvena*)—intended to exclude that—would result in being redundant; we say: do not say so. For the phrase "by way of being other" has as its referent that which is understood as "other than that," and thus it results in the very qualification of "being induced."

But even so, this is not a valid definition, because it suffers from the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*). To explain: in cases where something is imagined based on a property belonging solely to itself or a property belonging solely to another, there is an absence of the definitional element "due to connection with a property of another," and thus the definition is under-extended. For example:
"Having bound up the mass of darkness with its rays as if with fingers, the moon kisses the face of night, which has closed-lotus eyes."
Since these stars are far more numerous during the nights of darkness and sparse during the moonlit nights,
we infer that this moon was fashioned from the very stars themselves, which were melted down by the fire of twilight within the crucible of the sky.

Thus, in the first example cited here, because the mass of darkness—which resembles a mass of hair—is grasped by rays that resemble fingers, the kissing of the moon is imagined solely on the basis of its own attributes (*svamātradharma*). In the second, by means of another's attribute (*anyamātradharma*)—namely, the state of being sparse or dense in the form of stars—the moon is imagined to have been fashioned from a heap of stars rolled up like a ball of wool by a mouse situated within the fire of twilight. Furthermore, there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of causal, consequential, attributive, and essential poetic fancies (*hetu-phala-dharma-svarūpotprekṣā*), because the defining element "as something else" (*anyatvena*) is absent.
Likewise—
"This is that very spot where, while searching for you, I saw a single anklet fallen upon the ground;
it appeared as if bound in silence, as it were, out of the sorrow of separation from your foot.

In this example of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause), by means of the quality of silence—a characteristic common to those who are suffering—present in the anklet, the very sorrow that is the cause of that silence is fancied as its attribute (*dharma*), but not an identity with sorrow itself, because no suffix such as *matup* (possessive) is heard after the word "sorrow" (*duḥkha*). Thus, [the same applies to the following].

"In the example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the fruit—'The thorny forest edges have even today torn open the skin of the forehead of that Cōḷa king who fled in fear, as if to see what letters [of doom] he might experience'—the fruit of the trees is fancied as having the nature of a property (*dharma*), namely the objective of seeing the letters on the forehead, by means of the cause, which is the tearing of the forehead shared with a person intent on seeing such letters. However, there is no identity (*tādātmya*) with the subject (*dharmin*) who is intent on seeing the letters on the forehead, because the word 'to see' (*draṣṭum*) does not extend to the subject. Likewise:

"In the example of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the nature of an attribute (*dharmasvarūpa*): 'The ocean, as it were, grinds camphor-sandalwood with the tips of its waves; taking that [sandalwood], the moon, with his rays, seems to anoint the women who are the quarters of the sky'—here, by means of the perceived causes (namely, the ocean's shore acting like a grinding-stone and the moon's rays whitening the quarters of the sky), one merely fancies the acts of grinding and anointing performed by those two [the ocean and the moon]. However, there is no identity between those two [the ocean and the moon] and the agents of the grinding and the anointing."

Although the verbal roots in the expressions *pinaṣṭi* (he grinds) and *limpati* (he smears) denote an agent, according to the maxim "the verb has action as its primary meaning" (*bhāvapradhānam ākhyātam*), the agent is subordinate to the action which is the primary element; consequently, [that agent] cannot be construed with anything else. For this very reason, Daṇḍin, while illustrating the figure of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) in the verse "Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium," raised the following objection—anticipating that the comparison (*upamā*) between darkness and the sky might be based on their being the agents of smearing and raining respectively because of the hearing of the word *iva*:
"If the agent were the object of comparison, it would be subordinated to the verb."
"Being occupied with accomplishing its own function, it is not capable of depending upon another"—
thus [the opponent] has been refuted. [The Creator],
having fashioned those two auspicious shanks of his, which were rounded in their proportions and not too long...
"In the process of creating the remaining limbs, the Creator’s effort seemed as if it were directed toward producing fresh beauty.

Here, based on the cause—the total depletion of the treasury of beauty inferred from the creation of the shanks possessing unsurpassed loveliness—there is merely a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the Creator's exertion in producing beauty for the sake of fashioning the rest of the body; it is quite clear that this is not an identification with the state of possessing such an effort.

Furthermore, in a poetic fancy whose subject (*dharmi*) is something non-contextual (*aprakṛta*), there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) because the element of "the contextual" (*prakṛtam*) is absent. For example:
"The lunar orb, its essence extracted by the Creator for the sake of Damayantī’s face,
appears as if it has a hollowed center, possessing the dark blue luster of a deep mine."

Here, by means of *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) based on the poetic figure *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause-and-effect), where the phrase "containing a hollow in its center" serves as the cause, the lunar orb is imagined (*utprekṣita*) as having its essence extracted for the creation of Damayantī’s face—on the grounds that it possesses a dark spot (*kalaṅka*) which is dark due to the blueness of the space within its central cavity. It is not, however, the actual subject under discussion, Damayantī’s face itself, that is imagined as being constructed from the extracted essence of the moon in the manner described. [As the source text says: "It was produced as if from the essence accumulated from the collection of the digits of the moon."
"...may I behold once again her face, the auspicious abode of the bodiless god (Cupid).

Just as in this case, there is an absence of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the word *tathā*. Now, even if no connection is obtained with the word *tathā*, in the expression "Let a hundred Brahmins be fed," the syntactic connection of the action terminates with the subordinate element (*upasarjana*), bypassing the principal (*pradhāna*), because the number [of the hundred] is unfit for connection with the act of eating; so too here.

If it is argued that, having transcended the primary moon-disc, the description must culminate in a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding Damayantī’s face as being fashioned from a thunderbolt whose essence was extracted from the moon-disc—since the non-contextual (the moon) is not to be described—the answer is no; for even the description of the non-contextual, in the form of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise), is fit to be connected with the purpose of imparting excellence to the contextual subject.

Nor should it be argued that, just as in the other example of Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Praise), "The moon is like a smear," here too there is merely a possibility (*sambhāvanā*) and not *utprekṣā* (Poetic Fancy). For while *utprekṣā* is impossible there due to the absence of the complete set of conditions for *utprekṣā*—specifically, the absence of a cause that delights the hearts of connoisseurs—it is possible here; thus, since *Aprastutapraśaṃsā* can coexist with it, their commingling (*saṅkara*) is logically established. Therefore, if it is argued that this definition is untenable because it lacks pervasiveness (*avyāpti*), [we reply:]...

To this we reply: first of all, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "its essence stolen" (*hṛtasāra*), because the word *prakṛta* (the subject at hand) refers merely to that which is intended to be the object [of the comparison]. Nor, in this way, is there an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "the moon as if smeared," for although in that instance the quality of being smeared with collyrium actually belongs to something else in proximity to Sītā’s face, the fact of belonging to another is irrelevant to the conceptualization (*sambhāvanā*) of the moon being smeared; or rather, because the intended quality is one that delights the hearts of connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).

The phrase "by way of being other" (*anyatvena*) means "in another manner" (*anyena prakāreṇa*); thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding cause, effect, attribute, or essential nature. Where one subject (*dharmin*) is fancied as being identical with another subject, there that other subject is the "other manner. However, where a certain attribute itself is fancied as a cause, an effect, or an essential nature in relation to something else, there that very attribute is the "other manner. Since this applies consistently everywhere, or alternatively, because even in the examples of poetic fancy regarding cause, effect, attribute, and essential nature, the fancy occurs precisely through identity (*tādātmyena*).

For instance, in the examples of the poetic figures *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy as cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (poetic fancy as effect), such as "This is that very spot where you were being searched for" and "Of Cola, who had fled from Bhadīti," the attributes of the pain of separation and the sight of the letters on his forehead are not fancied as the cause or the effect [of the respective actions].

However, that silence and tearing of the bark caused by immobility, contact with thorns, and so forth—which belong to the nature of the *nūpī* tree and such—is here poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as being identical with the silence and tearing of the forehead intended for the purpose of reading the letters [of fate] caused by suffering. Indeed, one must necessarily maintain the identification (*tādātmyādhyavasāya*) of both types of silence and so forth; otherwise, it would be inconsistent to imagine that natural silence and the like—caused by factors such as immobility—are identical with the causes of suffering and so forth.

And even by the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, who maintains that in such instances as "this is that very spot," the property (*dharma*) itself—such as silence—is metaphorically identified (*adhyavasāya*) with the anklet and so forth as the cause of [the woman's] silence and other traits, he accepts two kinds of [metaphorical] identification regarding silence and the rest. For his words state: "In the case of causal metaphor (*hetūtprekṣā*), that property belonging to the subject which is imagined to be the cause is, through the force of metaphorical identification, treated as non-different from that [subject] and adopted as the ground for the metaphor."

Furthermore, it is necessary in some instances elsewhere to rely upon the identification (*tādātmyādhyavasāya*) of the causal factor (*nimittāṃśa*) within an example based on the poetic fancy of a cause (*hetūtprekṣā*). For example: "O lady of graceful form, I believe that the Goddess of Fortune, out of joy because the pride of beauty belonging to that moon—who is my innate enemy and cannot endure my blossoming during the night—has been forcibly brought to rest by the splendor of your face, has now clung to your feet."

In this case, as the cause for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding joy, the contact of the lotus-goddess with the feet—which is intended to be its result—must be stated as the ground (*nimitta*); however, that [contact] is entirely unestablished. Here, it must be justified by maintaining that the very natural connection between the beauty of the feet and [the lotus] is itself determined (*adhyavasita*) as the contact with the lotus-goddess, serving as the ground. Thus, since there is a necessary determination of identity (*tādātmyādhyavasāna*) regarding the causal factor, let the poetic fancy rest right there.

Nor should it be argued that no other ground (nimitta) for such [imaginative] identification must be sought there; for when the silence caused by immobility is identified with the silence caused by suffering, the ground is "occurring at the time of separation from the lotus-feet"; and when the tearing caused by contact with thorns is identified with the tearing performed for the purpose of reading the writing on the forehead, the ground is "occurring at the time of flight," which arouses the desire to know whether "this great king is experiencing such hardship even now, and how much more unbearable might it be for him beyond this"—all of which is clear.
This very position is also favored by Daṇḍin. As he says:
"Where the mode of being of a sentient or insentient entity, though established in one way, is imagined in another way, that they call *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy)."
Scorched by the midday sun, the elephant plunges into the lake;
I imagine he is intent on uprooting the lotuses that are the very dwelling-places of the sun.
"To bathe, to drink, or to eat lotus stalks—the elephant's plunging into the water is described by the poet through poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) as being for the sake of avenging that [past] enmity.

Here, the activity of the conscious elephant—consisting of plunging into the water—which exists in one way solely for the purpose of removing heat, is fancied in another way as being a plunge into the water for the sake of avenging that enmity; thus it has been applied in accordance with the author's own definition.

This very position is also accepted by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśikā*. For, having stated the definition of *utprekṣā* as "the imagining (*saṃbhāvanā*) of the subject (*prakṛta*) with something similar (*sama*) through a standard of comparison (*upamāna*)", he provides the example "He who does not tolerate my blossoming" (*unmeṣaṃ yo mama na sahate*).

Consequently, it is quite clear that, in accordance with his own definition, the natural beauty of the feet itself is imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as being the Goddess Lakṣmī, marked by joy arising from the victory over her own enemy.

Likewise, in examples of the poetic figure *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on the nature of an attribute, such as "He seems to grind with the tips of his waves," it is the act of impelling (*preraṇā*) and so forth that is fancied. Nor is the non-mention of the object (*viṣaya*), such as the act of impelling, a defect; for this is possible just as in the case of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), and because, since *utprekṣā* involves a process of identification (*adhyavasāya*), the swallowing up (*nigaraṇa*) of the object is appropriate therein. Nor should it be argued that, if the act of impelling and so forth lack the status of being the object—and thus the cause—another cause must be sought.

In the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that the spreading [of darkness] takes the form of smearing, the cause is its becoming a mass of foam and sandalwood paste at the edges. In the poetic fancy that the pervasion [of darkness] is the anointing of the women who are the quarters of the sky, the cause is its whitening them; thus, because another cause is clearly present, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśikā*, in stating that in such instances as "Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium," the spreading and so forth are imagined as being of the nature of smearing, has likewise relied upon the position that in examples of poetic fancy regarding the essential nature of an attribute (*dharmasvarūpotprekṣā*), there is only the fancy of identity (*tādātmyotprekṣaṇa*).

Similarly, in such instances as "The moon, as it were, kisses the face of the night," the connection between the moon and that which is called the "face"—namely, the beginning [of the night]—which has been identified with the face of the night, is imagined (utprekṣyate) as being a kiss. In the verse "vṛttānupūrve ca" ("round and well-proportioned"), one should understand that there is an imagination of identity (*tādātmyotprekṣā*) between the effortless creation of the remaining limbs and their being preceded by effort.

Furthermore, the common attribute (*anugāmidharma*) is not intended merely in its capacity as a shared quality; rather, like the common attribute in a simile (*upamā*), it is intended through all possible modes, such as the relationship of the original image and its reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*).
And so, for example:
In the verse: "She, wearing a garment with the hue of the rising sun, slightly bending under the weight of her breasts,

was like a moving, sprouting creeper bent down by an abundance of flower clusters," there is an identification [of the woman with the creeper] through the superimposition (adhyavasāya) of non-difference based on the relation between the original object and its reflection.

In the verse, "Mounted upon the elephant of youth, she is the abode of the goddess of grace, like the embodied Fortune of the conquest of the three worlds of Manojā," there is a connection with another attribute because the attribute, through an identification based on the employment of different compounds, is common to both the subject at hand and that which is not. Likewise, in the case of "As if with her fingers," there is no lack of definition (avyāpti), for since the attribute is uncommon to both the subject at hand and that which is not through an identification based on a difference in grammatical construction, the connection with another attribute is easily established. Nor is there a lack of definition in the case of "bhūyastarāṇi."

In that case, it is because there is a causal relation with another property (dharma) that is both apprehended (*upātta*) and implied (*ākṣipta*). For in that instance—where there is a poetic superimposition (*utprekṣā*) that the sky is composed of a mass of stars formed by mice moving through the midst of the twilight fire within the lunar form—the property residing in the stars, namely their state of being sparse or dense across various nights, serves as the apprehended cause (*nimitta*). By means of this cause, there is an implication of the property residing in the moon: its possession of increase and decrease that conforms to those states of sparseness and density.

And this is another distinction: in *dharmyutprekṣā* (poetic fancy on the substratum), based on the connection with the attributes of another thing, the locus of the attribute belongs to the *viṣayin* (the object of the fancy). This being the case, wherever a cause-attribute (*nimittabhūto dharmaḥ*) is not explicitly mentioned, in every such instance one must seek an attribute that can be imagined as relating both to the other thing (the *anyapadārtha*) and to the *viṣaya* (the subject of the fancy). In the example "The sky seems to rain collyrium," according to the view that the act of raining is fancied as residing in the sky, [the attribute of raining must be sought as belonging to the sky].

The common ground for the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) that darkness is pervading as far as the earth’s limits—likened to the raining of collyrium—is its quality of making all things dark and dense. However, when one conceives of the action of raining collyrium as having the sky as its agent in order to pervade the darkness, the grounds for this are the total and thick darkening of all objects. In the same way, in such expressions as "the shore of the ocean of passion," one should infer the underlying grounds, such as its capacity to cause agitation.

However, where a connection with the subject (*viṣaya*) or the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is not directly perceived—even though a property (*dharma*) has been introduced as a cause (*nimitta*)—in some cases that connection must be established by producing the state of being that [cause] or its likeness in some other property belonging to the subject; in other cases, it must be established by producing the state of being the locus of those properties or their likeness in either the subject or the meaning of another word.

In some cases, it is by means of both [the object and the subject] joined together; in some cases, by the implication of another property (*dharma*) brought about by the property already expressed. In that context, the production of the similarity of the cause (*nimitta*) for another property—just as in a simile (*upamā*), the commonality of a property is produced through modes such as the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*)—has been demonstrated. Likewise, the production of the similarity of the locus of the property for either the object (*viṣaya*) or the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*) occurs through the device of paronomasia (*śleṣa*) and other figures. Among these, the production of the similarity of the locus of the property for the object by means of paronomasia is as follows:

"In this [beauty], I imagine even sages were deluded; for the great Bhṛgu resorted to her mountain-like breasts, while Vyāsa, worthy of composing the *Mahābhārata*, took refuge at her thighs, his mouth delighted by the various *āradas*. Here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the delusion of sages such as Bhṛgu directed toward Damayantī, the cause—namely, the act of resorting to her breasts and so forth—is not actually situated in the object (the sages), but rather in the mountains and other things. Its presence in the object is established through the pun (*śleṣa*) on the words "Bhṛgu" and so forth. An example using Apahnuti (Concealment) is as follows:
Under the guise of the *kiṃśuka* trees, the fire seems to climb the tree on all sides and gaze upon the forest, both burnt and unburnt.

In this case, regarding the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) concerning the action of displaying the burnt and unburnt forest within the object that is the forest fire, the cause is the climbing of trees. Yet even that is not located in the object itself, but rather in the *kiṃśuka* flowers. Although there is no actual climbing of trees there, nevertheless, the very act of those [flowers] taking refuge in the tree is determined as "climbing" for the sake of the metaphor; and thus, through that concealment (*apahnuti*), by establishing the identity of the object with the *kiṃśuka* flower, the connection between the attributes is accomplished.
The production of the identity of the substratum of the quality with another referent through *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is as follows:
"The face of this woman, who is pregnant with longing, has a pale luster;
truly, I think it is now 'Rāja' (the King), since it desires to enjoy the earth."

In this instance, the desire to enjoy the earth is the cause for the metaphorical identification (*utprekṣā*) of the face with the moon; yet that [desire] resides in the object [the face], not in the moon, which serves as the other referent (*anyapadārtha*). Therefore, by means of the pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *rājā* (king), the moon is established as the substratum of the attribute, thereby fulfilling the requirement that the attribute belongs to it.
The combination of both—establishing the identity of the causal attribute with another attribute, and establishing the identity of the subject with the substratum of that attribute—is as follows:
"By virtue of being encircled by a seamless silken cloth formed by the coils of the Lord of Serpents slipping off due to the force of his drawing [the ocean], [the ocean]..."
At whose footbase the Mandākinī long encircled him, as if to quickly allay the pain caused by churning.

Here, within the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the cessation of the pain from churning the ocean—which is the object (*viṣaya*) of the Mandākinī—the cause for the encircling at the base of the feet is the identification [of that base] with the base of a peripheral mountain through *śleṣa* (pun). Furthermore, the identification of the object with its attributes (*taddharmāśrayatādrūpya*) is achieved through *apahnuti* (concealment), wherein the locus of the stated attribute—namely, the slough (*nirmoka*)—is concealed by the word *pariveṣa*, which signifies a pretext. Thus, it is accomplished by both means acting in combination.

The accomplishment of the connection of another property with the object [of comparison] is [the definition]. As for the implication of another property by means of a property already apprehended, that has indeed been demonstrated. Therefore, since this [definition]—namely, "from the connection with another property"—is followed by all types of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), it is not non-pervasive (*avyāpta*) anywhere; thus, everything is consistent.

The author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* has thus demonstrated its classification: Utprekṣā (Poetic Fancy) is of two kinds, namely, expressed (*vācyā*) and suggested (*pratīyamānā*). It is expressed when words such as *iva* are employed; it is suggested when they are not employed. Among these, the expressed variety is fourfold, based on the objects of determination being genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or substance (*dravya*), all of which are non-contextual (*aprakṛta*). Each of these is further divided into two types—consisting of the attribution of existence or non-existence—resulting in eight varieties.

Among those, there are sixteen varieties based on the cause (*nimitta*) having the form of a quality or an action. Furthermore, by means of the presence or absence of the expressed cause (*upātta*) and the unexpressed cause (*anupātta*), there are thirty-two types. Within these, since each can take the form of a poetic fancy regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*), the cause (*hetu*), or the result (*phala*), there are ninety-six varieties. Among these, the poetic fancy regarding the essential nature is itself [the base category]; therefore, the fancies regarding the cause and the result must be subtracted from it. Consequently, sixteen varieties are reduced. Moreover, it is impossible for the cause not to be expressed even in the poetic fancies regarding the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, when they function as causes or results.

Consequently, twenty-four varieties are fewer [than the total]; thus, including the *svarūpotprekṣā* (metaphor of essential nature), there are thirty-two varieties without omission. Since *hetūtprekṣā* (metaphor of cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (metaphor of effect) each have twelve varieties, there are fifty-six varieties of *vācyotprekṣā* (expressed metaphor).
