The calculation is exactly the same for *pratīyamānotprekṣā* (implied metaphor) as well. In that regard, even within *svarūpotprekṣā*, the non-mention of a ground (*nimitta*) is not possible; this constitutes a distinction.

Consequently, there are sixteen varieties of *svarūpotprekṣā* (imagination of the essential nature) therein; and since *hetūtprekṣā* (imagination of cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (imagination of effect) each have twelve varieties as previously stated, there are forty varieties of *gamyotprekṣā* (imagination where the suggested meaning is understood). Thus, when combined in this manner, there are ninety-six varieties of *utprekṣā*.

Vidyānātha, however, while accepting that a substance may also be conceived as having a cause or an effect, has disregarded the enumeration of its varieties based on whether the cause is unexpressed and whether it takes the form of a quality or an action—arguing that such a classification is like naming a child before it is born and does not bring about aesthetic charm. Consequently, he has presented a different classification: there are twenty-four varieties of *utprekṣā* when the cause is expressed (*vācyā*), because in the case where the cause is unexpressed (*anupāttanimittā*), eight varieties are subtracted due to the absence of the distinctions based on the cause being a quality or an action.

The imaginative conceits (*utprekṣā*) regarding cause and effect each have an increase in varieties due to their respective subdivisions. Thus, there are fifty-six varieties of expressed (*vācyā*) imaginative conceit. In the case of implied (*pratīyamānā*) imaginative conceit, however, even the imaginative conceit of essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*) has sixteen modes; for since the non-mention of a ground (*nimitta*) is possible there, eight of its subdivisions are eliminated. Consequently, there are forty-eight varieties of implied imaginative conceit. Thus, taken together, there are one hundred and four varieties of imaginative conceit. Now, examples are shown by way of illustration alone. An example of an imaginative conceit of essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*) where the ground is a quality (*guṇa*) that is explicitly mentioned (*upātta*) is as follows:
May that moon protect you— curved like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk— which rests upon the head of the Enemy of Smara, glowing tawny with fire,
and which shines as if it were the water of his own Mandākinī river, sprinkled there every day.
"Released from its calyx like a sprout white as crystal.

Here, because the word *aṅkura* (sprout) is a generic term (*jātiśabda*), a generic nature (*jāti*) is the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The quality (*guṇa*) of curvature (*kauṭilya*) is the apprehended cause (*nimitta*). In this same way, instances of poetic fancy regarding the nature of a generic entity (*jātibhāvasvarūpotprekṣā*) where the action is the apprehended cause should be illustrated.
An example of poetic fancy regarding the nature of a quality (*guṇabhāvasvarūpotprekṣā*) where the action is not the apprehended cause is as follows:

"The beeswax applied to his lower lip for the sake of the glow of the red lac-dye shone as if eager to dwell right there, having cast aside its honey-like sweetness in favor of that [lip] which shares the nature of nectar.

Here, eagerness (*autsukya*), a quality (*guṇa*), is the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The action of "adhering" (*lagana*) is employed as the cause. In this same manner, a poetic fancy regarding the essential nature of a quality (*guṇabhāvasvarūpotprekṣā*), where the cause is an employed quality, should also be illustrated.

An example of *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature) based on the cause (*nimitta*) of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*) that have been assumed [as belonging to the subject] is as follows:
"Then, as the pair [of Garuḍa and Aruṇa] flew toward the invocation of Indra’s weapon, they were reddened by the thick rays of twilight;
they fell apart, smeared with blood streaming from their hearts pierced by the sharp arrow."

Here, the act of smearing with blood is the object of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The quality of redness (*āruṇya*) is the apprehended cause (*nimitta*). In this manner, one should also cite examples of the poetic fancy of the nature of an action (*kriyābhāva-svarūpa-utprekṣā*), where the cause is an action that has been apprehended.
An example of the poetic fancy of the nature of a substance (*dravya-bhāva-rūpa-utprekṣā*) where the cause is an apprehended action is as follows:
"Each single [quality] possesses marvelous merit and shakes off all defects..."
Having abandoned one man and approached another, she was leaving him;
he, whose lotus-feet were worshipped by the world, spoke to her as she fell from the embrace of Acyuta like a lotus-stalk fallen from between his arms.

Here, because of the unity of the lotus (*paṅkaja*) and its substantial nature, it is imagined as a substance (*dravya*). The action of "not abandoning" (*aparityajana*), which is both expressed (*upātta*) and implied (*upagamya*), serves as the cause (*nimitta*). In this way, one should provide examples of the imagination of the nature of a substance (*dravyabhāva-svarūpotprekṣā*) where the cause is an expressed quality (*guṇa*). Thus, eight varieties of the imagination of the nature of genus (*jāti-bhāva-svarūpotprekṣā*) and so forth, with expressed causes, have been accounted for within the category of the conceit of being (*bhāvābhimāna*).

An example of the imagination of the nature of genus (*jāti-bhāva-svarūpotprekṣā*) with an unexpressed cause (*anupātta-nimitta*) is as follows: "When [the trees] have long relied upon a mass of wood as a shelter against rain and sun, and [the clouds] have arisen..."
"Among these young *tārākavaka* mushrooms, I perceive one that has blossomed as the moon.
Here, the genus (*jāti*) of the mushroom is the object of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The unmentioned quality (*guṇa*), such as whiteness and roundness, serves as the cause (*nimitta*).
An example of a poetic fancy regarding the essential nature (*svarūpa*) where the cause—the quality—is unmentioned is as follows:

"This lord of kings, who has conquered all his enemies, shines like grace incarnate among all his dependents. Here, the quality of *prasāda* (serenity/grace) is the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The grounds for this—such as his being a great bestower and his being pleasant to serve—are not explicitly stated.
An example of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) involving the existence of an action whose cause is unappropriated (*anupātta*) is as follows:
"The darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium. Like a gaze directed toward a wicked man, my vision has become fruitless."
Here, an action is the object of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The cause, such as pervasion (*vyāpana*), is not explicitly mentioned.
An example of the poetic fancy of substance or state where the cause is not mentioned is as follows:
"Whose form Umā beholds in the mirror while remaining within his body..."
"...as if another Ardhanārīśvara were produced from the two halves [of the original].

Here, a distinct substance in the form of another Ardhanārīśvara, produced from the other half, is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*). The unstated cause for this is the presence of the inverted forms of the male and female bodies within the reflection. Even though there is a poetic imagination of another Ardhanārīśvara, because the actual Ardhanārīśvara is in fact one, its status as a poetic imagination of a substance (*dravyotprekṣā*) is not contradictory. Or, for example:
"In the interior of a certain lake, the sky shone as if reflected..."
"In the water supported by reflections that are clearly manifest through the guise of the moats...

Here, the substance of Devapurī is the object of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). The excellence of its beauty residing in Kuṇḍinapura is the unmentioned cause (*nimitta*). Thus, four types with unmentioned causes have been illustrated. By considering the distinctions of the cause into the forms of quality (*guṇa*) and action (*kriyā*), its eightfold nature is to be inferred. In this way, sixteen varieties of poetic fancy regarding genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which possess the conceit of a state of being (*bhāvābhimānavatī*), are established.

Alternatively, one may consider it according to the method stated by Vidyānātha, without taking into account the distinction between the qualities and actions that serve as the causes [of the poetic fancy], because when the cause is not explicitly mentioned, such a formal classification is impossible. For example, in the verse "He sported within the depths of the lake," it could equally be said that the cause is the quality of possessing unsurpassed beauty, or that the cause is the action of partaking in unsurpassed beauty. Therefore, there are only twelve varieties.

Now, regarding the fancies of essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*) involving the conceit of non-existence: these are fancies of the non-existence of genus, quality, or action, where the cause is an explicitly mentioned quality, as follows:

"I behold this body of yours as if it were free from saffron-dust, your lower lip as if free from red lac, and your pair of eyes as if free from the application of collyrium—by means of their very natural qualities.

Here, the absences of saffron-powder (a genus), red lac-dye (a quality), and the application of collyrium (an action) are poetically imagined (*utprekṣyante*). Their causes are the naturally acquired yellow, reddish, and dark-blue colors, which are explicitly mentioned (*upāttāḥ*). Among these, examples where an action serves as the cause should also be cited.
An example of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on the absence of a substance that serves as the cause for an action already undertaken is as follows:
"Having beheld your face upon the earth, which is like the risen full moon,
I perceive the sky as being without a moon, due to its loss of splendor."

Here, the non-existence of the moon as a substance (*dravya*) is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*). The act of "avoiding" (*varjana-kriyā*) is the expressed cause (*nimitta*). Likewise, examples of the poetic imagination of the non-existence of a substance based on an expressed quality (*guṇa-nimitta*) should be cited. These same two verses—*idaṃ viśālākṣi vibhāvayāmi* and *padavīm amṛtāndhasām*—serve as examples of the poetic imagination of the non-existence of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, where the cause is unexpressed (*anupātta-nimitta*), provided that the fourth quarters are read as follows: [the first verse ends with] *...vibhāvayāmi* and [the second with] *...amṛtāndhasām*.

Thus, even those *svarūpotprekṣās* (imaginings of essential nature) characterized by the conceit of non-existence (*abhāvābhimānavatyaḥ*)—following the previously mentioned method—are shown to be approximately thirty-two or twenty-four varieties, being sixteen or twelve respectively. Among these, in some cases there is an identification (*tādātmyena adhyavasāyaḥ*) of the object of imagination (*viṣayin*), as in the verse beginning "May that moon protect you. In other cases, however, it is through association (*saṃsargitayā*), as in the verse beginning "entrusted for the sake of the brilliance of the lac-dye"; this variety involving eagerness (*autsukya*) should also be understood. Now, for *hetūtprekṣā* (imaginings based on a cause): an imagining of a genus (*jāti-hetūtprekṣā*) caused by a quality (*guṇa*) that has been adopted is as follows:
"The bird, bearing the mark of many *śaivala* plants and possessing a *rudrākṣa* bee, went again to Nala’s hand, as if from the delusion that it was a *kokanada* lotus of a lake.

Here, the delusion that it was a *kokanada* lotus is imagined as the cause for the action of reaching Nala’s hand; that very action of reaching is the occasion [for the figure]. In subsequent instances of causal imagination (*hetūtprekṣā*) as well, the result alone is everywhere the occasion. In this same way, an imagination of a cause based on a quality (*guṇahetūtprekṣā*) should also be understood when the occasion is a quality.
An *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) based on qualities and the cause of action is as follows:
"By Vivasvat, the cows whose other name is 'eyes' were surely led away along with his own thousand cattle; therefore, this blindness of people is indeed due to that [loss], and not by darkness."

Here, the act of seeing is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the cause for the quality of blindness. In this manner, other instances of the poetic figure of *kriyāhetūtprekṣā* (poetic imagination of an action as a cause) based on an action may also be cited.
An example of *kriyānimittā dravyahetūtprekṣā* (poetic imagination of a substance as a cause based on an action) is as follows:
"The heart of that learned man, who partakes in pure deeds, is eternally purified indeed."
"As if flowing from the sky like a stream of water, [the Ganges] flows from the lotus-foot of the Universal Form (Viśvamūrti) as He dwells within.

Here, the substance *gaṅgā* (the Ganges) is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the cause for the action of the wind. In this manner, causal poetic imagination (*hetūtprekṣā*) based on qualities (*guṇanimittā*) should also be illustrated.
Thus have been illustrated the causal poetic imaginations characterized by the attribution of sentience (*bhāvābhimānavatyaḥ*).
Then those possessed of the conceit of non-existence said: "Just as the sun is absent at night and the moon by day,
that Lord has created heat and fame on earth, which remain perpetually present."
"When the sun has set, how much [smaller] is the moon in its place?
Thinking thus with disregard, the bed of lotuses surely closes.
"From the intensity of her playing the lute, her right breast trembled."
"...not seeing the other [moon], which was hidden by the expanse of its [the mountain's] peak.

Here, in the first verse, the absence of the two substances—the sun and the moon—is imagined as the cause. In the second and third verses, the absences of the qualities and actions—respect and looking—are [imagined]; however, the actions of creation, merging, and trembling are the actual causes (*nimitta*). In this way, instances of *hetūtprekṣā* (causal fancy) where the cause is an absence (*abhāva*) based on a quality (*guṇa*) should also be illustrated. Thus, the sixteen varieties of *hetūtprekṣā* have been shown. Now, the *phalotprekṣā*s (fancies regarding effects):
In those palaces where the spreading radiance of the gazelle-eyed women’s faces is so clever at mocking the moonlight,
the moon wanders through the nights as if for their sake alone.
"Stretching out its hands toward the lattice-work,
it gazes upon your gold of such hue;
having emerged from your treasury-house, it surely dwells at sacred bathing-places."
"The sun set out toward the northern quarter, the birthplace of the finest horses, as if to turn back those standing in their chariots like ancient mounts.
"To the thousand oceans of milk, to the peak of Mount Kailāsa,"
"Surely the fame of Pratāparudra has been spread in all directions.

In these verses, respectively, the genus (jāti), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and substance (dravya)—namely, the face, radiance, whiteness of color, the turning [of the tide], the ocean, and Mount Kailāsa—are poetically imagined (utprekṣyante) as the results (phala). The actions of wandering, dwelling at holy sites, setting out, and spreading are the causes (nimitta). In this way, examples based on qualities (guṇanimitta) may also be cited.
An example of the poetic imagination of a result (phalotprekṣā) involving the personification of a non-existence (abhāvābhimānavatī) is as follows:
"Desiring to attain similarity with your face, the moon surely plunges into the ocean to rid itself of the mud of its dark spot.
"Those who are indifferent toward the female deer, their kinswomen acquired through dwelling in the forest,"
"The wives of the enemies of the Lord of the Trilinga country turn their faces away from the play of his glances;
the Siddha women, sporting in the bowers of the boundary mountains, offer imagined libations of moonlight as they sing of the playful glory of Śrī Vīrarudra, as if unable to touch the darkness."
"The dust arising from the victorious expedition of King Vīrarudra stands as if the sky were non-existent, having covered the entire sphere of the directions.

In these verses, the absences of mud, enmity, touch, and space are imagined as the results [of the king's expedition]. Among them, turning away [from the enemy] is one quality (*guṇa*); the others are actions (*kriyā*). Thus, the distinctions based on qualities and actions as causes should be illustrated. In this way, sixteen types of *phalotprekṣā* (imaginations of result) have been shown. This concludes the section on the imagination of wind-storms (*vātyotprekṣā*).

Now, examples of *gamyotprekṣā* (suggested fancy) are illustrated by way of a mere direction: "Here, the moon, supporting the earth with its rays—which are like arrows for the destruction of the crows of darkness—fled toward the western quarter out of fear of being slaughtered by [the sun]. Upon reaching it, the female pigeons that are the stars flew up."

Here, by means of the movement of the sun's rays—which have been released by the sun and take the form of hawks that destroy the crows of darkness—the sun’s act of sporting in the hunt, characterized by the swooping of hawks, is imagined; thus, first, there is a *kriyāsvarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy on the nature of an action). From that [imagined action], the moon’s fear is imagined as the cause for its departure to another quarter of the sky; thus, there is another *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy on a cause).

Therefore, the attainment of that [state] by those who have reached the further shore is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as the cause for their non-appearance in various places, being determined as their act of flying away; thus, this is another instance of *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause). All these [varieties] are to be understood through implication (*gamyāḥ*), because of the absence of words such as *iva*. Other [varieties] should likewise be understood by oneself, since they can be inferred through the previously mentioned modes in the absence of words like *nūnam* and so forth. Furthermore, since it is possible for the very verses cited earlier to serve as examples of implied poetic fancy (*gamyotprekṣā*) by not employing words such as *nūnam*, the implied poetic fancies have not been cited separately and in their entirety.

This, however, is being considered: whether the poetic figures of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding genus (*jāti*) and substance (*dravya*) are possible in implied (*gamyā*) *utprekṣās*, or not. If one holds the position that they are possible, [one may cite]:
"The rays of the sun that has set, having fallen away and being without support, truly became the market-stalls for saffron in the evening ointment-shops."

An example [of this] should be provided by such verses as: "That which, under the guise of a moat-enclosure, was not within the reach of capture by enemies, has attained the name 'coil' (kuṇḍalā), being as difficult as the difficult arguments (*phakkikā*) in the *Bhāṣya* spoken by the Serpent (Patañjali). This is the view of some who favor such [a usage]. However, the position is that for the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva*, these two [types of *utprekṣā*] are not possible. It is precisely with this intention that he stated in the section on *gamyotprekṣā*: "In this case, *svarūpotprekṣā* generally does not occur. What, then, is the figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*) for these two in his view? It is simply *rūpaka* (metaphor). For this very reason—

"In this verse— *pīyūṣaprasṛtirnavā...* [the body of the moon rises on the first day of the fortnight like a fresh handful of nectar for the gods, a sickle for the destruction of darkness, a lotus-stalk trembling from the sorrowful faces of those distracted by the celestial Gaṅgā, and an indescribable double manifestation of the god of love’s bow]— the author, by citing this as an example of *mālārūpaka* (chain metaphor), has accepted that there is indeed *rūpaka* (metaphor) even in expressions such as *svargaṅgāvimanaska*. Therefore, having set aside *jāti-utprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on genus) and *dravya-utprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on substance), the category of *gamyotprekṣā* (implied poetic fancy) should be enumerated."

This other point must also be understood: in *dharmyutprekṣās* (similes of the substratum), the cause is a quality (*dharma*) that follows both the superimposed object (*viṣayin*) and the actual object (*viṣaya*); whereas in *dharmotprekṣās* (similes of the quality), the cause is a quality that follows both the locus of the superimposed object (*viṣayyāśraya*) and the actual object. Therefore, in examples such as "She bore a creeper-like body" (*uvāha yā tanulatā*), the position that "purity" (*vaimalya*) is the cause is not tenable. This is because that quality of the body—which serves as the constituent of the reflected image (*pratibimba*) necessary for the possibility of identification (*tādātmya-sambhāvanā*)—is not a quality of the [actual] object (*viṣaya*).

Since all those who state the definition beginning with "where, through connection with another property... have treated only the property of the *viṣayin* (the subject of imagination) as the cause [of the poetic figure], enough of this excessive detail. Here we say:

"In the case of *utprekṣā*, the division of the *viṣayin* into the nature of genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth, which was not previously seen, possesses no such beauty as that of the *upamāna* (standard of comparison) in *upamā*."
In the absence of that [rasa], the figures of speech (alaṅkāras) do not merit a formal classification merely by their existence;
otherwise, its domain too would have to be divided in the same manner.

Even the division of *dharma* (the common property) into qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*) is not a cause of beauty, as in the case of *upamā* (simile); for that [division] too is deficient because it does not combine both the presence and the absence of those properties.
As if out of a mental apprehension to behold her beloved, her two eyes longingly turned inward;
yet even these two lacked the power to grasp that object which stood directly before them.
"In those [verses] such as, 'While they were looking with eyes like decorative blue lotuses, did their two ears become dejected?

For those whose hearts were fixed on the sight [of him], their ears did not hear the words of the fawn-eyed women,' we clearly perceive [the function of suggestion] even in the case of qualities (guṇa), actions (kriyā), and states of being (bhāva)."
The basis for the brilliance [of the expression] is its status as the cause (nimitta) in poetic fancy (utprekṣā).

In this regard, in the first example, the cause for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that the eyes have entered within in order to behold the beloved situated in the heart is the incapacity to perceive external objects. In the second, the cause for the fancy that the sense of hearing is intent upon looking [within] is the absence of the act of hearing. Likewise:

"These trees, occupying the center of the sacrificial altars of sages who practice meditation in the *vīrāsana* posture, shine as if they too have ascended to the heights of yoga, due to their immobility in the windless air."
There are many such examples regarding non-existence (*abhāva*) as a cause.
Furthermore, the various types of combination (*samuccaya*) among causes must be enumerated:
both existence and non-existence, when combined, also function as a cause.
"I recognize these white rows of swans as the fleeting grains of the very form of your fame;
having flown up, it is fitting that they have fallen and now float about, purifying the waters of the streams on all sides.
"Is it not worthy for the assembly of stars to belong to the Night? Is there any impropriety in this, that their Lord, whose mass of splendor is so countable, is not seen by them?"
"The chest of the Moon is clearly made of stone, possessing the luster of shimmering black stone; for even when pierced by these two [the sun and moon], alas, it does not melt quickly.
In many such instances, who could possibly conceal the fact that the presence of multiple causes is observed within poetic fancies (*utprekṣā*)?

In the first example, the two causes for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that the rows of swans are like tufts of fame are both the quality of whiteness and the action of floating over the victory. In the second, the two causes for the fancy that the chest of the Lord of Stars (the Moon) is made of stone are both its stone-like luster and its lack of fluidity. Furthermore: "Since even genus and substance can serve as the cause in a poetic fancy, one should know this enumeration of causes to be extensive."
"Your speech shall bestow upon Droṇa there a gift consisting of the enchanting power of good fortune attainable through luck;
it will be as beautiful as an island-lamp due to the brilliance of medicinal herbs, with the clouds resting upon its peak appearing like collyrium.

Here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of the palace of the demon Bāṇa being a lamp, the light of the medicinal plants and trees growing upon it and the clouds situated above acting as collyrium are the causes; thus, the causality of a genus (*jāti*) is observed.
"In the nights, the palace shines with the moon gleaming upon its summit, as if Śrīkaṇṭha himself were present there for the sake of protecting his devotees.
In this passage, the moon gleaming on the summit is the *nimitta* (the cause or ground) for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that Bāṇāsura’s palace is Śiva. Likewise—

With an ornament like the sun, a smile with white radiance, lips red as Mars, a gaze gentle as Mercury, hips heavy as Jupiter, a necklace white as Venus, feet slow-moving as Saturn, eyes blooming like blue lotuses, and a form that was the banner of victory over the three worlds, she appeared as if composed of the planets themselves.

In this instance, regarding the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that Vāsavadattā consists of all the planets, the cause is the ornaments and so forth which have assumed the form of those respective planets through *śleṣa* (paronomasia); thus, we observe that a combination of genus (*jāti*), action (*kriyā*), and quality (*guṇa*) functions as the cause. Nor should it be argued that in the examples cited, the connection with "radiance" (*dīpti*) and so on is the cause, and that this [connection] is merely a quality (*guṇa*) in the case of *śleṣa*; for if that were so, then even in cases such as "having reached such a state of emaciation," the connection with the action of "going" (*gamana*) and so forth would likewise be the cause, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that action (*kriyā*) could not function as a cause at all.

Furthermore, one must not say that in examples such as "na ca tathāpi bhāsvatālaṅkāreṇa," where figures like *alaṅkāra* (ornament) have attained the form of a *sīri* (plough) through *śleṣa* (punning), these [attained forms] are the cause [of the poetic figure], and not the unqualified genus (*jāti*) or substance (*dravya*). For if that were the case, then even in instances such as "kapālenonmuktaḥ sphaṭikadhavalenāṅkura iva," it would follow that only the state of being qualified by "the sprout released from a skull" and so forth is to be the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), and not the unqualified genus and so on; this would result in the inconsistency of the classification of the *viṣayin* (the object of comparison) according to its form as a genus and so forth.

Therefore, just as in the case of the possessor of the object (*viṣayin*), a division must also be made for the cause (*nimitta*) into four types based on its form—such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—and further into eight types by each being either existent or non-existent; thus, this division appears deficient. Moreover: "That which was asserted—that there is nowhere any possibility of the non-mention of the cause in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*)—that too is not correct."
"Did his gaze sink into the nectar [of her face], or did it remain fixed within the moon of her face? Did it perhaps dwell inside her breasts?
His sight finally left her waist, as if out of fear of stumbling upon something even more slender.
In this verse, while the cause is being poetically imagined (utprekṣā), the actual motive for sinking and clinging is not stated.
"That effect, perceived as a vision, is the long-delayed abandonment of face and breasts.

This might be argued: "In this case, the two metaphors (*utprekṣā*) of 'bathing' and 'clinging' have the abandonment of face and breasts as their delayed consequences, and those two [consequences] are fit to be the causes for the bathing and clinging. True. Nevertheless, this is not a metaphor of causality (*hetūtprekṣā*). For a metaphor of causality does not consist merely in the metaphorical imagination of something capable of being a cause; rather, it is the metaphorical imagination [of something] *as* a cause. As in the verse: "This is that very spot where, while searching for you... Here, indeed, the ablative case does not express causality. Likewise—
In the verse, "Alas, her two cheek-plates, having become such as they are,

have reached such a state of emaciation as if they were not seeing one another," the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the word *apaśyantāv iva* (as if not seeing) expresses the causality within the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that the failure to see each other is the cause for their reaching such emaciation.

"That the heart of Damana’s sister did not burst asunder under the weight of the fever of love and fly away was due to that very offense; for her dense, full breasts, by their firm constraint, held it back and bound it fast."

In this passage, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the two breasts acting as a restraint (*yantraṇā*) because they prevent the heart from bursting and flying out due to the heat of love. Here, the word *pratibadhnati* (restraining), which signifies the act of obstructing flight, effectively establishes the cause for the non-flying. In such cases, the mention of the result—which serves as the motive—is indeed necessary; otherwise, the syntactic connection with the ablative case (*pañcamī*) and so forth would be impossible.
Where no word expressing causality exists, even that which is capable of becoming a cause is merely a poetic fancy of essential nature (*svarūpotprekṣā*).
For this very reason, the author of the *Alaṅkārasarvasva* stated:

If it is argued that in the verse, "When he, having obtained consecration in this [kingdom], desired to stand firm against his enemies, the earth trembled as if overwhelmed by the fear of its wealth being plundered," although the cause of the trembling—the state of being overwhelmed (*vihvalitatva*), which is the object of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*)—is capable of functioning as the cause for the trembling even without words explicitly expressing that causality, this is nevertheless cited as an example of *svarūpotprekṣā* (fancy regarding the essential nature); we say: not so. For, in this way—

In the verse: "O Smara, do you remember the binding with the cords of my girdle whenever there was a slip of the tongue regarding one's lineage, or the lashings from the blue lotuses used as ear-ornaments when [your] eyes were bitten by falling filaments?"—here, *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause) would not be possible, because of the absence of words expressing the causality inherent in the act of remembering. Nor is this a desirable conclusion.
"Have you not done anything displeasing to me, nor have I acted contrary to your will?
Why then is your sight not granted to Ratī as she laments, and for no reason at all?

Following this statement, the introduction of this verse is appropriate only if it intends a poetic conjecture (*hetūtprekṣā*) regarding the reason why her sight is not granted—namely, that it is because of the recollection of an offense previously committed by her.

If, however, even in the absence of words expressing causality, a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) regarding a cause could arise through internal consistency between what precedes and what follows, then here too—due to the mention of a third poetic fancy—it is more logical to assume that, just as the fear of stumbling is the cause for the abandonment of the middle after a long time, so too the two initial fancies have "long-delayed abandonment of the face and breasts" and "immersion" respectively as their understood causes.

For even where there is a word expressing the nature of a fruit (*phala*) in relation to a result, there too, disregarding the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) of the fruit due to contextual propriety, the acceptance of a poetic fancy of the cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) is observed. As for example:
"That which his heart whispers to you in secret, that very thing his face proclaims openly;
this is indeed the fitting conduct of friendship between the moon—the friend of the flower-armed god (Kāma)—and the sacrifice of that [king]."

For here, by means of the word *tat* (that), which reflects upon the disclosure of the secret counsel formed in the heart, there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *sakhyaucitī* (the propriety of friendship), which ends in the suffix *ṣyañ* denoting the object of the action; thus, it is understood from the words that the disclosure of the secret is the work of the Moon—the friend of the God of Love who is the enemy of Mukha. Nevertheless, in this case, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) consists solely in [the disclosure] being the cause for the friendship, and not in the disclosure of the secret being the fruit of the friendship.

This is because the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that "friendship was formed with the aim of revealing the secret" is inconsistent; for a fancy regarding an effect cannot be sustained by the mere fact of being an effect without a stated purpose, just as a fancy regarding a cause cannot be sustained by the mere fact of being a cause. Thus, even where a word explicitly expresses the causality of a cause, it is sometimes observed that one must accept a fancy regarding an effect (*phalotprekṣā*), setting aside the fancy regarding the cause due to contextual propriety (*aucitya*). For example:
"Since the chest of the fair-browed daughter of Vidarbha was indeed agitated by flowers that had become the arrows of Love..."
"While she was wiping away the blood from her garland, she wiped it upon them, having driven a needle-point into one of them.

Here, although the suffix *ktvā* exists—which expresses the state of being prior in time and thus functions as a cause for the act of wiping—this act of driving in the needle is not to be imagined (*utprekṣya*) as the cause for the wiping of the enmity. Rather, the driving in of the needle is for the sake of wiping the enmity; thus, the wiping of the enmity itself is to be imagined as the result (*phala*). This is because that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) is what must be imagined, whether [the cause] is established or unestablished; and furthermore, because in this case, the imagination is possible precisely because the action is undertaken with that [result] as its purpose. Or, for example:
"The creation of the lotus by your hand is merely a preliminary sketch (*hastalekha*) for the sake of creating this very [face]," so says the Creator regarding the fawn-eyed woman.

Here, although the instrumental case is present in the phrase "by that creation of the lotus," the act of creating the lotus is not imagined as the cause for manifesting the quality of being a preliminary sketch belonging to the Creator’s act of creating the lotus; rather, the imagining of the creation of the lotus as a preliminary sketch is for the purpose of manifesting that [quality], and thus the manifestation itself is to be imagined as the result. What more need be said?
In certain instances, it is observed that a word which expresses the nature of a cause must, by propriety, be accepted as expressing its effect; for example:
"Beholding the breasts of the slender-limbed maiden, the youth shakes his head, as if uprooting her gaze that is submerged between them."

In this case, although the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed [by Pāṇini 3.2.126] in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), it can somehow be established that the fruit (*phala*) is also a cause by virtue of being the intended object (*uddeśyatā*). Thus, one must accept the metaphorical attribution (*utprekṣā*) of the fruit. And so, if even when disregarding the indication of being a fruit or the like, one should accept a metaphorical attribution of cause (*hetūtprekṣā*) and so forth according to propriety (*aucitya*), then what need is there to mention that one must follow propriety in the absence of contradictory words? In this manner, by this same principle, the non-mention of a cause in other instances should also be inferred as possible. Furthermore:
"Just as there is the state of having an expressed cause (*upātta-nimittatva*) and the state of having an unexpressed cause (*anupātta-nimittatā*),"
"It exists in each individually, and likewise it is seen when combined.
For example:
"The lion, son of Siṃhikā, perceived the sage-tree in the forest, which was budding and possessed a white luster, as being him [the moon]."
"Vomiting, as it were, the collection of lunar digits devoured by the peak of the waning fortnight.

Here, when the sage-tree (*munidruma*)—characterized by the emergence of its buds—is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyamāṇa*) as Rāhu, characterized by his vomiting of the collection of lunar digits, the dark color (*asitavarṇatva*) is employed as the ground for the poetic fancy regarding the substantive (*viśeṣya*). However, the ground for the poetic fancy regarding the attributes (*viśeṣaṇa*)—namely, the similarity between the buds and the lunar digits—is not explicitly stated. Or, for example:
"O King Pāṇḍya, O handsome one, in your courtyard the elephants appear with their chains..."
"Like mountains that have committed an offense against their enemy kings, they remain [there] because of the granting of shelter.

Here, the state of being fettered is employed as the cause for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the quality of "having committed an offense," which serves as the attribute; however, loftiness and other qualities, which would be the causes for the poetic fancy regarding the subject's form as "mountains," are not employed. Or, for example:
"Being worshipped at its feet by the dust raised from incessantly striking the surface of the earth..."
"By the minds of the people who had come for the purpose of studying [the Vedas], as if marked by the power of *aṇiman* (minuteness) due to the excellence of their speed.

Here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) where the minds are the subjects of the fancy (*viśeṣya*), the cause "marked by *aṇiman*" is employed. In the poetic fancy regarding the qualifying attribute "who had come for the purpose of studying," the cause consisting of "worship of the feet" is also employed. However, in the qualifying attribute of the study, "due to the excellence of speed," the cause—the fact that the speed of the minds is inferior to that of the horses being described—is not employed. Thus, here too, examples should be cited for the combination of the employment and non-employment of causes.

Therefore, this division [of the *viṣayī*] into eight types based on caste (*jāti*) and so forth, as well as the division of *dharma* into the forms of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*kriyā*), is deficient and includes even the consumption of grass. Consequently, in this context, setting aside that eightfold division of the *viṣayī* according to its caste and the like, and the division of *dharma* according to its form as quality or action, only as many varieties as are obtainable through other modes of division are truly striking.

However, in the cases of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) regarding essence (*svarūpa*), cause (*hetu*), and result (*phala*), further subdivisions are possible through different methods. For example, *svarūpotprekṣā* is twofold: *aviśiṣṭotprekṣā* (unqualified fancy) and *viśiṣṭotprekṣā* (qualified fancy).

When the qualification of the *viṣayin* (the subject of superimposition), though mentioned, is not understood as something to be superimposed—because of the absence of a qualification of the *viṣaya* (the object) in the form of its own nature or its cause, but rather because that qualification serves the *viṣayin* in another way—that is *aviśiṣṭotprekṣā* (unqualified fancy). But where even the qualification of the *viṣayin* is understood as something to be superimposed, due to the employment of a qualification of the *viṣaya* in the form of its own nature or its cause, that is *viśiṣṭotprekṣā* (qualified fancy).
Of these, the first is as follows: [Example omitted per instructions]

"In the verse: *'ratergṛhītānayena... babhūvendumatīnirāśam* (The minds of the kings, as they gazed upon Indumatī standing there in distress, became hopeless of her, as if their own bodies had been returned to them by the Lord after having been seized by Rati), the ground for the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that she is the form of Madana is her resemblance to the form of Madana. Therefore, that [resemblance] is understood as the object of the fancy. However, the qualifying element—that her body was returned by the Supreme Lord who was pleased by Rati’s entreaties—is not understood as the object of the fancy, because in that respect, there is an absence of both a subject (*viṣaya*)—whether expressed or implied—and a ground (*nimitta*) for the fancy."

However, since no one other than Śukra is able to restore the body of Madana burnt by the Supreme Lord or the body of Kaca burnt by the Asura, this qualification is employed to justify the restoration in the subject; thus, this is an *aviśiṣṭotprekṣā* (unqualified poetic fancy).

An example of a distinguished *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is: "O King Sundarapāṇḍya, the sage-tree in your courtyard has blossomed buds and possesses a white luster. In the first example, because the subject (*viṣaya*) is explicitly mentioned, the status of the attribute of the object of fancy (*viṣayiviśeṣaṇa*) as the object of fancy is understood; in the second, it is understood through the mention of the cause (*nimitta*). Furthermore, in the cases of fancy regarding cause (*hetu*) or effect (*phala*), the status of being the object of fancy is understood either through the relation of cause and effect between two things that are unestablished, two that are established, or both; in the second case, it is understood through the mention of the cause.

Regarding the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) of cause and effect, there are two varieties each, depending on whether the cause and effect are both unestablished (*asiddha*) or both established (*siddha*). In examples such as "This is that very spot where, while searching for you... and "Of the King of Cola, who had fled in fear...", the anklet and the thorny tree are unestablished [in their literal sense], yet they are conceived as being related by way of cause and effect to the suffering of separation and the sight of the script on the forehead, respectively. [An example of the established-unestablished variety is: "These two soles, red from tossing about upon the ground—how could we describe the feet of that slender lady, so tender as young shoots? In this case, the redness of the soles is established, while the act of "tossing about" is unestablished; thus, the two are conceived as being related by way of cause and effect.
"In order to increase the fullness of the ocean, I suspect this moon draws forth how many waters from the moonstone;

and due to separation from his beloved, how many [waters] does he draw from the eyes of the sorrowful female ruddy goose (*kokī*)?"—in such instances as these, the feet, the moon, and so forth are themselves the subjects of the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*), insofar as they are imagined through the relation of cause and effect with the spreading [of light] and the increasing of the ocean, respectively. We shall also demonstrate some of its other varieties in the section on *samāsokti* (condensed expression).

As for the distinction of this [figure] shown by Sarvasva: "In some cases it is based on a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) regarding the attribute (*dharma*); in some cases it is accompanied by concealment through words such as *chala* and the like; and in some cases, although an *upamā* (simile) is initiated at the time of the syntactic connection of the word-meanings due to the expression of similarity, it culminates in *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) through the power of the intended meaning of the sentence and by way of the propriety of the agent's mental operation"—in that regard, why was the quality of being based on *śleṣa* regarding the attribute introduced? Is it that the state of being the cause (*nimittatā*) [of the common property] is established through the connection (*śleṣa*) by way of its being "pervasive" (*anugāmitā*)? Or rather, is it that just as purity is seen in the aspect of the property (*dharma*), so too is its being "ornamented" (*alaṅkṛtatā*) seen through the connection? In the first case, whatever distinctions there may be regarding the pervasive nature and so forth of the common property in a simile (*upamā*)—all those factors which effect its commonality—are also possible as factors effecting the causality of the property in a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). In the verse: "Was he abandoned by those of opposing qualities out of fear of him, as if they were rival kings, because he was a conqueror of enemies and a conqueror of friends through his prowess, and possessed both discerning vision and a crooked gaze?"—here there is the figure of speech *virodhābhāsa* (apparent contradiction). For here, in the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the abandonment of their own substrates due to their possession of contradictory attributes, the cause is the coexistence of those qualities that appear to be contradictory within Nala.
"Certainly this slender-waisted girl has learned impatience from the speed of the sunbeams hurrying as messengers for her beloved;

In this instance, there is an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth). Although here the speed of the swan acting as Nala’s messenger is poetically imagined (*utprekṣā*) as the cause of Damayantī’s fickleness, even so, in that poetic fancy, the mere fruit of study is not the motive; rather, it is embellished by the *arthāntaranyāsa*—"for he who arises immediately after something is said to have been produced from that"—which serves to dispel the doubt: "How can there be fickleness in one place due to the speed of another? Similarly:
"Perhaps, like Gaurī, I too may some day become fortunate enough to perform the union of half-bodies with my husband."
"Thus, as it were, the Creator fashioned for her a dark thread of a line of hair in the middle.

In this instance, one should infer that there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*) regarding the causal aspect (*nimittāṃśa*), and so forth. Therefore, although in both cases [of *samāsokti* and *apahnuti*] there is merely the mention of "punning" (*śliṣṭatva*), the mention of others should also be understood by way of implication (*upalakṣaṇa*). "When the city's playful women hurriedly reached the bank due to the collision with a whale, the Siprā river there shines as if laughing aloud with pearls, under the guise of her mass of shimmering foam"—this was cited as an example of *svarūpotprekṣā* (imagination of the essential nature). However, that too should be understood as an illustration for cases where both *hetūtprekṣā* (imagination of cause) and *phalotprekṣā* (imagination of effect) involve concealment (*sāpahnavatva*). Among these, an example of *sāpahnavahetūtprekṣā* (imagination of cause with concealment) is as follows:

"In the verse: 'When the Mind-born [Cupid] was rendered "infatuated" (mugdha) by his delusion, as he gave his bow to fashion your eyebrows from the body of that fortunate one—since he was then conquerable by the knitting of your brows, it was at that time that he possessed this form,'"—here, while the word *mugdha* applies to Madana, the actual cause of his state, beauty (*saundarya*), is concealed as the cause; instead, the causality of his delusion (*mauḍhya*), which is presented as the reason for his giving his own bow to fashion Nala’s eyebrows, is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*).

An example of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the fruit of concealment (*sāpahnavaphalotprekṣā*) is as follows: "When the Mind-born [God of Love] was defeated by the knitting of your eyebrows, he was at that time in this form: out of delusion, he took up his bow to fashion the earth for you from the beautiful body of Nanda."

Here, although the state of being called "deluded" (*mugdha*) belongs to Madana, the actual cause—beauty—is concealed, and instead the causality of "delusion" resulting from the surrendering of his own bow for the purpose of fashioning Nala’s eyebrows is poetically imagined (*utprekṣita*).
An example of *sāpahnavaphalotprekṣā* (poetic imagination with concealment as the result) is as follows:
"Surely an elephant, scorched by the sun, [seeks] lotuses to ward off those [scorching] rays."
"The elephant does not enter the lake to bathe; for an elephant's bath is indeed fruitless.

Here, with respect to the elephant’s entry into the lake, the actual result—bathing—is denied its status as a result, and the warding off of lotuses is imagined as the result. Nor is it the case that in a *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy regarding the essential nature), the specific charm consists solely in the denial of an actual existing nature, nor that in *hetūtprekṣā* and *phalotprekṣā* there is merely the denial of a well-known cause or result.

On the contrary, in the two instances of *hetūtprekṣā* and *phalotprekṣā* cited above, even the denial of the well-known cause and effect is supported by a reason (*sahetuka*), and not without a reason (*nirhetuka*) like the denial of the essential nature of the subject matter cited; for it is precisely here that there exists an excellence of aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*). Therefore, it is more appropriate to regard these two as well as *sāpahnavotprekṣā* (metaphor with denial) as being merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*). Other matters to be considered here will be discussed in the section on *samāsokti* (condensed expression).

As for the statement that in examples such as "the musk-tilaka upon the surface of the forehead," the simile (*upamā*) that was initially introduced concludes, by propriety (*aucitya*), in a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): if propriety resides merely in the identification (*tādātmya*) of the musk-tilaka with its connection to a locus such as the forehead, then the figure would conclude in a metaphor (*rūpaka*). Therefore, one must admit that the propriety lies in the *possibility* of that identification, and thus its conclusion in poetic fancy must be asserted. Accordingly:
"May the fish at the feet of Murāri protect you with their lotus-like hands joined in reverence; may the lake of his navel [protect you], and the one named Kaustubha in his heart."

In such instances where there is a perception of metaphor (*rūpaka*), as in the verse beginning, "The necklaces made of emeralds are bees upon the lotus-face; the peacock-feather crests are the side-glances of the women of Ghoṣa upon the mass of hair," one must likewise admit the presence of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). And so it is said:

"Deprived of that beautiful lotus by a winged bird as the Goddess of Fortune was departing from the pond, the flock of ruddy geese on the bank cried out, resembling the tinkling anklets of her moving lotus-feet.
"The universe, the abode of the worlds, shines like a pavilion; the cosmic egg appears as its supporting pillar."

"In the passage beginning with: 'Then a certain man with matted hair, wearing a deerskin and a bark garment, bold of speech and as if blazing with the splendor of Brahman, entered the penance grove like the first stage of life embodied,' there is the perception of a simile; yet, in such cases, the ultimate resolution lies in poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). Thus it is said.
"The Varaṇa mountain, whose wings are its massive jeweled door-panels, embraced and dwelt with that proud lady, the celestial realm, who had come from the lap of the mountain of the immortals.
"That water, variegated with sesame seeds and purified by faith, which was offered as *svadhā* to the ancestors by their sons— "

In instances where there is a perception of metaphor (*rūpaka*), such as: "The nectar itself, inlaid with the luster of its sprouts, attended upon the moon as the abode of the ancestors," one must likewise admit that [the identification] culminates in that [metaphor]. This is because the logic is the same: it consists in the employment of qualifiers conducive to the imaginative identification (*tadātmya-sambhāvanā*) [of one thing with another]. Similarly:
"Of the full moon, whose body possesses a nourishing splendor, [shining] with the brilliance of wide-spreading rays..."

"This pale parasol of Desire, raised high by the beauty of the evening twilight, does not rise in the expanse of the sky over this world that seeks to conquer it— [the world] whose sole passion is now the exertion to shatter the pride of those people swollen with self-importance."
This should also be understood as an example of concealment (*apahnuti*). Further details will be considered in the section on the figure of speech *nidarśanā*.

Now, an objection may be raised: it is improper to include suggested (*gamyā*) poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) among the figures of speech, because it constitutes the suggestion of a figure (*alaṅkāradhvani*). To this it is replied: when the object of comparison (*viṣaya*), the object of superimposition (*viṣayin*), and the cause (*nimitta*) are all expressed, that case where poetic fancy is understood merely through the non-employment of words such as "as if" (*iva*) and so forth, attains the status of a figure of speech precisely because it is extremely clear and thus functions as something directly expressible (*vācyāyamāna*). This is as illustrated in the examples provided.

Where there is no mention of the subject (*viṣayin*) that is to be compared, and where the suggested metaphor (*utprekṣā*) is understood through the expressed fact (*vastu*) or the expressed ornament (*alaṅkāra*), it is a "hidden" (*gūḍha*) metaphor; in that very case, where the subject to be compared is not mentioned and the suggested metaphor is conveyed by the expressed fact or ornament, there exists the "suggested metaphor" (*utprekṣādhvani*). For example:
"Seeing the warriors of Vīrarudra victorious in battle, the thorny trees in the forest drag away the hair of their enemies' wives."

Here, by means of the *vastu*— the seizing of the hair— the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is suggested that [the eyes] were as if their passion ignited by the sight of the warrior embraced by the Goddess of Victory.
"Their eyes took refuge in Nala’s lofty breasts, which had surged high in the ocean of his passion, having overflowed the shore with the nectar-essence of gazing upon her moon-like face."

Here, through the metaphor (*rūpaka*) consisting of a partial manifestation (*ekadeśavivartin*), a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*)—as if out of fear of submerging—is understood. In this same manner, examples may be cited elsewhere as well.
Thus ends the section on Poetic Fancy (Utprekṣā).

Having stated the definition: "Where, due to the non-mention of the object (*viṣaya*), the subject (*viṣayin*) is presented [as that very object], that shall be *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), which has the life-force of the poet’s bold assertion (*kaviprauḍhokti*)," they describe its fourfold variety: non-difference where there is difference; difference where there is non-difference; non-connection where there is connection; and connection where there is no connection.
Examples of these are as follows:

"In the act of her creation, was the Creator perhaps the moon, the bestower of luster?"
"Is he Love himself, whose sole essence is the sentiment of passion, or is it the month of spring, the source of flowers?
For how could that ancient sage, dulled by the study of the Vedas and with his curiosity turned away from worldly objects, have been able to create this heart-stealing form?"
A burning heat that cooks the spreading moisture of tears; a thickening of breath perceived through the nostrils;
sighs that cause the flickering flames of lamps to sway; and a body submerged in pallor—what more shall I say? All night long, at the window facing your path, [I have remained thus].
"The state of her [the woman] exists, whose moonlight is blocked by the parasol of her hand.

Here, there is non-difference despite the difference between the lotus and so forth on one hand, and the face and so forth on the other; there is difference despite the non-difference of the form and so forth from the forms established in the world; there is non-connection despite the connection of the form with the creation of the ancient Prajāpati; and there is connection despite the non-connection of the burning of separation and so forth with the power to cook a stream of water—these are composed in their respective order.

In this regard, the following is considered and investigated: regarding the statement "because of the non-mention of the object" (*viṣayasyānupādānāt*), does "non-mention" mean that there is absolutely no means of conveying the object, or that there is no word expressive of it? In the first case, even in instances such as "the lotus is not in water," the definition would fail to apply; for words such as "lotus" convey the intended object—the face and so forth—through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

In the second [definition], there would be non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "The moon seems to kiss the face of the night," where there is an exaggeration (*atiśayokti*) based on the pun (*śleṣa*) of the word "face" (*mukha*), because the absence of any word denoting the object other than the word denoting the subject (*viṣayin*) is intended. Even so, there remains non-pervasion in cases such as "The eyes have opened like lotuses at the rising of the sun," where there is an exaggeration consisting of a determination (*adhyavasāya*) based on the difference between the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*) and the indicated meaning (*lakṣyārtha*) of the word "opened" (*unmīlita*).

In this context, because the word *unmīlita* (manifested) functions as an indicator (*lakṣaka*) of the expansion that constitutes its own referent (*viṣayin*), it denotes the object (*viṣaya*) only as something distinct from its own direct denotation (*vācya*). Even when considering the absence of any indicator of the object other than the indicator of the referent—[as in the following example]:
"O Hero, this is the distinction between your hand [the palm] and the trunk of the Kalpa tree:
one adorns the ear, while the other eclipses the ear."

In this case, there is an over-extension (avyāpti) of the definition regarding the hyperbole (atiśayokti) based on the pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *karṇa*. This is because the subject (*viṣaya*) and the object (*viṣayin*) are expressed by two distinct words, *karṇa*. If it is argued that what is intended is the absence of a separate expression for the subject that is distinct from the expression for the object, even so, consider the following verse: "Was her pair of breasts, swelling with the new offering brought forth by her youth, born from her chest? For, having crossed even the impassable river of bashfulness, that slender maiden entered the heart of Nala. [In this verse, the breasts are the object (*viṣaya*), and the "river of bashfulness" is the subject (*viṣayin*); yet they are not expressed by distinct words.]

In this case, there would be a lack of extension (*avyāpti*) in the case of the hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) of the pair of breasts with a pair of jars. This is because, in that instance, there exists a word denoting the object (*viṣaya*)—namely, "born from the chest" (*uraḥprabhavatva*)—which is distinct from the word denoting the superimposed object (*viṣayin*). If it is argued: "What is intended is the absence of a word denoting the object that is distinct from the word denoting the superimposed object, and which functions through the qualifier that delimits the objecthood (*viṣayatāvacchedaka-prakāreṇa*); however, 'being born from the chest' is not the delimiter of the objecthood of the breasts, as it is common to many things," even so—
"O lady of beautiful thighs, upon investigation, the Vaiśeṣika system is considered by me to be the most excellent;
indeed, they call that philosophy 'Aulūkya,' and it is truly capable of defining the true nature of darkness."

In such cases as "the owl's vision," there is an unavoidable lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the definition of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*)—which, according to the Vaiśeṣika school, consists of the determination of identity with the sight of a specific bird—because the phrase "in the Vaiśeṣika system" exists as a statement of the object in its specific character (*viṣayatāvacchedaka-prakāreṇa*). Furthermore, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the figure of speech called *ananvaya* (non-comparison), as in "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa," because in that case there is no distinct statement of an object different from the subject itself.

If it is argued that there is no such over-extension because the intended relation here is that between the "object" (*viṣaya*) and the "subject" (*viṣayin*), wherein that which is determined as non-different from something is the object, while that which is so determined is the subject; even so, the over-extension remains unavoidable in cases of *śliṣṭarūpaka* (punning metaphor), such as "the swan of the mind's lake. For the conceptual distinction that mere superimposition of identity constitutes *rūpaka*, whereas the determination of non-difference constitutes *atiśayokti* (hyperbole), has already been refuted in the very examination of the definition of *rūpaka*. Furthermore, there is over-extension in the examples of *samāsokti* (speech of abbreviation) based on similarity.
"To whom would this voluminous *Citra-mīmāṃsā* not bring delight?
It is like Anūru to the sun, or like the crescent moon to Śiva.
